Revision notes

Study notes — foundations

Weeks 1 and 2. Less drug-heavy, more principle-heavy — and the safety rules here are the ones that show up inside every other unit.

The Say it out loud answers can be covered so you have to retrieve them.

Kinetics vs dynamics

  • Kinetics = what the body does to the drug (ADME)
  • Dynamics = what the drug does to the body (receptors)
  • First pass — oral only. SL, IM, transdermal, IV all skip it; only IV skips absorption too
  • Half-life sets the dosing interval · steady state at 4–5 half-lives
  • Low albumin → more free drug → toxicity at a normal dose
  • Liver failure → accumulation → reduce dose. Kidneys cannot compensate

Adverse reactions

  • Type I minutes — anaphylaxis · Type IV days — rash. Timing classifies it
  • Anaphylaxis → stop the drug first, then airway and help
  • Idiosyncratic = unexpected, unexplained (agitation from a sedative)
  • Teratogenic risk peaks first trimester — organogenesis
  • Blood dyscrasia → infection + bleeding precautions

Safety rules that recur everywhere

  • Leading zero yes (0.5 mg) · trailing zero never (5.0 mg reads as 50)
  • Spell out units — "U" misreads as 0 or 4 · write mcg
  • A naked decimal = tenfold overdose risk → clarify, never guess, never rewrite
  • Two identifiers that travel with the patient — name + DOB, not room number
  • After an error: assess the patient first, then notify, document, report
  • Near miss → ISMP · adverse event → MedWatch
  • Scope: nurses do not alter a dose, rewrite an order, or discontinue a drug
  • Refusal: competent adult may refuse — assess why, inform, notify, document
  • Teach-back checks your explanation, not the patient

Challenges to therapy

  • Inhibitor → levels up (grapefruit) · inducer → levels down (St John's wort)
  • Supplements are regulated but not approved — ask by name
  • Stacked OTC products → duplicate ingredients → unintended overdose
  • Cost and literacy are barriers you can act on — ask before labelling non-adherence

Say it out loud

  • Steady state after? 4–5 half-lives
  • Albumin 1.8, normal dose →? more free drug, toxicity
  • Rash at 60 hours is type? IV, cell-mediated
  • Order reads ".5 mg" →? clarify — do not give or rewrite
  • Grapefruit does what to levels? raises them — CYP3A4 inhibition
Revision notes

Study notes — autonomic

Condensed for revision, not reference. Read it top to bottom in about ten minutes; everything here is derivable from the four receptors.

The four receptors — everything else follows

  • α1 SQUEEZE · vessels · stimulate → BP↑ · block → BP↓, orthostasis
  • β1 ONE HEART · stimulate → HR↑ force↑ · block → HR↓ BP↓
  • β2 TWO LUNGS · stimulate → bronchodilate · block → bronchospasm
  • M MOIST + MOVING · stimulate → SLUDGE · block → dry, dilated, retained, confused
  • α2 is not on your list — skip clonidine, dexmedetomidine, guanfacine

Reverse it to get adverse effects

  • Blockers cause the opposite of stimulation. You never memorise an adverse-effect list — you derive it.
  • Nonselective β blocker = β1 + β2 → the asthma problem

Prototypes

  • epinephrine α+β · anaphylaxis · verify route & concentration
  • norepinephrine α1 · shock · extravasation → phentolamine
  • phenylephrine α1 · expect reflex bradycardia
  • albuterol β2 · rescue · tremor + tachycardia expected · K⁺↓
  • metoprolol β1 · apical pulse 1 min · never stop abruptly
  • propranolol β1+β2 · question in asthma
  • prazosin α1 block · first dose at bedtime · syncope
  • tamsulosin · tell the eye surgeon — floppy iris
  • bethanechol M agonist · rule out obstruction first · empty stomach
  • pyridostigmine · 30–60 min before meals
  • atropine M block · bradycardia · success = HR rises

Traps

  • Therapeutic vs side effect. Albuterol worked if wheeze↓ and air moves — not if HR rose.
  • Cholinergic vs myasthenic crisis. Both = weakness. Discriminator is SLUDGE alongside it → too much drug.
  • Retention is anticholinergic. Urination is cholinergic. These mirror each other — the commonest mix-up.
  • New confusion in an older adult = check the med list before blaming age or infection. Beers: anticholinergics.
  • Anticholinergic burden — three mild drugs stack into one strong effect.
  • Hold parameters come from the written order, not a remembered number.

Must-not-confuse

albuterolsalmeterolrescue / maintenance
metoprololpropranololβ1 only / β1+β2
bethanecholatropineopposites — one voids, one retains
SLUDGEdry/dilatedcholinergic / anticholinergic

Say it out loud

  • Which receptor opens bronchi? β2
  • Antidote for norepinephrine extravasation? phentolamine
  • Why pyridostigmine before meals? peak strength for swallowing
  • Atropine working looks like? HR rises, perfusion improves
  • Beta blocker in diabetes hides what? tachycardia of hypoglycemia — teach sweating/hunger
Revision notes

Study notes — cardiovascular

The whole unit hangs off four levers and one electrolyte. Learn those and the drug lists stop being lists.

The four levers

  • CO = HR × SV   BP ≈ CO × SVR
  • Rate ↓ beta blockers, diltiazem, verapamil, digoxin
  • Contractility ↓ beta blockers, non-DHP CCB · ↑ digoxin, dobutamine
  • Volume / preload ↓ furosemide, HCTZ, spironolactone, nitrates
  • Vessel tone / afterload ↓ ACEI, ARB, ARNI, amlodipine, α1 blockers
  • Low BP? Ask which lever is on the floor — bradycardic → rate drugs; dry → the diuretic

Potassium — the thread

  • ↑K ACEI · ARB · ARNI · spironolactone
  • ↓K furosemide · hydrochlorothiazide
  • Low K + digoxin = toxicity at a normal level — they compete at the Na/K-ATPase
  • Peaked T = high K · flat T + U wave = low K

Derive, don't memorise

  • RAAS blocked → vasodilation + less aldosterone → BP↓, K↑, creatinine may rise
  • ACE cough/angioedema = bradykinin builds up. ARBs skip bradykinin → less cough
  • Amlodipine edema = capillary pressure, not fluid overload — no weight gain, no crackles, diuretic won't fix
  • Loops lose Ca, thiazides keep Ca — from where they act

Reversal pairs

  • heparin → protamine · warfarin → vitamin K · digoxin → immune Fab

Signature dangers

  • Angioedema on ACEI → airway emergency, drug stopped for good
  • Digoxin toxicity → anorexia/nausea first, then yellow halos, then bradycardia. Normal level does not exclude it
  • HIT → platelets fall but the risk is clotting. Stop all heparin incl. flushes. Never transfuse platelets
  • Statin + dark urine → myoglobin = kidney injury, not blood
  • Nitrate + PDE-5 → refractory hypotension. Sildenafil ~24 h, tadalafil ~36 h — an hour apart is not safe
  • Amiodarone → HEART · LUNGS · THYROID · LIVER. New cough = report
  • Beta blocker + diltiazem/verapamil → additive AV block
  • Entresto → 36-hour washout from any ACEI
  • Non-DHP CCB in reduced-EF HF → contraindicated

Must-not-confuse

amlodipinediltiazemvessels / AV node
antiplateletanticoagulantplatelet plug / cascade
anticoagulantthrombolyticprevents / dissolves
INRDOACwarfarin only / renal function
iron dark stoolmelenawell / dizzy & weak
folateB12same anemia, only B12 has neuro signs

Say it out loud

  • Why does low K cause digoxin toxicity? they compete at the same pump site
  • Ankle edema on amlodipine — what rules out overload? stable weight, clear lungs
  • Platelets 80k on heparin + leg pain? HIT — stop all heparin
  • Apixaban, INR 1.1 — concerning? no, INR is not used for DOACs
  • Creatinine 0.9→2.1 on digoxin, K normal? renal clearance fell — level is rising
Revision notes

Study notes — respiratory

One question decides most respiratory items: symptoms NOW, or preventing future symptoms?

Rescue vs maintenance

  • RESCUE — albuterol. That is the list.
  • MAINTENANCE — salmeterol, formoterol, tiotropium, ICS, montelukast
  • Ipratropium = SAMA, acute adjunct · tiotropium = LAMA, maintenance
  • LABA in asthma must sit inside an ICS-containing plan — never alone
  • Frequent rescue use = poor control, not a refill

Two ways to open an airway

  • Sympathetic → dilates. β2 agonist presses the accelerator
  • Parasympathetic → constricts. Anticholinergic releases the brake
  • → side effects differ: tremor/tachycardia vs dry mouth

Hypoxia

  • Early restless · anxious · tachycardic · pale — looks like anxiety; do not sedate
  • Late cyanosis · confusion · bradycardia · distress
  • SpO₂ 95–100%, ≥92% in illness · PaO₂ = oxygenation · PaCO₂ = ventilation
  • hypoxia = tissues · hypoxemia = arterial blood

Inhaler order

  • bronchodilator → device-specific wait → ICS → rinse & spit → spacer if prescribed
  • No single universal wait time — follow the device

Signature dangers

  • Silent chest — drowsy + diminished breath sounds = emergency. A wheeze that returns with better air movement is progress
  • Montelukast → agitation, vivid dreams, mood change, suicidal thoughts. Outranks headache/tremor reported alongside
  • Theophylline 10–20 mcg/mL. Early: N/V, restless, tachycardic. Late: arrhythmia, seizure. Quitting smoking raises the level
  • Benzonatate swallowed whole — chewed it numbs the throat, kills the gag reflex. Lethal to small children
  • Pseudoephedrine → BP↑ HR↑ — caution in HTN
  • Oxymetazoline >3 days → rebound congestion. More spray makes it worse
  • Acetylcysteine → can trigger bronchospasm
  • ICS → thrush + hoarseness. Rinse and spit. Not for an attack

Must-not-confuse

albuterolsalmeterolrescue / maintenance
ipratropiumtiotropiumSAMA / LAMA
guaifenesinacetylcysteinethins / dissolves
nasal steroiddecongestantdays to work / instant
1st gen antihist.2nd gensedating & drying / not

Recognition only

  • biologics (omalizumab, dupilumab) · cromolyn · surfactants — class, role, route. Do not sink time here.

Say it out loud

  • Wheeze gone but patient drowsy? silent chest — emergency
  • Why rinse after ICS? prevents thrush and hoarseness
  • Patient quits smoking on theophylline? clearance falls, level rises, watch toxicity
  • Nasal spray day 10, worse? rebound — stop the spray
  • Productive cough + fever, wants a suppressant? assess infection first
Revision notes

Study notes — pain & CNS

Her framework for every drug here: WHY → ASSESS → ACT → REASSESS/TEACH. Most items test the ACT step — give, question, hold, or escalate.

The one-line rules

  • Sedation rises BEFORE the respiratory rate falls — a drowsy patient is the finding, not a normal rate
  • Opioid + benzodiazepine = more than additive respiratory depression
  • Naloxone wears off before the opioid does — waking up is not the same as safe
  • Paralysis ≠ sedation or analgesia
  • Acetaminophen 4,000 mg/day max across ALL products · overdose is initially silent
  • Ketorolac ≤ 5 days total, never with another NSAID
  • Never stop abruptly: antiseizure drugs, antidepressants, baclofen, levodopa, benzodiazepines

Tell these apart

serotonin syndromeNMSclonus & hyperreflexia / lead-pipe rigidity
NMSEPSfever + rigidity / movement, no fever
MAOI crisisserotonin syndrometyramine food / serotonergic drug added
anticholinergicNMSdry, flushed, hot / rigid and febrile
fine tremorcoarse tremorexpected on lithium / toxicity
akathisiaagitationdrug effect — more drug worsens it / illness

The shortcut: fever + rigidity → NMS. Fever + twitchy reflexes → serotonin syndrome. Severe headache + very high BP → MAOI crisis. Movement problems, no fever → EPS.

Hypnotic is not anxiolytic

  • Zolpidem = hypnotic only. Insomnia; taken in bed; 7–8 hours allowed
  • Boxed warning: complex sleep behaviours. A prior episode is a contraindication — stop and call the prescriber
  • Benzodiazepines: anxiety, spasm, seizure rescue — one mechanism, several jobs
  • Older adults: non-drug sleep measures and fall precautions first

Lithium — one mechanism explains it all

  • The kidney treats lithium like sodium
  • → dehydration or low sodium = more reabsorbed = level rises on the same dose
  • → so vomiting, diarrhea, fever, sweating, hot weather, NSAIDs and thiazides all raise it
  • The trap: toxicity causes vomiting and diarrhea, which worsens the dehydration
  • Hold and escalate on coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion
  • Monitor kidney and thyroid; levels timed per order

Antiseizure red flags — one each

  • Phenytoin → nystagmus + ataxia = early toxicity · gum overgrowth · many interactions
  • Levetiracetam → mood & behaviour change; ask directly about self-harm · renal dosing
  • Lamotrigine → rash, especially with mouth sores — stop, urgent evaluation · slow titration
  • Diazepam rescue → respiratory depression; airway ready, monitor after

Movement & migraine

  • Carbidopa/levodopa: give ON TIME — late means unable to move, speak or swallow
  • Carbidopa blocks peripheral conversion → vitamin B6 is compatible with the combination
  • High-protein meals can blunt the response — individualise timing
  • Benztropine = anticholinergic for drug-induced parkinsonism and dystonia. Overheating, retention, confusion in older adults
  • Baclofen withdrawal → seizures, delirium. A missed home dose is a real emergency
  • Sumatriptan = acute only. Avoid in CAD, prior stroke/TIA, uncontrolled HTN; chest symptoms get evaluated, not excused

Recognition level only

  • Propofol — apnoea, hypotension; trained personnel and airway readiness
  • Succinylcholine — hyperkalemia · malignant hyperthermia → dantrolene
  • Know the names and the dangers. You are not expected to manage them.
Revision notes

Study notes — endocrine

Two questions answer most endocrine items: which direction is this moving the hormone, and what did the body stop doing while the drug was on board?

The feedback rule — and what it costs

  • Give a hormone → body reads it as high → own production stops → gland atrophies
  • Never stop prednisone abruptly → adrenal crisis: hypotension, weakness, hypoglycemia
  • Long-term steroid + surgery or illness → needs MORE, not the usual dose
  • Low cortisol + high ACTH → the gland. Low cortisol + low ACTH → upstream
  • Decide replace or suppress first: Addison’s and hypothyroid replace; Cushing’s and Graves suppress

Gluco vs mineralo — name the job

prednisonefludrocortisoneinflammation, immunity, glucose / sodium & water
infection, diabetesheart failure, HTNthe cautions, straight from the job
hyperglycemiahypokalemiathe lab that moves on each

Pituitary — up or down on the same axis

  • somatropin ↑ GH · octreotide ↓ GH (→ gallstones, bradycardia)
  • Leuprolide is an agonist that ends in suppression — expect the flare, symptoms worsen 1–2 weeks first
  • cetrorelix = antagonist → immediate block, no flare · watch ovarian hyperstimulation
  • desmopressin = a water drug → every problem is dilution: ↓ sodium, ↑ weight, headache

Thyroid & bone — the one-liners

  • Levothyroxine: empty stomach · same brand · TSH is the monitor · adverse = too much thyroid (tachycardia, anxiety, heat)
  • Cardiac disease or older adult → start low, go slow; acute MI is a contraindication
  • Methimazole / PTU → fever or sore throat = agranulocytosis. Report now, get a CBC
  • Methimazole avoided in pregnancy · PTU avoided in liver disease
  • Iodine paradox: high dose inhibits release → thyroid storm, pre-op. Dilute, use a straw
  • Alendronate: full glass of water, upright 30 min. Cannot sit up = cannot take it
calcitriolcalcitoninraises calcium / lowers it
calcitriol toxicityhypercalcemiasame thing — weakness, constipation, thirst
calcitonin-salmonfish allergyask before the first dose

Diabetes — who can actually go low

  • Only the drugs that force insulin out: insulin, sulfonylureas (glipizide), meglitinides (repaglinide)
  • Metformin, acarbose, DPP-4, GLP-1, SGLT-2 are glucose-dependent → rarely low alone
  • repaglinide: no meal, no dose
  • acarbose: treat lows with GLUCOSE, not sucrose — the drug blocks the enzyme that splits sugar
  • metformin: hold for contrast → renal dip → accumulation → lactic acidosis
  • canagliflozin: DKA can happen at a normal glucose. UTIs, dehydration, foot care
  • liraglutide slows gastric emptying · thyroid C-cell warning · pancreatitis
  • Insulin moves K⁺ into cells → treats hyperkalemia; watch potassium on a drip
  • Clear before cloudy — regular drawn up before NPH. Glargine, detemir, degludec: never mixed
  • Only regular insulin goes IV · NPH is the cloudy one (protamine) — roll, do not shake
  • Hypoglycemia clusters at the peak; long-acting insulins have no peak
  • Pioglitazone (TZD) → fluid retention → avoid in heart failure; report swelling and weight gain

Low vs high — and the rescue

  • LOW = sympathetic alarm: tremor, sweating, tachycardia, anxiety, hunger — fast, looks like anxiety
  • HIGH = polyuria, thirst, flushed dry skin, fruity breath — slow
  • A beta blocker masks the warning signs — sweating may be all that is left
  • Glucagon: turn on the side (vomiting), then carbohydrate once awake — glycogen is now empty
Exam technique

How to work a Select All That Apply item

SATA questions are not harder content — they are five independent decisions wearing one stem. Working them in a fixed order turns them from a guess into a checklist.

StepWhat you doWhy it works
1 · Read the stem twiceName exactly what is being asked: report urgently, teach, assess first, or safe practice. Underline itMost SATA errors are stem errors. “Which require prompt reporting” and “which are expected” have opposite answers from the same five options
2 · Cover the optionsBefore reading them, say what you would expect a correct option to containStops the options leading you. If you already know the shape of the answer, a plausible-sounding wrong option has less pull
3 · One at a timeTreat each option as its own true/false question about this client. Mark it T or F before moving onThis is the whole technique. SATA is not “pick the best” — it is five independent yes/no decisions that happen to share a stem
4 · Never count firstDo not decide “it is probably three” and then hunt for threeThe number correct varies deliberately — two, three, four. Deciding the count first makes you add a wrong option or drop a right one to hit your number
5 · Re-read the stemCheck your marked options against the question one final timeCatches the option that is true in general but false for this client — the commonest trap in the format
Signal in an optionWhat it usually meansCaution
always · never · allUsually false — clinical practice rarely holds absolutelyNot a rule. “Never stop a steroid abruptly” and “never give a paralytic without sedation” are both true
“will improve on its own”Often false when the effect does not develop toleranceOpioid constipation is the classic — drowsiness eases, constipation does not
A different drug or classOften the planted distractorDaily visual acuity testing among antipsychotic monitoring; allergic rhinitis among triptan contraindications
A normal findingFalse when the stem asks what to reportMild early nausea on an SSRI is expected; sodium of 124 is not
Treat-only-if-severeUsually false in pain items“Withhold until pain is above 8” sounds cautious and is poor practice

Worked example. “Which statements about inhaled corticosteroid therapy should the nurse include?” Run them one at a time. Rinse and spit — true, it prevents thrush. Take it daily even when symptom-free — true, that is what a controller does. Use it at the first sign of wheezing — false, it has no rapid bronchodilator effect, and this is the dangerous one. Report white patches — true, that is thrush. Use a spacer if prescribed — true. Four correct, and you never had to guess a number: each decision stood alone.

Scoring, and what it means for strategy. Most nursing programmes give no partial credit — one wrong box loses the whole item. That sounds like a reason to be cautious and select fewer, but it is not: leaving out a correct option costs exactly as much as adding a wrong one. There is no safety in picking two. Mark every option you have judged true, and stop there. If you genuinely cannot decide on one option, decide it on the clinical fact alone — not on how many you have already selected.

When you get one wrong, diagnose which failure it was. Did you misread the stem, miss a fact, or talk yourself out of a correct option to reach a tidier number? Those need three different fixes, and only the middle one is a content problem. Track which it is for a week and the pattern usually turns out to be the same one every time.

Ch 01 · pp. 4–7 · Slides 6, 9

Where drugs come from — and what they’re called

CategoryDefinitionExamples from lecture
Natural — plantDerived from plant material.digoxin
Natural — animalDerived from animal sources.insulin
Natural — inorganicElements and mineral salts. Karch’s Table 1.3 lists their therapeutic uses.aluminum antacid, hyperphosphatemia · fluoride cavities, osteoporosis · gold rheumatoid arthritis · iron iron-deficiency anemia
SyntheticMade or modified in the lab; includes prototype drugs — the model drug of a class that the rest are compared against.Learn the prototype, infer the class.
Orphan drugDeveloped for a rare disease; small market, so development is incentivized by law.Rare = orphan.
OTCAvailable without prescription — common use, but not risk-free. Patients often omit them from med lists.Always ask what they take that isn’t prescribed.
Behind-the-counter (BTC)A third category students miss. Available without a prescription, but carrying more legal restriction than ordinary OTC drugs — kept behind the pharmacy counter.Not OTC, not prescription. Karch names it as its own key term.
What makes a chemical a drugIt must show demonstrated therapeutic value or efficacy without severe toxicity or damaging properties. Efficacy alone is not enough.dronabinol (Marinol) — a synthetic version of delta-9-THC from cannabis, used for chemotherapy nausea and AIDS-related weight loss. Cannabis itself is Schedule I federally.
Generic vs. brandSame active ingredient; may differ in fillers, appearance, and price.Generic name is lowercase; Brand is capitalized.
Ch 01 · pp. 8–11 · Slide 7

Drug development and approval

A genuine sequence — each stage answers a different question, and nothing skips ahead.

StagePhaseQuestion it answersSubjects
01PreclinicalTwo purposes: (a) does it have the presumed effect in living tissue, and (b) does it cause adverse effects? Tested in vitro (outside a living organism) and in vivo (inside or on one).No humans. Biologic differences mean computer models alone are inadequate.
02Phase IIs it safe? Dose range and toxicity.Small group of healthy volunteers
03Phase IIDoes it work? Effectiveness in the target condition.Patients who have the disease
04Phase IIIIs it better? Compared against existing treatment or placebo.Large, diverse patient population
05FDA approvalMarketing is authorized for specific indications.—
06Phase IVPost-marketing surveillance. Rare and long-term effects that trials were too small or too short to catch.The whole treated public

Phase IV is why drugs get withdrawn after approval. A trial of 3,000 people cannot detect a reaction that occurs in 1 of 50,000 — nurse reporting is how those signals surface.

Ch 01 · pp. 12–14 · Slide 8

Legal regulation of medications

The deck names the Controlled Substances Act schedules and pregnancy categories without detail; both are commonly tested, so they’re expanded here.

ScheduleAbuse potentialExamplesPrescribing
C-IHighest No accepted medical useHeroin, LSD, MDMACannot be prescribed
C-IIHigh Severe dependence risk; accepted medical useMorphine, fentanyl, oxycodone, hydromorphone, methylphenidateNo refills. New script each time
C-IIIModerate Moderate–low physical, high psychologicalBuprenorphine, ketamine, testosterone, codeine combinationsUp to 5 refills / 6 months
C-IVLow Low relative to C-IIIBenzodiazepines (lorazepam, diazepam), zolpidem, tramadolUp to 5 refills / 6 months
C-VLowest Limited quantities of narcoticsAntidiarrheals and cough preparations with low-dose codeine, pregabalinSome available OTC by state
Pregnancy categoryMeaning
AAdequate, well-controlled human studies show no fetal risk in the first trimester.
BAnimal studies show no risk, but human studies are inadequate — or animal risk was not confirmed in humans.
CAnimal studies show an adverse effect; no adequate human studies. Benefit may warrant the risk.
DPositive evidence of human fetal risk, but benefit may still outweigh it in serious disease.
XContraindicated in pregnancy. Risk clearly outweighs any benefit.
YearThe disasterThe law it produced
1930s“Elixir of sulfanilamide” was distributed in a vehicle of ethylene glycol that had never been tested in humans. Ethylene glycol is toxic; hundreds died and many more became very ill.Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938 — gave the FDA power to enforce standards for testing drug toxicity and monitoring labeling.
1960sThalidomide (Thalomid) was used as a sleeping aid during pregnancy, resulting in the birth of many babies with limb deformities.Kefauver–Harris Act of 1962 — gave the FDA regulatory control over testing and evaluating drugs, and set standards for efficacy and safety.

Which law wins: the FDA regulates development and sale, but local laws further regulate distribution and administration. In most cases the strictest law prevails — and rules vary from state to state and even within a state, so know the ones where you practice.

The pregnancy categories are being phased out. The FDA required a pregnancy category on every new drug starting in 1979. In 2014 it added guidelines covering the drug’s presence in human milk, and in 2015 it moved from letter categories to risk levels. Newly approved and revised labels carry no letter — instead they state risk for fertility, pregnancy, and lactation. High risk in pregnancy means research showed fetal toxicity; high risk in lactation means the drug is known to enter human milk and could harm the infant; low risk means no problems shown so far. Learn the letters as your lecture presents them, but expect risk levels on a current insert.

Ch 02 · Slides 3, 10–11

Core concepts

The four definitions the rest of the course is built on. Pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics are the pair most often confused — keep the direction of the arrow straight.

TermWhat it meansMemory hook
PharmacologyThe study of the biological effects of chemicals (drugs) on living systems.The whole field.
PharmacotherapeuticsPharmacology narrowed to therapy — using drugs to prevent, diagnose, treat, or relieve suffering.Pharmacology with a patient in front of it.
PharmacodynamicsWhat the drug does to the body — receptor binding, enzyme inhibition, selective toxicity.Dynamics = Drug’s action on you.
PharmacokineticsWhat the body does to the drug — absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion.Kinetics = movement; the body moves the drug.

Every drug has both therapeutic and adverse effects. There is no drug with only the effect you want — that idea underpins the entire second half of this deck.

Ch 02 · pp. 21–22 · Slide 10

Pharmacodynamics — how drugs act on the body

Karch frames this as four ways drugs work, then explains the receptor machinery underneath. The four-way list is the one most likely to appear as a question.

Drugs usually work in one of four waysMeaning
01Replace or substitute for missing chemicals. Insulin and thyroid hormone are the pattern.
02Increase or stimulate cellular activity.
03Depress or slow cellular activity.
04Interfere with the functioning of foreign cells — invading microorganisms or neoplasms — causing cell death. Drugs acting this way are chemotherapeutic agents.
Receptor site typeHow binding produces an effect
Gated ion channelBinding changes the opening of an ion channel, altering the flow of components into and out of the cell.
Transmembranous receptorSpans the entire cell membrane. The chemical interacts with the receptor outside the cell and affects the portion inside it.
G protein–coupled receptorStimulation makes the receptor contact the G protein, which activates an enzyme or opens a channel as a second messenger.
Intracellular receptorDrugs able to enter the cell react with receptors inside it.
MechanismWhat the drug doesThink of it as
AgonistBinds the receptor and activates it, producing the same effect as the body’s own chemical.A key that turns the lock.
AntagonistBinds the receptor and blocks it, preventing the natural chemical from acting.A key that fits but won’t turn — and jams the lock.
Partial agonistBinds and activates, but produces a weaker response than a full agonist.A key that turns halfway.
Enzyme inhibitionBlocks an enzyme rather than a receptor, interrupting a chemical pathway.Removing a step from the assembly line.
Selective toxicityAttacks the invading organism or abnormal cell while sparing healthy host cells.The goal of every antibiotic and chemo agent — and never perfect, which is why they have side effects.
Ch 02 · Slides 11–13

Pharmacokinetics — ADME

What the body does to the drug, in order. Each stage has a factor that can go wrong and a patient population where it does.

StageDefinitionWhat affects itClinical consequence
AAbsorption
drug → bloodstream		Route (IV, IM, SC, oral, sublingual, inhalation, topical), blood flow to the site, food in the stomach, drug formulation.IV = 100% bioavailable, no absorption phase. Oral is slowest and most variable.
DDistribution
blood → tissues		Perfusion of the tissue, protein binding, and barriers — the blood–brain barrier and the placenta.Only unbound (free) drug is active. Low albumin → more free drug → toxicity at a normal dose.
MMetabolism
biotransformation		Primarily the liver, via the CYP450 enzyme system. Oral drugs undergo the first-pass effect.Liver impairment → drug accumulates. First-pass is why some oral doses are much larger than IV.
EExcretion
drug → out		Mainly the kidneys; also bile, lungs, sweat, and breast milk.Renal impairment → accumulation and toxicity. Breast milk matters for the nursing mother.

First-pass effect: an orally absorbed drug travels through the portal vein to the liver and is partly metabolized before it ever reaches systemic circulation. Any route that bypasses the portal system — IV, IM, sublingual, rectal, transdermal — escapes it.

RouteAbsorption?First-pass?Dr. Kaur’s teaching point
IVNoNoEnters the bloodstream directly — there is no absorption step at all.
OralYesOften yesAbsorbed from the GI tract; many drugs pass through the liver first.
IM / SubQYesNoAbsorbed from tissue into blood; usually bypasses first-pass.
Sublingual / buccalYesNoAbsorbed through oral mucosa; bypasses first-pass.
RectalYesPartial / variableSome venous drainage bypasses the liver, some does not.
Transdermal / inhaledYesNoAbsorbed through skin or lungs; bypasses first-pass.

She corrected this in Week 2 because it gets confused: absorption and first-pass are related but not the same thing. “No first-pass” does not mean “no absorption.” IV is the one route with neither. Topical medications are usually intended for a local effect, though some systemic absorption can occur.

Ch 02 · Slides 11–13

Time course and dosing terms

TermDefinitionWhy the nurse cares
OnsetTime from administration until the drug begins to produce an effect.Tells you when to start looking for a response.
PeakTime at which the drug reaches its highest concentration.When the effect — and the risk of adverse effects — is greatest. Peak levels are drawn here.
DurationHow long the effect lasts.Determines when the next dose is due.
Half-life (t½)Time for the serum concentration to fall by half.Guides dosing frequency. Long half-life → less frequent dosing, greater accumulation risk.
BioavailabilityThe fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged.IV is 100% by definition; oral is always less.
TroughThe lowest concentration, drawn just before the next dose.Paired with peak for drugs needing serum monitoring.
Critical concentrationThe amount of drug that must be present at the site of action to produce the desired therapeutic effect.Below it, nothing therapeutic happens; well above it, toxicity. A named learning objective in Karch’s Chapter 2.
Dynamic equilibriumThe actual concentration the drug reaches in the body — the net result of absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion happening at once.Explains why the dose given is not the concentration achieved. Also a named objective.
Active transportMovement of a substance across a cell membrane that requires energy.Contrast with passive diffusion, which does not.
Ch 02 · Slide 14

Factors influencing drug response

Why the same dose of the same drug produces different results in two patients.

FactorHow it changes the response
WeightStandard doses assume an average adult. Higher body mass may need more; lower needs less. Many drugs are dosed per kg.
AgeThe two extremes are the risk. Infants have immature liver and kidneys; older adults have declining function and altered body composition.
GenderDifferences in body-fat percentage and muscle vascularity affect distribution and absorption — the IM scenario in the deck.
Physiological factorsTime of day, hydration, electrolytes, and normal variation.
Pathological factorsLiver and kidney disease are the two that change everything — they impair metabolism and excretion.
GeneticsInherited enzyme variation makes patients fast or slow metabolizers of the same drug.
ImmunologicPrior sensitization sets up allergic response on re-exposure.
PsychologicalExpectation and belief affect outcome — the placebo effect is real and measurable.
EnvironmentTemperature, noise, and surroundings alter response, especially for sedatives and analgesics.
ToleranceRepeated exposure → decreased response → larger doses needed for the same effect.
AccumulationDrug is taken in faster than it is eliminated → concentration builds → toxicity.
Ch 03 · Slides 18–19

Adverse effects and types of reaction

An adverse effect is any undesired drug effect. Reactions are either predictable (extensions of known pharmacology) or unpredictable.

TypeWhat happensPredictable?Example
Primary actionThe intended effect, but too strong — an overdose of the therapeutic action itself.PredictableAn antihypertensive causing hypotension.
Secondary actionAn effect the drug produces in addition to the intended one — ordinary side effects.PredictableAn antihistamine causing drowsiness.
Drug allergyImmune-mediated hypersensitivity. Requires prior sensitizing exposure — not dose-related.UnpredictableRash or anaphylaxis on a second course of penicillin.
IdiosyncraticA strange, unexpected reaction not explained by the drug’s known pharmacology; often genetic.UnpredictableExcitation from a drug that normally sedates.

Why adverse effects happen at all: drugs act on multiple body systems at once, patients differ in sensitivity, dosing may be wrong for the individual, and individual variation is unavoidable.

Ch 03 · Slide 20

Allergic reactions

Severity here is genuinely ordinal — the stripe and pill encode where a presentation sits on that scale.

SeverityPresentationNursing action
MildRash, hives (urticaria), itching.Stop the drug, notify the provider, document, monitor for progression.
ModerateAngioedema (swelling of face, lips, tongue), wheezing.Stop the drug immediately, assess the airway, notify provider urgently, prepare for escalation.
SevereAnaphylaxis — airway closure, bronchospasm, circulatory collapse. Life-threatening.Stop the drug, call for emergency help, maintain airway, epinephrine, oxygen, IV fluids. Document and flag the allergy on the chart.
Hypersensitivity typeMechanismTiming & example
Type IIgE-mediated, immediate.Minutes — anaphylaxis, urticaria.
Type IICytotoxic; IgG/IgM against cell surfaces.Hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia.
Type IIIImmune complex deposition.Hours to days — serum sickness, vasculitis.
Type IVDelayed, T-cell mediated.48–72 hours — contact dermatitis, some severe skin reactions.

The universal first step for any suspected drug allergy is the same: stop the drug, treat the reaction, document it. Severity changes what “treat” means, never the order.

Ch 03 · pp. 38–48 · Slide 21

Organ and tissue toxicity

Grouped by system, with what you assess and the lab that tracks it — this is the table most worth knowing cold. Chapter 3’s objectives are the clinical significance of adverse reactions, the four types of allergic response, drug-induced tissue damage, and applying clinical judgment to them.

SystemToxic effectsWhat to monitor
DermatologicKarch’s range: from a simple rash to potentially fatal exfoliative dermatitis. Also stomatitis (mouth inflammation) and Stevens–Johnson syndrome.Skin and oral mucosa assessment. SJS is a medical emergency — blistering with mucous membrane involvement.
GastrointestinalNausea, vomiting, diarrhea, ulceration and GI bleeding.Intake and output, abdominal assessment, stool for occult blood.
LiverHepatotoxicity — the liver metabolizes most drugs, so it takes the exposure.AST, ALT, bilirubin. Watch for jaundice, dark urine, right upper quadrant pain.
KidneysNephrotoxicity — the kidneys concentrate drugs during excretion.BUN, creatinine, GFR. Urine output, edema, daily weights.
Blood / bone marrowBlood dyscrasia — Karch’s term for bone marrow suppression caused by drug effects on the rapidly multiplying cells of the marrow. Produces lower-than-normal levels of blood cells.CBC with differential. Infection signs, fatigue and pallor, bruising and bleeding.
SuperinfectionNormal flora destroyed → overgrowth of resistant organisms.Watch for oral thrush, vaginal yeast infection, and new-onset diarrhea (C. difficile) during antibiotic therapy.
NeurologicEPS (extrapyramidal symptoms), NMS (neuroleptic malignant syndrome), anticholinergic effects.Abnormal movements, rigidity. NMS = high fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability — life-threatening.
SensoryOtotoxicity (hearing and balance), ocular toxicity (vision).Ask about ringing in the ears, hearing loss, dizziness, and vision changes — patients rarely volunteer these.

Anticholinergic effects — the classic mnemonic: dry as a bone (dry mouth), red as a beet (flushing), blind as a bat (blurred vision), mad as a hatter (confusion), hot as a hare (hyperthermia). Add urinary retention and constipation.

Ch 03 · Slide 22

Teratogenicity

AspectDetail
DefinitionA drug effect that causes birth defects in the developing fetus.
ExamplesIsotretinoin, some anticonvulsants, chemotherapy agents.
Timing of riskFirst trimester is the highest-risk period — organogenesis. Risk is greatest before many patients know they are pregnant.
Nursing responsibilityCheck pregnancy status before administering, educate on effective contraception, and confirm the patient understands why it matters.
Ch 03 · Slides 23, 25

Managing toxicity and adverse reactions

The response scales with severity — but assessment and documentation never drop out.

SituationAction
AlwaysContinuous assessment. You cannot catch what you are not monitoring for.
Mild effectsSupportive care — comfort measures, timing adjustments, symptom relief. The drug usually continues.
ModerateHold the drug and notify the provider.
SevereStop the drug. Give the antidote if one exists, provide urgent supportive therapy, escalate immediately.
Poisoning / overdoseToo much drug causes damage across multiple body systems. Requires urgent supportive care and antidote therapy where available.
AfterwardNotify the provider, document thoroughly, and educate the patient so it is not repeated.
Ch 04 · Slides 4, 26

The nurse’s role in drug therapy

Five verbs, in the order they happen around a single dose.

StepVerbWhat it looks like in practice
01AssessBefore giving: confirm identity, check vitals and relevant labs, review allergies and current meds.
02AdministerGive safely using the Five Rights, then document immediately.
03Assess againMonitor after giving — is the therapeutic effect happening, and are adverse effects appearing?
04InterveneMake the regimen tolerable: timing with meals, comfort measures, managing side effects.
05EducateTeach the patient the drug, its purpose, what to watch for, and why adherence matters.
06PreventPrevent errors and keep the whole-patient view — the holistic check that catches what protocol misses.
Ch 04 · pp. 49–60

The nursing process and the CJMM

Verified against Karch. Two things here differ from what most students write down: the process has six elements, not five, and Karch says “nursing conclusion,” not “nursing diagnosis.” Table 4.1 in the book aligns the two frameworks — that alignment is reproduced below.

StepNursing processCJMM cognitive skillWhat you actually do
01AssessmentRecognize cuesSystematic, organized data collection — physical, intellectual, emotional, social, cultural, and environmental. The goal is to spot the cues that explain the complaint or signal danger.

Dr. Kaur’s six assessment domains (Wk2 slide 8): patient — two identifiers, age, weight, pregnancy or lactation where relevant · medication history — prescription, OTC, vitamins, herbals, substances, and the last dose · allergies — what actually happened; allergy or intolerance? · current status — vitals, symptoms, ability to swallow, pain, mental status · labs and organ function — renal, hepatic, electrolytes, glucose, drug levels when ordered · understanding — why they take it, their concerns, and whether they can obtain and take it safely.
02AnalysisAnalyze cuesWork out what the cues mean together in this patient’s situation.
03Nursing conclusions
generate hypotheses		Prioritize hypothesesState the actual or potential concern the assessment points to, then rank concerns by likelihood and danger.
04PlanningGenerate solutionsPrioritize the gathered information and plot the interventions that will meet the goals and desired outcomes.
05Intervention /
implementation		Take actionCarry it out — administer the drug, provide comfort measures, teach the patient.
06EvaluationEvaluate outcomesDetermine the effects of what you did, which feeds straight back into further assessment and intervention.

Why the CJMM exists: it was developed by the NCSBN — the body that writes the NCLEX — as a framework for measuring clinical judgment and decision making. That is why Next Gen NCLEX items are phrased in its language rather than the classic five-step vocabulary.

Karch key termDefinition
NursingThe art of nurturing and caring for the sick, combined with the scientific application of chemistry, anatomy, physiology, biology, nutrition, psychology, and pharmacology to the clinical situation.
Nursing processThe problem-solving method used to deliver efficient care: gather information, analyze it into a nursing conclusion, prioritize the concerns, set goals and outcomes, intervene, and evaluate.
AssessmentInformation gathering about the patient’s current status, including past history and physical examination. Provides the baseline and the clues to whether therapy is working.
HypothesisA proposed explanation built from limited data, used to generate a plan of action and direct further investigation.
Nursing conclusionA statement of an actual or potential concern, drawn from assessment of the clinical situation, that directs the nursing interventions needed.
PlanningPrioritizing what assessment found and using the nursing conclusions to plot the interventions that meet the goals and desired outcomes.
InterventionsActions taken to meet the patient’s needs — drug administration, comfort measures, and patient teaching.
EvaluationDetermining the effects of the interventions that were instituted, leading to further assessment and intervention.
Health literacyThe patient’s ability to find, understand, and use information and resources to inform health-related decisions and actions. Low health literacy drives nonadherence and home dosing errors — assess it before you teach.
Ch 04 · Wk1 s5 · Wk2 s10

The Rights of medication administration

Week 1 taught five. Week 2 expanded it to ten. Dr. Kaur presents them as a safety framework and warns that programs and facilities organise them differently — so use them with clinical judgment, not instead of it.

#RightWhat you verify
01PatientUse two identifiers.
02MedicationMatch the order and MAR against the label.
03DoseCalculate it — then check it for reasonableness.
04RouteCorrect formulation and correct route.
05TimeSchedule, interval, and when the last dose was given.
06ReasonWhy is this patient receiving this drug?
07AssessmentAre the required vitals and labs safe for this dose?
08Education / refusalExplain it; respect questions and the patient’s right to refuse.
09DocumentationDocument what was actually given.
10ResponseEvaluate the effect and any adverse effects.

Her exact caution: the rights help catch errors — they do not replace assessment, clarification, or stopping when something does not make sense. Her warm-up case makes the point: an order for metoprolol 25 mg with a hold parameter of systolic < 100, and a BP of 88/54. The dose is “right.” You still hold it.

RightWhat you verifyWhere it goes wrong
Right patientConfirm identity with at least two identifiers — typically name and date of birth.Room number is not an identifier. Patients move.
Right drugCheck the label against the order and the MAR.Look-alike / sound-alike names.
Right doseVerify the dose being prepared and given, including the calculation.Decimal-point errors; wrong concentration on hand.
Right routeOral, IV, IM, subcutaneous, sublingual, inhalation, topical — as ordered.Giving an IV-only formulation by another route.
Right timeCorrect time, frequency, interval, and relation to meals.Missing the meal relationship changes absorption.

Many programs add right documentation, right reason, right response, and right to refuse. This deck teaches five — answer five unless the question says otherwise.

Ch 04 · p. 55, Box 4.3

Medication errors and patient teaching

Karch opens this section with the report that put medication safety on the national agenda.

FactFigure
The landmark studyThe Institute of Medicine’s To Err Is Human: Building a Safer Health System, published in 2000.
Reported deaths44,000 reported hospital deaths per year from medication errors — the report judged the true number likely closer to 98,000.
Annual costEstimated at over $21 billion per year to the healthcare system.
Why the risk is risingAn aging population, more drugs available, heavy OTC and alternative-therapy use, and shorter hospital stays that push complex regimens into the home.
Box 4.3 — teach every patientWhat to cover
Name, dose, and actionPatients often see several providers. Urge them to carry a written or electronic list of everything they take, for any provider and for emergencies.
Timing of administrationFrequency, spacing from other drugs, and relation to meals.
Storage and preparationRefrigeration, mixing with a specific liquid, and any special handling — confirm they can actually carry it out.
What to avoidSpecific prescriptions, OTC drugs, and alternative therapies that would interact. Patients frequently do not count OTC or herbal products as “drugs” and take them alongside prescriptions.
Comfort measuresHow to cope with expected adverse effects — which reduces anxiety and prevents nonadherence. Example: schedule a diuretic for a day when bathrooms are close by.
Wk2 · Slides 11–12

Error-resistant notation and safety habits

From the ISMP list of error-prone abbreviations and dose designations. These are the notation choices that turn into tenfold dose errors.

Write thisNot thisBecause
0.5 mg.5 mgAlways a leading zero. A missed decimal point reads as 5 mg — ten times the dose.
5 mg5.0 mgNever a trailing zero. Reads as 50 mg.
mLcc“cc” is easily misread; ISMP recommends mL.
unitsU  or  IU“U” can be read as a zero or a four.
mcgambiguous symbolsSpell it out rather than using a symbol that can be misread.
Habits that prevent errors
Compare the medication with the MAR or order at key points in the process.
Use barcode scanning and independent double-checks when policy requires them.
Clarify orders that are incomplete, illegible, contradictory, or unsafe.
Do not bypass alerts or use workarounds just to get it done.
Know hold parameters, monitoring needs, and maximum or safe-dose information.
Minimise interruptions during preparation and administration.

When something does not match: STOP → verify → clarify.

If a medication error occurs

Her framing: patient safety first, learning comes next. The order matters — the patient is step one, the paperwork is not.

StepAction
01Assess and protect the patient.
02Notify the appropriate clinician and obtain any needed treatment.
03Follow the organisation’s medication-error policy.
04Document the clinical facts and the patient’s response.
05Complete the required safety or incident report.
06Use external reporting when indicated.
External reportingWhat it is for
FDA MedWatchSerious adverse events, product problems, therapeutic failure or inequivalence, and product-use errors.
ISMP MERPMedication errors, close calls, and hazardous conditions — reported for learning and prevention.
Wk2 · Slides 9, 13

Patient education as a safety intervention

Her reasoning: the patient is the last person who can catch an error — so give them enough information to do it.

Teach every patient
Medication name and purpose.
How and when to take it.
Important side effects, and when to seek help.
Interactions or precautions that matter.
What to do about a missed dose, when applicable.
Storage, the measuring device, and safe disposal.
TechniqueHow it works
Teach-backPut the burden on your own explaining, not on the patient’s memory: “Just so I know I explained it clearly, can you tell me how you will take this medicine when you are home?”
Respecting refusalPause, assess the reason, provide information, notify or clarify as appropriate, and document the clinical facts.
Plan the outcome before you give the drugExamples
Expected therapeutic effectPain decreases · blood pressure moves toward goal · infection symptoms improve · blood glucose responds.
Safety parametersWhat should make you pause, hold, or clarify: an abnormal vital sign · an allergy concern · an unsafe lab · duplicate therapy · a dose outside the expected range.

Ch 05 · pp. 61–62

Routes of administration

Route determines how fast the drug arrives and whether it meets the liver first. Onset times are typical ranges, not guarantees.

RouteTypical onsetFirst-pass?Key nursing point
Intravenous (IV)30–60 secNoFastest and least reversible — 100% bioavailable. Cleanse the site aseptically and assess the line for patency; do not start if there are signs of vein irritation or infiltration. Check compatibility before running drugs in the same line, and label, date, and time the line.
Intramuscular (IM)10–20 minNoInject deep into muscle at a 90-degree angle. Karch’s recommended sites: ventrogluteal, vastus lateralis, deltoid. Withdraw slowly, engage the safety device, do not recap, dispose in the sharps container.
Subcutaneous (SC)15–30 minNoSlower than IM; small volumes only. Rotate sites with repeated dosing.
Sublingual / buccal3–5 minNo — bypassesAbsorbed straight into systemic circulation. Do not swallow.
Oral (PO)30–90 minYesSafest and most convenient, slowest and most variable. Food and GI status change absorption.
Rectal5–30 minPartialUseful when the patient is vomiting or unconscious. Absorption is erratic.
Inhalationseconds–minNoLarge surface area, rapid uptake. Mostly local respiratory effect.
TransdermalhoursNoSteady sustained levels. Remove the old patch before applying the new one.
TopicalvariesNoLocal effect intended; broken skin increases systemic absorption.

Preventing medication errors: verify the order against the MAR, never give a drug someone else prepared, question any order that is illegible or seems wrong, avoid dangerous abbreviations, and use two identifiers every time. Report errors that reach the patient and near misses — near misses are how systems get fixed.

Karch Table 5.1 · Ch 05

The three measuring systems

Karch teaches three. Dr. Kaur de-emphasized apothecary and avoirdupois for Week 2 — kept here for the textbook and for your dosage course, but metric is what she is testing.

SystemSolid measureLiquid measure
Metric
the standard		 gram (g)
1 g = 1,000 mg
1 mg = 1,000 mcg
1 kg = 1,000 g		 liter (L)
1 mL = 0.001 L
1 mL = 1 cubic centimeter = 1 cc
Apothecary

60 gr = 1 dram (dr)
8 dr = 1 ounce (oz)		 minim (min)

Why metric wins: in 1995 the U.S. Pharmacopeia Convention set standards requiring every prescription to carry the metric measure for quantity and strength, and established that drugs may be dispensed only in metric form. You still need the other two for conversion — finding the equivalent value between two systems.

Pick one and stay with it

The one setup: Desired ÷ Have × Quantity

Karch names three acceptable methods. Dr. Kaur models one, and explicitly lists “memorising three different calculation methods” as de-emphasized. Use hers. The other two are shown once below so you recognise them if a question is phrased that way.

Dose to give = D ÷ H × Q
D = desired / ordered dose  ·  H = dose on hand  ·  Q = quantity containing H

Keep the units visible as you work. They should cancel, or lead you to the unit the question asked for.

Order: 375 mg PO. On hand: 250 mg per 5 mL. How many mL?
  1. Formula (desired over have). (375 ÷ 250) × 5 = 7.5 → 7.5 mL
  2. Ratio–proportion. 250 mg : 5 mL :: 375 mg : x → 250x = 1875 → 7.5 mL
  3. Dimensional analysis. 375 mg × (5 mL / 250 mg) = 7.5 mL. Units cancel, leaving mL → 7.5 mL
Karch’s own example (p. 66). An order is written for 324 mg of aspirin by mouth. The tablets available are 81 mg. How many tablets should the nurse give?
  1. Ratio and proportion, set up as Karch does: amount available / one tablet = amount prescribed / number of tablets
  2. 81 mg / 1 tablet = 324 mg / X → 81X = 324
  3. Answer: 4 tablets

Why dimensional analysis is worth learning: it carries the units through the arithmetic, so if your units do not cancel to the unit you were asked for, you know you set it up wrong before you get a number.

Week 2 · Slides 18, 21

Before you calculate

Her framing: a correct calculation with the wrong unit can still harm a patient. Most errors are caught here, before any arithmetic happens.

StepThe six-step process
01Read the order.
02Identify what is available.
03Match or convert the units.
04Calculate.
05Round correctly.
06Ask: does this make sense?
Safety setupWhat to check
Units matchConvert the order and the available dose into the same unit before calculating.
Decimal is safeUse a leading zero. Never use a trailing zero.
Quantity is clearTablet? mL? vial? package? Know exactly what Q represents.
Rounding rule knownDo not round early. Follow your course or facility direction.
Answer is reasonableWould this really need 0.02 tablets? 20 tablets? 75 mL? Pause if the answer looks strange.

Do not let the calculator make the clinical decision for you. The reasonableness check is the step students skip, and it is the one that catches a tenfold error.

Week 2 · Slides 23–27

Dr. Kaur’s worked examples

The four she modelled in class, in her setup and with her reasonableness checks.

Tablets. Order: acetaminophen 650 mg PO. Available: 325 mg per tablet.
  1. D = 650 mg, H = 325 mg, Q = 1 tablet. Units already match.
  2. 650 ÷ 325 × 1 → 2 tablets
  3. Reasonableness: 650 mg is twice 325 mg, so 2 tablets makes sense.
Oral liquid. Order: amoxicillin 600 mg PO. Available: 400 mg / 5 mL.
  1. Why Q = 5 mL: the 400 mg on hand is contained in 5 mL, so Q is the 5 mL — not 1.
  2. 600 ÷ 400 × 5 mL → 7.5 mL
  3. Safety habit: measure with an appropriately marked oral dosing device in mL. Never a household spoon.
Weight-based, two steps. Order: cefazolin 25 mg/kg/dose. Patient weighs 20 kg. Prepared concentration 100 mg/mL.
  1. Step 1 — find the ordered dose. 25 mg/kg × 20 kg = 500 mg per dose
  2. Step 2 — convert to what is available. 500 ÷ 100 × 1 mL → 5 mL
  3. Never skip the dose-range or maximum-dose check when the order or policy requires it.
Infusion pump. Infuse 1,000 mL over 8 hours. What rate will you program?
  1. mL/hr = total volume (mL) ÷ time (hr) — hours in the denominator.
  2. 1,000 ÷ 8 → 125 mL/hr
  3. The pump is a tool. Verify the programmed rate against the order before starting the infusion.
Critical-care drip — the format your course uses. Order: propofol 12 mcg/kg/min IV. Weight: 154 lbs. Dose on hand: 500 mg propofol in 50 mL NS. How many mL/hr does the nurse set the pump to? Round to the nearest whole number.
  1. Convert the weight. 154 lb ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg
  2. Put the bag in mcg. 500 mg × 1000 = 500,000 mcg
  3. Concentration. 500,000 mcg ÷ 50 mL = 10,000 mcg/mL
  4. Dose per minute. 12 × 70 = 840 mcg/min
  5. Dose per hour. 840 × 60 = 50,400 mcg/hr
  6. Rate. 50,400 ÷ 10,000 = 5.04 → 5 mL/hr
BSA dosing — chemotherapy orders. Order: cisplatin 65 mg/m². BSA: 1.97 m². How many mg does the nurse administer? Round to the nearest whole number.
  1. BSA dosing is a single multiplication — no conversion, no concentration. dose per m² × BSA
  2. 65 mg/m² × 1.97 m² = 128.05 mg
  3. Round. 128 mg
  4. Sanity check. BSA is near 2, so the answer should be close to double 65 — and 128 is.
Paediatric weight-based dose to a volume. Order: furosemide 2 mg/kg. Weight: 23 lbs. Dose on hand: 8 mg/mL suspension. How many mL? Round the lb conversion to the nearest tenth, and the answer to the nearest tenth.
  1. Convert the weight, and round it now. 23 ÷ 2.2 = 10.4545… → 10.5 kg
  2. Ordered dose. 2 mg/kg × 10.5 kg = 21 mg
  3. Convert to volume. 21 mg ÷ 8 mg/mL = 2.625 mL
  4. Round. 2.6 mL
  5. The instruction that matters. This question says to round the kilogram conversion first, which overrides the usual “do not round early” rule. Here it happens not to change the answer — unrounded gives 2.6136, still 2.6 — but on other numbers it will. Follow whichever rounding the question states.

    Drug interactions

    TypeMechanismClassic example
    Drug–drugOne drug alters another’s absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion — interactions map onto ADME.Two protein-bound drugs compete; the displaced one becomes free and toxic.
    Drug–foodFood changes absorption or inhibits metabolizing enzymes.Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4 → less metabolism → higher drug levels. Alcohol; timing with meals.
    Drug–labThe drug alters a laboratory value without a matching change in the patient’s condition.A result can look abnormal because of the drug, not the disease — know what your patient is taking before interpreting labs.
    Ch 06 · pp. 72–80

    Challenges to safe and effective drug therapy

    This chapter is not about lifespan dosing, which is what its title suggests. Karch's five objectives are media and advertising, OTC drugs, herbal and alternative therapies, emergency preparedness, and healthcare costs.

    ChallengeWhat Karch saysNursing implication
    Information overloadPatients arrive influenced by advertising, the internet, and the alternative-therapy industry. The era of the provider being seen as always right is over — patients come with requests and demands.Expect to be asked about specific drugs by name. Correcting bad information is part of the job.
    Media influenceDirect-to-consumer prescription advertising became legal in the 1990s. If an ad states what a drug treats, it must also state contraindications, adverse effects, and precautions — so many ads simply never state the indication, freeing them to use pure imagery.When a patient requests an advertised drug, find out what they think it does.
    OTC drugsMany were “grandfathered in” before modern testing standards, so they were never evaluated to the standard new drugs face. Ipecac is the cautionary case — a standard for years, until the FDA announced in 2003 it was not effective for its intended use.OTC drugs can mask the signs and symptoms of an underlying problem, delaying real diagnosis. Duplicate ingredients across cold and allergy products cause accidental overdose.
    Self-careSelf-diagnosing and determining one’s own treatment needs. The FDA weighs it when considering OTC status — lovastatin was rejected for OTC in 2009 and 2010 because high lipids have no symptoms and need a blood test.Ask specifically about products for headache, colds, and constipation. Patients do not consider OTC drugs “real” drugs and omit them from drug histories.
    Herbal & alternative therapiesThe FDA treats them as dietary supplements, not medications, so they are not tightly regulated. Also includes nondrug measures — imagery, massage, acupuncture, relaxation.Not benign: unexpected effects, toxic reactions, interactions with prescription and OTC drugs, and unknown ingredients that alter potency. The clinician’s job is to balance what the patient wants to use against the prescribed regimen.
    Emergency preparednessSince 9/11, the CDC and Office of Homeland Security address exposure to biologic and chemical weapons. Biologic weapons — “germ warfare” — are bacteria, viruses, or parasites used at scale to incapacitate or destroy a population. The 2001 anthrax mailings and the COVID-19 pandemic are the reference events.Karch directs nurses to cdc.gov and its A–Z index for evolving guidance.
    The opioid crisisOver 75% of drug overdose deaths in 2022 involved an opioid. The CDC reports 224 deaths per day from opioid overdose in 2022, and two-thirds were caused by synthetic opioids — often illicitly manufactured fentanyl.Tighter prescribing has lowered prescription-opioid deaths while illicit-opioid deaths rose. Responses: reversal agents in the hands of first responders and the public, safer delivery research, better chronic pain treatment, more rehabilitation access.
    Illicit & recreational drugsNonprescription drugs with no known therapeutic use, taken to enhance mood or increase pleasure. Alcohol and nicotine are legal drugs that cause serious problems. Marijuana is legal in some states but not sanctioned federally; heroin is illegal at both levels.They interact with prescribed drugs and alter the patient’s response. They also mask underlying medical problems. Karch points to nida.nih.gov.
    Healthcare costsCosts have skyrocketed. Patients are discharged far earlier, and many procedures that once required days of hospitalization no longer involve admission at all.Less monitoring means more responsibility falls on the patient and family — which makes teaching critical, and the nurse is usually the one who does it.
    Insurance coveragePrivate: employment-based, direct-purchased, TRICARE. Public: Medicare (federal), Medicaid (state), Veterans Affairs. Plan types include EPO, HMO, POS, and PPO.High Deductible Health Plans trade a lower premium for higher per-service cost, often paired with an HSA. Tier systems and generic-only coverage change what a patient can actually afford — and some patients have no coverage at all.

    Karch’s own Key Points for this chapter: OTC drugs are deemed safe by the FDA when used as directed and need no prescription; they can mask disease, interact with prescriptions, and be taken above the recommended dose to the point of toxicity. Herbal and alternative therapies are dietary supplements and are not tightly regulated; they can produce unexpected effects and toxic reactions, interact with prescription drugs, and contain unknown ingredients that alter effectiveness and toxicity.

    Ch 06 · Wk2 slides 32–37

    Why a correct plan still fails

    Week 2 moved Chapter 6 from broad healthcare trends to patient-level barriers you can actually assess and act on. This is the more exam-useful framing of the two.

    BarrierThe question it raises
    Access & costCan the patient obtain this medication consistently?
    AdherenceIs the regimen realistic? Any missed or altered doses?
    Health literacyDoes the patient understand the purpose and the instructions?
    PolypharmacyPrescription plus OTC plus supplement burden increases complexity.
    Information qualitySocial media, advertising, and websites can mislead.
    Care transitionsDischarge, home care, and multiple prescribers all increase error risk.

    Her strongest instruction: never assume “noncompliance” before you assess the barrier. The opening move is “Walk me through how you take your medicines at home.”

    StepCost, adherence and home care
    Ask“Walk me through how you take your medicines at home.”
    IdentifyCost · transportation · side effects · schedule · literacy · beliefs · swallowing · memory.
    SolvePharmacist or prescriber · simplified regimen · a generic option where appropriate · assistance programmes · pill organiser or reminders.
    TeachPurpose · schedule · warning signs · follow-up · teach-back.

    On generics: an FDA-approved generic must meet standards for the same active ingredient, strength, dosage form, route, and bioequivalence to the reference product. That makes a generic switch a legitimate cost solution, not a compromise.

    Ch 06 · Wk2 slides 33–34, 36–37

    OTC, supplements, online information and disposal

    Her one-line thesis: “natural” and “over the counter” do not mean risk-free.

    TopicWhat to know
    Ask about everythingOTC pain, cold, sleep and allergy products · vitamins and minerals · herbal products and teas · energy or weight-loss products · cannabis, CBD or other substances when clinically relevant.
    Why it mattersDuplicate ingredients, interactions, adverse effects, and altered lab or clinical findings.
    How supplements are regulatedThe FDA regulates dietary supplements but does not approve them for safety and effectiveness before marketing the way it approves drugs. Product quality and evidence vary.
    Your responseDocument use, check interactions, avoid judgment, and use reliable references.
    Evaluating medication information onlineAsk
    WhoWho wrote or reviewed it — and are they qualified? Who funds or sponsors the site?
    WhereWhere does the information come from? Are references provided?
    WhenWhen was it last updated?
    WhyWhy does the site exist — education, sales, advocacy, or advertising?
    CorroborationDoes it match other reliable sources?
    Good starting pointsFDA · MedlinePlus / NIH · DailyMed · your institution’s drug database.
    Do not rely onA social post, an influencer, an ad, or a “.org” label alone as proof that information is accurate. A domain ending is not evidence.
    Two things patients ask aboutThe answer
    Buying medicines onlineUse a state-licensed pharmacy. Be wary of sites selling prescription medication without a valid prescription, prices that seem too good to be true, or products of unknown origin. FDA BeSafeRx helps patients verify safer options.
    Disposing of medicinesFor most unused or expired medicines the FDA recommends a drug take-back or mail-back option. Follow product-specific instructions; flushing is reserved for certain medicines on the FDA flush list when take-back is not readily available.
    Substance useUse a safety lens, not a stigma lens
    AssessWhat substances, how often, when was the last use? Any withdrawal, intoxication, interaction, or overdose concern?
    RespondNonjudgmental language. Address immediate safety, notify the care team as needed, follow withdrawal and overdose protocols.
    Educate & connectHarm-reduction education, naloxone where indicated, treatment and referral resources, and clear medication instructions.
    Ch 29 · Wk slides 5–6

    1The autonomic nervous system — the map

    Start here. This unit runs in seven steps: what the ANS is → the four receptors → drugs that turn the sympathetic side up, then down → the parasympathetic side up, then down → a side-by-side review. The med chart and medication index sit at the end as reference, not reading.

    Two branches constantly balancing each other. Dr. Kaur’s framing: learn the patterns first, then the drugs make sense. Every drug in this unit either turns one branch up or turns it down.

    Organ / functionSympathetic — fight or flight (the accelerator)Parasympathetic — rest and digest (the brake)
    Heart rateIncreasesDecreases
    Blood pressureIncreasesFalls as vessels relax
    BronchiDilate — more airflowConstrict, secretions increase
    PupilsDilateConstrict
    GI activityDecreasesMotility and secretions increase
    BladderEmptying becomes harderContracts → urination
    SalivationDecreases — dry mouthIncreases
    MessengerBranchActs at
    Acetylcholine (ACh)Parasympathetic — rest and digestMuscarinic receptors. Broken down by acetylcholinesterase.
    Norepinephrine / epinephrineSympathetic — fight or flightAdrenergic receptors: alpha and beta.

    Don’t confuse the messenger with the receptor. ACh and norepinephrine are the messages; receptors are the receivers. An agonist mimics or activates; an antagonist blocks.

    From the textbook — detail the lecture skippedWhy it matters
    SNS = thoracolumbarIts CNS cells originate in the thoracic and lumbar spinal cord. Short preganglionic axon, ganglia beside the spinal cord, long postganglionic axon.
    PNS = craniosacralIts neurons originate in the cranium and sacral cord. Long preganglionic axon, ganglia near or within the target organ, short postganglionic axon. The vagus is the 10th cranial nerve.
    The sweat gland exceptionSympathetic postganglionic fibres to the sweat glands release ACh, not norepinephrine — so they are sympathetic but cholinergic. A favourite exam trap.
    The adrenal medullaIt never develops postganglionic axons. Its chromaffin cells secrete epinephrine and norepinephrine straight into the bloodstream — which is why epinephrine acts as a hormone as well as a neurotransmitter.
    SphinctersPNS stimulation relaxes the GI and urinary sphincters while the bladder wall contracts — the two together are what allow voiding.
    “Feed and breed”Karch’s alternative name for rest-and-digest, alongside “rest-and-digest.”
    Both preganglionic neurons use AChIn both branches the preganglionic neurotransmitter is acetylcholine. The branches differ at the postganglionic step.
    Ch 29 · Wk slides 7–8, 38

    2The four receptors — the whole unit in one table

    Her stated study question: “If this receptor is stimulated or blocked, what happens to the patient?” Learn this table and you can rebuild every drug effect below it.

    ReceptorAnchorMain locationStimulate →Block →
    α1SQUEEZEBlood vesselsVasoconstriction → BP risesVasodilation → BP falls, orthostatic dizziness
    β11 HEARTHeartRate and contractility riseHR and BP fall, cardiac workload drops
    β22 LUNGSBronchiBronchodilationBronchoconstriction risk — the asthma/COPD safety issue
    MMOIST + MOVINGParasympathetic targets throughoutHR down, secretions up, GI motility up, bladder contracts, pupils constrictDry, dilated, retained, confused
    OrganReceptor turned ONWhat you would see in the patient
    Blood vesselsα1Constriction → blood pressure rises
    Heartβ1Rate and force increase
    Lungsβ2Bronchodilation
    GI tractmuscarinicMotility and secretions increase
    BladdermuscarinicDetrusor contracts → voiding
    Eyes and glandsmuscarinicPupils constrict, saliva increases

    Alpha-2 is not on your list. Dr. Kaur teaches four receptors — α1, β1, β2 and muscarinic. The textbook also covers α2 agonists (clonidine, dexmedetomidine, guanfacine); those are flagged not required in the medication index so you can skip them.

    Then reverse it. Blockers produce the opposite of stimulation — which is how you predict a drug’s adverse effects without memorising them.

    Ch 30 · Wk slides 9–13

    3Adrenergic agonists — turning the sympathetic system up

    Also called sympathomimetics. Laid out in Dr. Kaur’s own six-box reference format from slide 29: what it is, why it’s given, what it does, how you know it worked, what to watch for, and what you assess.

    MedicationReceptorsWhy givenExpected responseAdverse effectsNursing safety
    Epinephrineα1 β1 β2Anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest, severe bronchospasm in selected emergenciesAirway opens, BP and perfusion improveTachycardia, hypertension, dysrhythmiasHR, rhythm, BP, respiratory status, perfusion. Verify route and concentration — they differ by indication.
    Norepinephrinemainly α1, some β1Severe hypotension and shockBP and perfusion improveExcessive vasoconstriction; extravasation can injure tissueContinuous BP and perfusion monitoring. Monitor the IV site closely — phentolamine is the antidote for norepinephrine or dopamine infiltration.
    Phenylephrineα1Raises blood pressure; also in some decongestantsBP rises through vasoconstrictionReflex slowing of heart rate; hypertensionCaution in hypertension and vascular disease. Check BP before giving.
    Albuterolβ2Bronchodilation — wheezing, asthmaLess wheezing, better air movement, easier breathingTremor, jitteriness, tachycardia, palpitations, chest discomfort; potassium may fallBreath sounds, respiratory effort, HR, oxygenation — before and after. Overuse signals poor control.
    Safety patternWhat it means
    Before givingHR and rhythm, BP, respiratory status, perfusion, and relevant IV access.
    After givingDid the target response occur? Recheck the system you were treating.
    Common effectsTremor, anxiety, headache, palpitations, tachycardia.
    Red flagsSevere hypertension, chest pain, dysrhythmia, worsening ischemia, poor peripheral perfusion.
    TeachingAvoid accidental duplication with OTC stimulants and decongestants. Report severe palpitations or chest pain.

    The pattern to hold on to: almost every adverse effect of this class looks like too much fight-or-flight. And her closing question after any drug — “what evidence tells me it worked, and what tells me it harmed?”

    Ch 31 · Wk slides 17–20

    4Adrenergic antagonists — turning the sympathetic system down

    Blockers produce the opposite of stimulation. Predict the adverse effects from that alone.

    MedicationReceptorsWhy givenExpected responseAdverse effectsNursing safety
    Metoprololβ1 selectiveHypertension, rate control, cardiac conditionsHR, BP and cardiac workload fallBradycardia, hypotensionHR, BP, symptoms. Follow the ordered hold parameters rather than a memorised number.
    Propranololβ1 and β2 — nonselectiveCardiac conditions, migraine preventionHR and BP fallβ2 blockade can worsen bronchospasm in susceptible patientsCheck respiratory history first. A red flag in asthma and COPD.
    Prazosinα1HypertensionVasodilation → BP fallsOrthostatic hypotension and dizzinessTeach slow position changes; report severe dizziness or syncope.

    StepBeta blocker safety check
    01HR and rhythm — is the patient already bradycardic or symptomatic?
    02BP — hypotension, dizziness, syncope, poor perfusion?
    03Respiratory history — nonselective agents may worsen bronchospasm.
    04Diabetes — beta blockers can blunt the tachycardia that warns of hypoglycemia.
    05Follow the ordered hold parameters and policy; notify for concerning symptoms or vitals.
    06Never stop abruptly. Sudden withdrawal can worsen cardiac symptoms.

    Her emphasis: clinical judgment beats a memorised cutoff. Do not rely on a single remembered “hold number” — assess the patient, verify the ordered parameters, then act.

    Ch 32 · Wk slides 23–25

    5Cholinergic agonists — increasing acetylcholine effects

    Direct agonists mimic ACh. Indirect agents block the enzyme that breaks it down, so ACh sticks around longer. Different indications, same underlying idea.

    MedicationTypeWhy givenExpected responseNursing safety
    BethanecholDirect muscarinic agonistNonobstructive urinary retentionBladder contracts → voiding improvesRule out obstruction first. Assess bladder, HR, BP, GI effects.
    PyridostigmineIndirect — inhibits ACh breakdownMyasthenia gravisSkeletal muscle function improvesMonitor strength, swallowing, and respiratory effort.
    DonepezilAcetylcholinesterase inhibitorAlzheimer diseaseMay support cognition or slow symptom declineDoes not cure the disease. Monitor tolerability, especially GI effects.
    SLUDGEToo much cholinergic activity
    SSalivation
    LLacrimation — tearing
    UUrination
    DDiarrhea
    GGI upset and cramping
    EEmesis
    AntidoteReverses
    AtropineCholinergic drug overdose, and poisoning by certain mushrooms.
    PralidoximeIrreversible cholinesterase inhibitors — nerve agents and organophosphate pesticides.

    Irreversible cholinesterase inhibitors are not therapeutic drugs. Karch covers them because they are nerve agents: absorbed by inhalation or through skin, they bind acetylcholinesterase permanently. ACh floods the system — the heart slows and becomes ineffective, pupils and bronchi constrict, secretions pour, and sustained muscle contraction immobilises the diaphragm so breathing stops. The one exception in clinical use is echothiophate iodide, applied topically to the eye.

    Beyond SLUDGE, cholinergic toxicity also brings bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm with secretions, and severe weakness. Higher-risk patients: asthma, bradycardia, peptic ulcer disease, and GI or GU obstruction.

    Ch 33 · Wk slides 26–27

    6Anticholinergics — blocking rest-and-digest

    Blocking muscarinic receptors shifts the body toward a sympathetic-like pattern. Same blockade, different target organs — always connect the drug to the reason it was prescribed.

    MedicationRoute / targetWhy givenExpected responseNursing safety
    AtropineSystemic — heartSymptomatic bradycardiaHR rises, perfusion improvesHR and rhythm. Watch dry mouth, retention, confusion, blurred vision.
    IpratropiumInhaled — airwaysCOPD careBronchodilation, fewer airway secretionsBreath sounds and respiratory effort before and after.
    OxybutyninBladderOveractive bladder, urgencyBladder relaxes, urgency decreasesWatch for retention and constipation.
    ScopolamineTransdermal patchMotion sickness, nausea preventionNausea preventedDry mouth and blurred vision are common. Wash hands after handling the patch.
    PatternWhat you see
    DRYDry mouth, reduced sweating, thick secretions
    DILATEDBlurred vision, photophobia, pupil dilation
    RETAINEDUrinary retention, constipation, slower GI motility
    CONFUSEDDizziness, confusion or delirium, fall risk

    Older adults especially: new confusion, constipation, urinary retention or falls may be medication-related. Reduced sweating causes heat intolerance, and several anticholinergic drugs together produce additive “anticholinergic burden.”

    7Cholinergic vs. anticholinergic — side by side

    Her exam strategy, verbatim: if you forget a side effect, go back to the parasympathetic pattern and reverse it.

    Body systemCholinergic agonistAnticholinergic
    HeartHR decreasesHR increases
    EyesPupils constrictPupils dilate, blurred vision
    MouthSaliva increasesDry mouth
    GIMotility and secretions increaseMotility decreases → constipation
    BladderContracts → urinationRelaxes → retention risk
    SweatingMay increaseDecreases → heat intolerance
    DrugActionIts opposite
    Albuterolβ2 agonist → bronchi openPropranolol — β1+β2 blocker → bronchospasm risk
    Phenylephrineα1 agonist → vessels constrictPrazosin — α1 blocker → vessels relax

    Take-home anchors. α1 squeeze · β1 one heart · β2 two lungs · M moist and moving. For every medication: why → how → expected response → safety.

    Ch 42 · Wk 6 slides 5, 10

    1The pump and the pipes — where every CV drug acts

    Dr. Kaur opens with physiology on purpose. There are only four levers that change blood pressure, and every drug in this unit pulls on one of them. If you learn the levers, you never have to memorise which class lowers BP — you can derive it.

    EquationWhat it saysWhich drugs live here
