    • Benign prostatic hyperplasia (tamsulosin, doxazosin)
    • PTSD-related nightmares (prazosin, off-label)
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, headache, nasal congestion, fatigue
    • Serious: first-dose syncope, falls and fracture, reflex tachycardia, priapism
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Orthostatic BP before starting and after each dose increase
    • Fall risk — gait, balance, home layout, night-time toileting
    • Urinary symptoms: stream, frequency, nocturia, sense of incomplete emptying
    • Timing — whether the patient can take the first dose safely at home
    2Vitals
    • BP lying, sitting and standing — a drop above 20 mmHg systolic on standing is significant
    • HR — reflex tachycardia may accompany the BP fall
    • Recheck 2–6 h after the first dose, when syncope risk peaks
    3Labs
    • Renal function and PSA before starting BPH therapy (the drug can alter PSA interpretation)
    • Electrolytes if on a diuretic
    • No routine drug levels needed
    4Patient education
    • Take the first dose at bedtime — it can cause fainting
    • Rise slowly; sit on the edge of the bed before standing
    • Do not drive after the first dose or a dose increase
    • Tell your eye surgeon you take tamsulosin before cataract surgery — it changes how the iris behaves during the operation
    • Report fainting, or an erection lasting over 4 hours, urgently
    Special populations
    • Older adults: markedly increased risk for orthostatic hypotension, dizziness and falls with fracture; assess orthostatic vitals, start at the lowest dose, and put fall precautions in place.
    • Cataract surgery: tamsulosin causes intraoperative floppy iris syndrome — the ophthalmologist must be told in advance, even if the drug was stopped.
    • On other antihypertensives or PDE-5 inhibitors: additive hypotension; space doses and monitor BP.
    • Women: prazosin and doxazosin are used for hypertension; tamsulosin is not indicated.
    • Syncope history: consider a supervised first dose.
    Direct-acting cholinergic agonists
    muscarinic agonistsbethanechol · pilocarpine
    Example drugsbethanechol · pilocarpine
    Mechanism of action
    • Bind muscarinic receptors directly, mimicking acetylcholine
    • Bladder detrusor contracts and the sphincter relaxes → voiding
    • GI motility and secretions increase
    • Pupils constrict; salivation increases
    Therapeutic uses
    • Nonobstructive urinary retention, including postoperative and postpartum
    • Neurogenic bladder with retention
    • Xerostomia and glaucoma (pilocarpine)
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: salivation, sweating, abdominal cramping, urinary urgency, flushing
    • Serious: bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, cholinergic crisis (SLUDGE)
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Rule out obstruction before giving — making a blocked bladder contract can rupture it
    • Bladder scan for residual volume; palpate for distension
    • Time to first void and volume after the dose
    • Bowel sounds and abdominal comfort
    • Respiratory history — it can provoke bronchospasm
    2Vitals
    • HR and BP before and 30–60 min after — expect bradycardia and hypotension
    • RR and lung sounds for wheeze
    • Orthostatic BP before ambulating
    3Labs
    • BUN and creatinine for renal function with retention
    • Electrolytes if vomiting or diarrhea occur
    • No routine drug level
    4Patient education
    • Take on an empty stomach, an hour before or two hours after meals, to reduce nausea
    • Stay near a toilet — it works within 30–90 minutes
    • Rise slowly; it can lower blood pressure
    • Report wheezing, fainting, severe cramping or a very slow pulse
    • Do not double a missed dose
    Special populations
    • Asthma and COPD: contraindicated or high risk — bronchoconstriction and increased secretions can precipitate an attack; keep a bronchodilator available.
    • Older adults: greater risk of falls from bradycardia and orthostatic hypotension, and of urgency incontinence; ensure fast toilet access and assess orthostatic vitals.
    • Peptic ulcer disease: increased gastric acid can worsen or perforate an ulcer — contraindicated.
    • Bradycardia or heart block: further slowing is dangerous; contraindicated.
    • GI or GU obstruction: absolutely contraindicated — forcing contraction against a blockage risks rupture.
    Cholinesterase inhibitors
    indirect cholinergic agonistspyridostigmine · neostigmine · donepezil
    Example drugspyridostigmine · neostigmine · donepezil
    Mechanism of action
    • Inhibit acetylcholinesterase so ACh is not broken down
    • ACh accumulates at the synapse and its effect is prolonged
    • Improves transmission at the neuromuscular junction
    • Central agents raise ACh in the brain
    Therapeutic uses
    • Myasthenia gravis (pyridostigmine)
    • Reversal of neuromuscular blocking agents (neostigmine)
    • Alzheimer disease and Parkinson-related dementia (donepezil, rivastigmine)
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: nausea, diarrhea, increased secretions, muscle cramps, insomnia
    • Serious: cholinergic crisis, bradycardia, bronchospasm with copious secretions, respiratory failure
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Muscle strength, swallowing and speech, and ptosis before and after dosing
    • Respiratory effort and cough strength — weak respiratory muscles are the emergency in myasthenia
    • Distinguish cholinergic crisis (too much: SLUDGE plus weakness) from myasthenic crisis (too little: weakness without SLUDGE)
    • Baseline cognition and function for the Alzheimer agents
    2Vitals
    • HR — bradycardia is the cardiac warning sign
    • RR, SpO2 and ability to clear secretions
    • BP for hypotension
    3Labs
    • Liver function for donepezil and rivastigmine
    • Electrolytes if GI losses are significant
    • Renal function — affects clearance
    • No routine therapeutic level
    4Patient education
    • Take pyridostigmine 30–60 min before meals so swallowing is strongest when eating
    • Take the dose on time — a late dose can mean sudden weakness
    • Wear medical identification for myasthenia gravis
    • Report increasing weakness, drooling, or trouble breathing immediately — it can mean either too much or too little drug and needs assessment
    • Donepezil: give at bedtime; nausea and vivid dreams are common early and usually settle
    • Donepezil slows symptoms; it does not cure or reverse the disease
    Special populations
    • Older adults: bradycardia and syncope are more likely, and falls follow; check HR before dosing and assess for dizziness. GI effects can cause weight loss — weigh weekly.
    • Asthma and COPD: increased secretions and bronchoconstriction; monitor respiratory status closely.
    • Peptic ulcer disease: increased gastric acid may worsen ulceration.
    • Bradycardia or conduction disease: additive slowing; a pacemaker may be needed before therapy.
    • Myasthenia gravis: the crucial nursing judgement is telling cholinergic from myasthenic crisis — both present with weakness, and the treatments are opposite.
    Anticholinergics
    muscarinic antagonistsatropine · ipratropium · oxybutynin · scopolamine
    Example drugsatropine · ipratropium · oxybutynin · scopolamine
    Mechanism of action
    • Competitively block muscarinic receptors
    • Parasympathetic tone falls, leaving a sympathetic-like picture
    • Heart rate rises, secretions dry, GI and bladder smooth muscle relaxes, pupils dilate
    Therapeutic uses
    • Symptomatic bradycardia (atropine)
    • COPD maintenance bronchodilation (ipratropium, tiotropium)
    • Overactive bladder and urgency (oxybutynin)
    • Motion sickness and postoperative nausea (scopolamine)
    • Drying secretions before anaesthesia (glycopyrrolate)
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary hesitancy, reduced sweating
    • Serious: urinary retention, paralytic ileus, confusion and delirium, tachydysrhythmia, hyperthermia, acute angle-closure glaucoma
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Bladder: voiding pattern, distension, and post-void residual — retention is the effect that most often forces a stop
    • Bowel: sounds, last movement, abdominal distension
    • Mental status, especially any new confusion in an older adult
    • Vision changes and eye pain — eye pain with halos suggests acute glaucoma
    • Total anticholinergic burden across the whole medication list
    2Vitals
    • HR and rhythm — expect a rise with atropine; report a rate over 100 with symptoms
    • Temperature — reduced sweating causes hyperthermia in hot weather
    • RR and lung sounds before and after inhaled agents
    • BP for orthostatic change
    3Labs
    • Renal function — retention can cause post-renal injury; check BUN and creatinine
    • Electrolytes if there is significant constipation or reduced intake
    • No routine drug levels
    4Patient education
    • Dry mouth: sip water, use sugar-free gum or lozenges, keep up dental care — dry mouth causes cavities
    • Constipation: increase fluid and fibre, stay active; report no movement for three days
    • Report inability to urinate — this needs same-day attention
    • Avoid overheating; reduced sweating means heat is dangerous — no saunas or hard exercise in hot weather
    • Blurred vision is expected; do not drive until you know how it affects you
    • Scopolamine patch: apply behind the ear, wash hands thoroughly afterward — touching your eye causes a dilated pupil
    • Ipratropium: avoid spraying into the eyes; rinse the mouth after use
    Special populations
    • Older adults: listed on the Beers criteria as potentially inappropriate — new confusion, delirium, constipation, urinary retention or falls are often the drug rather than the disease; assess cognition at baseline and at each visit, and review total anticholinergic burden.
    • Benign prostatic hyperplasia: high risk of acute urinary retention; assess voiding and residual volume, and use with caution or avoid.
    • Narrow-angle glaucoma: pupil dilation can precipitate an acute attack — contraindicated; teach the patient to report eye pain, halos or sudden vision loss immediately.
    • Hot environments and exercise: impaired sweating causes heat intolerance and hyperthermia — a particular danger for outdoor workers, athletes and older adults in summer.
    • Children: more susceptible to hyperthermia and CNS effects; monitor temperature and behaviour closely.

    Why it is built by class, not by drug. Karch teaches prototypes — the model drug its class is compared against. Learn epinephrine and you can reason about any adrenergic agonist; learn atropine and every anticholinergic follows the same dry–dilated–retained–confused pattern.

    Exam weighting. Every class here except the β1 agonists appears in Dr. Kaur’s decks. textbook only marks a class that is in Karch but not in her slides — learn it for completeness and for the α1 / β1 / β2 symmetry, but weight your revision toward the lecture classes.

    Sources. Karch’s Focus on Nursing Pharmacology, 10th ed. (Tucker), Ch 29–33; Dr. Kaur’s NURS-11 lecture decks; the AGS Beers Criteria® and FDA prescribing information for the special-population notes. No commercial study sites were used.

    Ch 46 · Wk 6 D2 slides 3–4

    1Antiarrhythmics — recognition level, and why that is enough

    Dr. Kaur is explicit about the depth here: class + prototype for recognition, and for the exam, what happens to rate and conduction and which adverse effect is dangerous. You are not expected to select an antiarrhythmic. You are expected to notice when one is hurting your patient.

    ClassMechanismPrototypeThe nursing risk
    ISodium channel blocker — slows impulse conductionlidocaineCNS toxicity (confusion, slurred speech, seizures) and new rhythm problems
    IIBeta blocker — less sympathetic drive at the SA and AV nodemetoprolol · propranololBradycardia and hypotension
    IIIPotassium channel blocker — prolongs repolarisationamiodaroneQT prolongation and multi-organ toxicity
    IVNon-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockerdiltiazem · verapamilBradycardia and AV block

    The four questions that replace memorising a class. Her pearl: do not memorise a class in isolation. For any antiarrhythmic ask — what does it do to rate, to conduction, to blood pressure, and to repolarisation? Answer those four and the monitoring plan writes itself: rate and conduction → apical pulse and rhythm; blood pressure → BP before dosing; repolarisation → QT and the electrolytes that govern it.

    The paradox at the centre of this class. Every antiarrhythmic is also proarrhythmic — a drug that changes electrical behaviour to fix one rhythm can create another. That is why “the rhythm looks different” is never automatically good news, and why potassium and magnesium appear in the monitoring line: low K⁺ or low Mg²⁺ destabilises repolarisation and makes drug-induced dysrhythmia far more likely. Notice that this is the same potassium thread running through Day 1.

    Ch 46 · Wk 6 D2 slide 5

    2Amiodarone — four organs, one explanation

    Her memory hook is HEART · LUNGS · THYROID · LIVER. Rather than memorising four unrelated toxicities, understand why a rhythm drug reaches four organs at all — then the list is unforgettable.

    Why the toxicity is multi-organ. Amiodarone is intensely lipophilic. It leaves the blood and loads into fat, lung, liver, thyroid and skin, giving it an enormous volume of distribution and a half-life measured in weeks to months. Two consequences follow directly: toxicity is cumulative rather than dose-by-dose, and stopping the drug does not stop the exposure — it lingers for months. On top of that, the molecule contains iodine, which is why the thyroid is involved at all. Every item below is downstream of those two facts.

    OrganWhat goes wrongWhat you assessWhat the patient reports
    H — HeartBradycardia, AV block, QT prolongation and the dysrhythmia that can followHR, BP, rhythm and ECG; potassium and magnesiumFainting, palpitations, feeling the heart pause
    L — LungsPulmonary toxicity and fibrosis — the most feared, and often irreversibleLung sounds, respiratory effort, SpO2; baseline chest imaging and pulmonary function as orderedA new cough or new shortness of breath — report it, never dismiss it as a cold
    T — ThyroidHypo- or hyperthyroidism, because the drug carries iodineThyroid function tests as ordered; weight, HR, temperature tolerance, energyFatigue, cold intolerance and weight gain — or tremor, heat intolerance and weight loss
    Li — LiverHepatic injury and enzyme elevationLiver function tests as ordered; jaundice, right upper quadrant tendernessYellowing of eyes or skin, dark urine, unusual fatigue

    Two more that students miss. Photosensitivity and a slate-grey or bluish skin discolouration with long-term use — same lipophilic loading, this time into skin. And amiodarone raises digoxin and warfarin levels, so if either is on the MAR, anticipate toxicity and a dose reduction. That is a Day 1 drug and a Day 2 drug colliding on one medication list.

    Ch 46 · Wk 6 D2 slide 6

    3Adenosine — where the administration is the pharmacology

    Her pearl: “this is not a medication you casually push and walk away from.” Almost everything unusual about giving adenosine follows from a single number.

    The number that explains everything: a half-life of roughly 10 seconds. Adenosine is taken up by red blood cells and endothelium almost immediately. Give it slowly and it is destroyed before it reaches the heart — the dose simply fails. So: rapid IV push, through the port closest to the patient, followed immediately by a saline flush to drive the drug centrally before it disappears. The technique is not a ritual; it is the only way the drug can work.

    ElementDetail
    IndicationSelected regular supraventricular tachycardias
    ActionBriefly blocks conduction through the AV node, interrupting the re-entry circuit so the SA node can resume control
    Administration1. Rapid IV push · 2. Immediate flush · 3. Continuous ECG, with resuscitation capability immediately available
    Common effectsFlushing, chest discomfort or pressure, lightheadedness — brief, and expected
    SeriousBrief pauses or asystole, marked bradycardia, bronchospasm
    Teach beforehandWarn the patient they may feel flushing, chest pressure or a strange impending sensation — and that it passes in seconds

    The judgement this drug tests. A brief pause or a few seconds of asystole on the monitor after adenosine is the expected mechanism, not a complication — the drug is deliberately stopping conduction so the rhythm can restart cleanly. Recognising that is the difference between calmly watching the monitor and calling a code on a working drug. That said, “expected” is exactly why continuous ECG and resuscitation readiness are required: you have to be able to tell a two-second pause from one that is not ending. Caution in asthma — adenosine can provoke bronchospasm.

    Ch 45 · Wk 6 D2 slides 7, 9

    4Angina — supply versus demand, and why that decides the drug

    Her framing: understanding the physiology makes the medications easier to remember. Angina is a mismatch. Either supply fell or demand rose — and every antianginal drug attacks one side of that equation.

    Oxygen supplyOxygen demand
    Coronary blood flow must meet myocardial need. Reduced flow — atherosclerosis, spasm, thrombus — produces ischemia.
    raised by: nitrates (dilate coronaries), treating the obstruction    		Heart rate · contractility · preload · afterload — the same four levers from Day 1.
    lowered by: beta blockers, non-DHP CCBs, nitrates (preload)
    DrugWhich side of the equationRescue or preventionNursing focus
    NitroglycerinBoth — vasodilation lowers preload (demand) and dilates coronaries (supply)Rapid rescue (sublingual); long-acting forms preventChest pain and BP; sit or lie down before a dose
    Beta blockers
    metoprolol · propranolol    		Demand — lowers HR and contractilityPreventionHR and BP before dosing; never stop abruptly
    Diltiazem · verapamilDemand — slows HR and AV conduction; also dilatesPreventionHR and BP; watch conduction; verapamil constipation
    AmlodipineDemand — lowers afterload by vasodilatingPreventionBP; watch hypotension and edema

    Her pearl, and the distinction the exam will test. Beta blockers and calcium channel blockers are prevention and control — not rapid rescue. A patient with chest pain right now does not take their metoprolol early; they take sublingual nitroglycerin and follow the emergency plan. Confusing a maintenance drug for a rescue drug is the same error as confusing salmeterol with albuterol — and you have already met that pattern in the autonomic unit.

    When chest pain is not angina. Chest pain that is new, worsening, prolonged, or occurring at rest may be acute coronary syndrome and needs urgent evaluation, not another nitroglycerin tablet and a wait. Stable angina is predictable: same trigger, same duration, relieved by rest or nitrate. Anything that breaks that pattern is a change in condition.

    Ch 45 · Wk 6 D2 slides 8, 30

    5Nitroglycerin — high-yield because the patient uses it alone

    Her reason for weighting this drug: patients self-administer it at home, without a nurse present. The teaching is the intervention.

    ElementDetail
    ActionConverted to nitric oxide → venous and arterial dilation → preload falls, cardiac workload falls, coronary flow improves
    Common effectsHeadache (very common, from cerebral vasodilation), flushing, dizziness
    SeriousHypotension and syncope — the reason the patient sits or lies down first
    AssessChest pain and blood pressure before and after each dose. Hold and reassess if BP is below the ordered parameter.
    Teaching pointWhy it matters
    Sit or lie down firstThe drug drops blood pressure quickly. Standing patients faint and fall.
    Headache is expectedPatients who are not warned assume the drug is harming them and stop taking it.
    Store the tablets properlyOriginal dark glass container, tightly closed, away from heat, light and moisture — not in a pill organiser or a pocket. Nitroglycerin degrades, and a degraded tablet fails during an emergency.
    Know the emergency planIf chest pain is new, unrelieved, or worsening, activate emergency services — follow the plan your provider gave you rather than repeating doses indefinitely.
    Expect a tingle or burnA slight fizzing under the tongue suggests the tablet is still active. Do not swallow or chew a sublingual tablet.

    The absolute interaction — and why “separate them by an hour” is wrong. Never combine nitrates with PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil). Both act on the same pathway: nitrates raise cGMP, PDE-5 inhibitors block its breakdown. Stacking them produces profound, refractory hypotension. Her slide 30 makes the point precisely — a patient-chosen one-hour gap is not safe teaching, because sildenafil persists around 24 hours and tadalafil up to 36. Ask about these drugs before giving a nitrate, and ask plainly: patients often do not consider them medication, and may be embarrassed to volunteer them.

    Ch 47 · Wk 6 D2 slides 10–12, 31

    6Lipid-lowering — know atorvastatin well, recognise the rest

    She sets the study weighting explicitly: atorvastatin in depth; the other classes at recognition level only. Do not spend equal time on them.

    ElementAtorvastatin — the prototype
    GoalLower LDL-C and reduce cardiovascular events — MI and stroke. The target is the risk, not just the number.
    ActionInhibits HMG-CoA reductase → less hepatic cholesterol synthesis → the liver pulls more LDL out of the blood
    Common effectsMyalgias, mild GI upset, headache
    SeriousSevere muscle injury / rhabdomyolysis; possible liver injury
    AssessAsk directly about severe muscle pain or weakness — patients attribute it to exercise or age and do not report it. Lipid and liver monitoring as ordered.
    TeachTake it consistently · report severe muscle pain or weakness or dark urine · report pregnancy promptly · avoid grapefruit juice

    Why “muscle pain + dark urine” is the pairing she keeps repeating. In rhabdomyolysis, skeletal muscle breaks down and releases myoglobin into the blood. Myoglobin is filtered by the kidney and turns the urine dark brown or tea-coloured — that is not blood, it is muscle protein — and it is directly toxic to renal tubules. So the dark urine is not an incidental extra symptom: it is the sign that muscle injury has become kidney injury. Muscle ache alone is common and often benign; muscle pain with weakness with dark urine is the emergency.

    Recognition onlyRole
    EzetimibeReduces cholesterol absorption in the gut; adds further LDL lowering, often alongside a statin
    FenofibrateMainly lowers triglycerides; combined with a statin it raises muscle-injury risk
    PCSK9 inhibitorsInjectable LDL lowering for selected patients — typically when statins are insufficient or not tolerated

    Pregnancy. Cholesterol is required for fetal development, so statins are stopped in pregnancy — which is why “report pregnancy promptly” is on her teaching list rather than being an afterthought.

    Ch 48 · Wk 6 D2 slides 13–14

    7“Blood thinner” is three different drugs — and the difference is the clot

    Her pearl: “blood thinner” is not specific enough. All three raise bleeding risk, but their indications, monitoring and reversal are entirely different.

    CategoryPrototypesWhat it actually doesUsed for
    Antiplateletaspirin · clopidogrelStops platelets sticking together — acts on the platelet plug, before fibrinArterial clotting: MI, stroke prevention, stents
    Anticoagulantheparin · enoxaparin · warfarin · DOACsInterferes with the clotting cascade — prevents fibrin forming or extendingVenous clotting and stasis: DVT, PE, atrial fibrillation
    Thrombolyticalteplase · tenecteplaseBreaks down a clot that already exists by digesting fibrinEmergencies: selected acute ischemic stroke, massive PE, STEMI

    Why arterial and venous get different drugs — the reasoning, not the list. Arterial clots form in fast, high-pressure flow where platelets dominate — a pale, platelet-rich “white clot.” So you attack platelets: aspirin, clopidogrel. Venous clots form in slow, stagnant flow where the cascade dominates — a fibrin-and-red-cell-rich “red clot.” So you attack the cascade: heparin, warfarin, DOACs. That single distinction explains why a patient in atrial fibrillation gets apixaban rather than aspirin, and why a stent patient gets clopidogrel rather than warfarin.

    Bleeding — what should worry youFindings
    NeurologicSudden severe headache · new weakness or confusion · decreased level of consciousness — suspect intracranial bleeding
    GI / GUBlack tarry stool · vomiting blood or coffee-ground emesis · frank hematuria or bleeding that will not stop
    HemodynamicTachycardia · hypotension · dizziness · pallor · syncope — the body compensating for volume it has lost

    Her warning, and it is the one students fail. Do not normalise clinically important bleeding simply because the patient is on an antiplatelet or anticoagulant. “Of course they are bruising, they are on heparin” is how a GI bleed gets missed for a shift. The medication explains a tendency; it never explains away melena, hematemesis, a severe headache, or a falling blood pressure. Assess severity, review the last dose and every other bleeding-risk drug on the list, get the ordered labs, and escalate.

    Ch 48 · Wk 6 D2 slides 15–20, 26

    8The anticoagulants side by side — monitoring and reversal are the whole difference

    Her instruction: do not treat all anticoagulants as one medication. The table below is the one to be able to reproduce from memory.

    DrugRouteMonitoringReversalThe signature point
    HeparinIV / SQaPTT or anti-Xa + plateletsProtamine sulfateHIT — see below
    Enoxaparin
    LMWH    		SQBleeding + platelets + renal function; no routine aPTTProtamine (partial only)Renally cleared — accumulates when kidneys decline
    WarfarinPOPT / INRVitamin KConsistent vitamin K intake; many food and drug interactions
    Apixaban · rivaroxaban
    DOACs    		POBleeding + renal function; routine INR is not usedSpecific agents exist; not INR-guidedAdherence — short half-life means a missed dose quickly removes protection

    INR belongs to warfarin alone. Her slide 34 tests exactly this: an apixaban patient with an INR of 1.1 is not concerning, because INR is not used to dose DOACs — reading it as “subtherapeutic” is the trap. Warfarin needs INR because it works indirectly, by reducing production of vitamin K–dependent clotting factors, and each patient’s response differs. DOACs inhibit a single factor directly and predictably, so they are dosed by patient characteristics — renal function, age, weight — not by a titration lab.

    Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia — the counterintuitive one. Platelets fall, so the instinct is to think bleeding. It is the opposite. HIT is an immune reaction in which antibodies activate platelets, consuming them while driving new clot formation. The patient becomes thrombocytopenic and prothrombotic at once — which is why her case presents as a platelet drop plus new leg pain. If suspected: stop all heparin (including flushes) and escalate; a non-heparin anticoagulant is started. Giving platelets would be the wrong reflex. Her wording is worth keeping: HIT is a prothrombotic complication, not simply “low platelets = bleeding.”

    Warfarin teaching — what correct sounds likeWhy
    “Keep vitamin K intake consistent”Consistency, not avoidance. The dose is titrated to your usual diet. Swearing off spinach forever swings the INR just as much as suddenly eating a bowl of it — what destabilises INR is change.
    “I will not double a missed dose”Doubling spikes the INR into bleeding range. Call for instructions.
    “I will check before taking anything new”Includes OTC drugs, NSAIDs and supplements. Ibuprofen is not safe just because it is over the counter — NSAIDs add both bleeding risk and GI injury.
    “I will keep my INR appointments”The lab is the safety system for this drug.
    Enoxaparin — SQ techniqueDetail
    SiteSubcutaneous abdomen is common — at least 2 inches from the umbilicus; rotate sites
    Air bubbleDo not expel the air bubble in a prefilled syringe — it delivers the full dose and seals the track
    AfterDo not rub the site — rubbing causes bruising and hematoma
    MonitorBleeding, platelets, renal function — no routine aPTT titration
    Ch 48 · Wk 6 D2 slide 21

    9Thrombolytics — the only drugs that dissolve a clot

    First-semester focus, in her words: know the purpose, the major bleeding risk, and the need for strict screening.

    ElementDetail
    Prototypesalteplase · tenecteplase
    ActionPromote conversion of plasminogen to plasmin → digests the fibrin mesh of an existing clot
    IndicationSelected acute ischemic stroke; other emergencies such as massive PE and STEMI
    SeriousMajor bleeding — especially intracranial hemorrhage
    SafetyStrict eligibility screening · frequent neurologic and bleeding checks · time-sensitive therapy

    Why the screening is so strict. These drugs cannot tell the difference between the clot causing the stroke and a clot that is holding something closed — a recent surgical site, a healing ulcer, a small vessel in the brain. That is the entire reason for the eligibility checklist: recent surgery, recent bleeding, uncontrolled hypertension, prior intracranial hemorrhage. And it is why an ischemic stroke must be distinguished from a hemorrhagic one by imaging first — giving a thrombolytic into a brain bleed is catastrophic.

    The one-line distinction to carry into the exam. Anticoagulants prevent a clot forming or extending. Thrombolytics dissolve a clot that is already there. Aspirin stops platelets clumping in the first place. Three drugs, three different moments in the life of a clot.

    Ch 49 · Wk 6 D2 slides 22–25, 32

    10Anemia — pharmacology starts with the cause

    Her pearl: treat the cause, not just the hemoglobin number. Three different deficiencies, three different drugs, and giving the wrong one can let real damage continue while the blood count looks better.

    CauseDrugWhat it replaces or does
    Iron deficiencyferrous sulfateReplaces the iron needed to build hemoglobin
    Folate or B12 deficiencyfolic acid · vitamin B12Replaces the missing vitamin — both produce megaloblastic anemia
    CKD — low erythropoietinepoetin alfaStimulates the marrow to produce red cells
    Ferrous sulfateDetail
    Expected effectsDark stools, constipation, GI upset — expected, not adverse
    AbsorptionVitamin C improves absorption (take with orange juice); calcium, antacids and dairy reduce it. Food improves tolerance but lowers absorption — a real trade-off, so follow the plan the provider set.
    TeachConstipation is common — fluids, fibre, activity, and ask about a stool softener. Liquid iron stains teeth — dilute it and drink through a straw.
    Store safelyIron overdose is a leading cause of poisoning death in young children. Keep it out of reach in a child-resistant container — the tablets look like sweets.

    Dark stool versus melena — the discrimination she tests twice. Iron makes stool dark or greenish-black but formed and otherwise normal, in a patient who feels fine. Melena from GI bleeding is black, tarry, sticky and foul-smelling, and it comes with dizziness, weakness, pallor or tachycardia. Her pearl: dark stool can be expected with iron; black tarry stool plus dizziness and weakness is a different clinical picture. The stool colour alone does not decide it — the patient’s symptoms do.

    The folate trap — genuinely important. Folate and B12 deficiency look identical on a blood count: both cause megaloblastic anemia with large red cells. Give folate to someone who is actually B12 deficient and the anemia improves — the count normalises, everyone is reassured — while the neurologic damage continues silently and can become permanent. The discriminator is neurologic: numbness, tingling, balance problems point to B12. That is why her slide says identify the underlying cause, and why B12 may need injection when absorption is the problem — as in pernicious anemia or after gastric surgery, where oral replacement cannot be absorbed at all.

    Epoetin alfaDetail
    ActionStimulates bone marrow red cell production — replaces the erythropoietin failing kidneys no longer make
    CommonHypertension, headache, injection-site reactions
    SeriousThrombosis, MI and stroke if hemoglobin rises too high or too fast
    MonitorHgb and Hct · blood pressure · iron status
    TeachResponse is not immediate — it takes weeks. Adequate iron is required or the drug cannot work.

    Her framing is the exam point: safe erythropoiesis, not maximal. More hemoglobin sounds better, but raising it too high thickens the blood and drives clotting events — which is why there is a target range rather than a target of “normal.” And the drug is useless without iron: you can tell the marrow to build red cells, but it cannot build them out of nothing. That is why iron studies are monitored alongside hemoglobin.

    Ch 42–49, 51 · whole-unit integration

    11The pattern map — build the pattern, then add the exceptions

    Her closing slide, expanded. Four patterns cover most of the cardiovascular unit; the signature details hang off them. Learn the pattern first — it is what lets you reason about a drug you half-remember.

    PatternDrugsWhat you monitor
    Slows heart rateBeta blockers · diltiazem · verapamil · digoxin · amiodarone · adenosineHR and BP before dosing; watch for bradycardia and AV block. Two of these together is additive.
    Raises potassiumACE inhibitors · ARBs · ARNI · spironolactoneK⁺ and renal function. Risk multiplies when they are combined or kidneys decline.
    Lowers potassiumFurosemide · hydrochlorothiazideK⁺, Mg²⁺ — and remember low K⁺ potentiates digoxin and destabilises rhythm.
    Increases bleedingAntiplatelets · anticoagulants · thrombolyticsBleeding assessment · platelets · INR for warfarin only · renal function for LMWH and DOACs
    Reversal / rescueDrugThe clinical picture that calls for it
    Heparinprotamine sulfateMajor bleeding on heparin — falling BP, rising HR, visible or occult blood loss
    Warfarinvitamin KMajor bleeding or a dangerously high INR
    Digoxindigoxin immune FabSevere toxicity — bradycardia or dysrhythmia with the GI and visual picture

    Her pearl about antidotes, which is the right way to hold them. Do not memorise an antidote alone — connect it to the toxicity or bleeding pattern that tells you reversal may be needed. “Heparin → protamine” is a flashcard. “Falling BP, rising HR, black stool, patient on heparin → this may need reversal” is nursing.

    Look-alikes she wants you to separateThe discriminator
    Antiplatelet vs anticoagulant vs thrombolyticPlatelet plug → cascade → dissolving an existing clot. Arterial vs venous vs emergency.
    Heparin vs warfarin vs DOACaPTT/platelets vs INR vs no routine lab. Protamine vs vitamin K vs specific agents.
    Rescue vs preventionSublingual nitroglycerin rescues. Beta blockers and CCBs prevent. Never substitute.
    Dark stool vs melenaIron: formed, patient well. Melena: tarry, foul, with dizziness and weakness.
    Folate vs B12Same anemia; only B12 has neurologic signs, and folate can mask it.
    Low platelets in HITThrombocytopenia that causes clotting, not bleeding.

    How she tells you to study, and it is worth following. Build a prototype card for each drug — why · action · common adverse effect · danger · check · teach. Then practise give versus question against real vital signs, labs and symptoms. Then explain every wrong answer: why is that distractor less safe or less relevant? Her final line: do not copy the slide word for word — retrieve it and apply it to a patient.

    Ch 45–49 · med chart

    Medication chart — rhythm, ischemia, lipids, blood & anemia

    The Day 2 half of the cardiovascular unit, in the same rubric format: example drugs, mechanism, uses, effects, nursing considerations in the four required parts — assessment vitals labs education — and specific special populations.

    Class III antiarrhythmics
    potassium channel blockersamiodarone · sotalol · dofetilide
    Example drugsamiodarone · sotalol · dofetilide
    Mechanism of action
    • Block potassium channels → prolong repolarisation and the refractory period
    • Amiodarone also has class I, II and IV activity — which is why it affects rate, conduction and repolarisation
    • Intensely lipophilic: loads into fat, lung, liver, thyroid and skin; half-life of weeks to months
    • The molecule contains iodine — the source of thyroid toxicity
    Therapeutic uses
    • Serious ventricular dysrhythmias
    • Atrial fibrillation — rhythm control and conversion
    • Cardiac arrest protocols
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: bradycardia, hypotension, nausea, fatigue, photosensitivity
    • Serious — HEART: QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, AV block
    • Serious — LUNGS: pulmonary toxicity and fibrosis, often irreversible
    • Serious — THYROID: hypo- or hyperthyroidism
    • Serious — LIVER: hepatic injury
    • Long-term: corneal deposits, slate-grey skin discolouration
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Lung sounds, cough and respiratory effort at every encounter — a new dry cough or new breathlessness is pulmonary toxicity until proven otherwise, and patients dismiss it as a cold
    • Baseline and ongoing: chest imaging, pulmonary function, thyroid and liver studies as ordered
    • Rhythm and QT interval — the drug’s own mechanism creates dysrhythmia risk
    • Scan the MAR for digoxin and warfarin — amiodarone raises both to toxic levels
    • Vision and skin changes on long-term therapy
    • Thyroid symptom review: weight, energy, temperature tolerance, tremor
    2Vitals
    • HR and BP before dosing; continuous ECG during IV loading
    • Rhythm and QT — report lengthening
    • RR and SpO2 with any respiratory complaint
    • Temperature tolerance and weight as thyroid indicators
    3Labs
    • Potassium and magnesium — low levels amplify QT risk and torsades
    • Thyroid function (TSH, T4) at baseline and periodically
    • Liver enzymes at baseline and periodically
    • Digoxin level and INR if either drug is co-prescribed
    • Renal function
    4Patient education
    • Report a new cough or new shortness of breath right away — do not wait to see if it passes; this is the most important thing you can tell us
    • Report fainting, palpitations or a very slow pulse
    • Report major fatigue, weight change, feeling unusually cold or hot, or tremor — these can be thyroid effects
    • Use sunscreen and protective clothing; your skin burns easily and may develop a grey-blue tint with long use
    • Report yellowing of the eyes or skin, or dark urine
    • Keep every lab and eye appointment — this drug is monitored across several organs
    • Avoid grapefruit juice; check before starting any new medicine
    Special populations
    • Patients on digoxin or warfarin: amiodarone raises the level of both — anticipate digoxin toxicity and INR elevation; doses are usually reduced and levels followed. This is the most common dangerous interaction in this unit.
    • Existing lung disease: baseline impairment makes pulmonary toxicity harder to detect and more dangerous — establish a clear baseline and investigate any change.
    • Thyroid disease: the iodine content can destabilise either direction; monitor thyroid studies more closely.
    • Older adults: greater risk of bradycardia, hypotension and falls, and slower clearance prolongs an already very long half-life.
    • Hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia from any cause (including the Day 1 diuretics): sharply increases torsades risk — correct electrolytes before and during therapy.
    • Stopping the drug does not stop exposure: because of tissue loading, effects and interactions persist for weeks to months after discontinuation.
    Nitratesnitroglycerin · isosorbide mononitrate · isosorbide dinitrate
    Example drugsnitroglycerin · isosorbide mononitrate · isosorbide dinitrate
    Mechanism of action
    • Converted to nitric oxide → raises cGMP → smooth muscle relaxes
    • Venous dilation predominates → preload falls → cardiac workload and oxygen demand fall
    • Coronary dilation improves supply
    • Tolerance develops with continuous exposure — which is why a nitrate-free interval is built into long-acting dosing
    Therapeutic uses
    • Acute angina — sublingual nitroglycerin is the rescue
    • Prevention of anginal episodes (long-acting forms)
    • Acute coronary syndrome and heart failure (IV) in selected settings
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: headache (very common), flushing, dizziness, lightheadedness
    • Serious: symptomatic hypotension and syncope, reflex tachycardia; profound refractory hypotension if combined with a PDE-5 inhibitor
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Ask directly about PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) before giving any nitrate — patients often do not consider them medication and may be reluctant to mention them
    • Characterise the chest pain: onset, quality, duration, what relieves it, and whether this episode differs from the usual pattern
    • BP before every dose, against the ordered parameter
    • Check how the patient stores and dates their sublingual tablets — degraded tablets fail in an emergency
    • Ask how often the rescue drug is being used — increasing use signals worsening disease
    • Confirm the patient knows the emergency plan
    2Vitals
    • BP before and after each dose — and have the patient sitting or lying down first
    • HR — reflex tachycardia may accompany the BP drop
    • Pain score before and after, with time to relief
    • Continuous BP monitoring for IV infusion
    3Labs
    • No routine drug level
    • Electrolytes and renal function in the broader cardiac picture
    • Troponin if the presentation suggests acute coronary syndrome rather than stable angina
    4Patient education
    • Sit or lie down before taking it — it lowers your blood pressure quickly and people faint
    • A headache is expected and not a sign the drug is harming you; it usually eases with continued use
    • Store tablets in the original dark container, tightly closed, away from heat and moisture — not in a pill organiser or your pocket
    • Let the tablet dissolve under your tongue; do not chew or swallow it
    • Follow the emergency plan your provider gave you — if chest pain is new, worse, or not relieved, call 911 rather than continuing to take tablets
    • Never take erectile-dysfunction medication with this, and tell any provider who offers you one that you take nitrates
    • Check the expiry date; replace tablets as directed
    Special populations
    • Anyone taking a PDE-5 inhibitor: absolute contraindication. Both drugs act on the same cGMP pathway, so the effect is additive and can be fatal. Separating doses by an hour is not adequate — sildenafil persists roughly 24 hours and tadalafil up to 36. Ask every patient, not only the ones you expect.
    • Older adults: markedly higher risk of orthostatic hypotension, syncope and falls; sit or lie for every dose and assess orthostatic BP.
    • Hypotension or volume depletion: nitrates lower preload, which a hypovolemic patient cannot afford — correct volume first.
    • Right ventricular infarction: these patients are preload-dependent and can become severely hypotensive — nitrates are used with great caution or avoided.
    • Severe aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: reducing preload can drop cardiac output dangerously.
    • Continuous long-acting therapy: a daily nitrate-free interval is required or tolerance develops and the drug stops working.
    Statins
    HMG-CoA reductase inhibitorsatorvastatin · rosuvastatin · simvastatin
    Example drugsatorvastatin · rosuvastatin · simvastatin
    Mechanism of action
    • Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of hepatic cholesterol synthesis
    • The liver responds by upregulating LDL receptors → more LDL pulled out of the blood
    • Also stabilise atherosclerotic plaque and reduce vascular inflammation — part of why they cut events beyond the LDL number
    Therapeutic uses
    • Lowering LDL-C
    • Reducing MI and stroke risk in established or high-risk atherosclerotic disease
    • Secondary prevention after an acute coronary event
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: myalgias, mild GI upset, headache
    • Serious: rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury; hepatotoxicity; new-onset diabetes in predisposed patients
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Ask specifically about muscle pain, tenderness or weakness at every visit — patients blame age, exercise or the weather and will not raise it unprompted
    • Ask about urine colour when muscle symptoms are present — dark, tea-coloured urine changes this from a nuisance to an emergency
    • Establish whether muscle symptoms are new, worsening, or associated with exertion
    • Baseline liver function before starting
    • Review the MAR for interacting drugs — fibrates, amiodarone, and several antibiotics and antifungals raise statin levels and muscle risk
    • Pregnancy status and contraception
    2Vitals
    • No specific vital-sign parameter for dosing
    • BP and HR as part of overall cardiovascular assessment
    • Urine output and colour if muscle injury is suspected
    3Labs
    • Creatine kinase (CK) when muscle symptoms occur — not routinely, but promptly when they do
    • Liver enzymes at baseline and if symptoms develop
    • Lipid panel to assess response
    • Creatinine — rhabdomyolysis causes acute kidney injury
    • HbA1c or glucose in patients at risk of diabetes
    4Patient education
    • Report severe muscle pain, tenderness or weakness — especially with dark or tea-coloured urine. That combination needs same-day attention
    • Take it consistently, at the same time each day; some statins work best in the evening
    • This drug lowers your risk of heart attack and stroke — you will not feel it working, which is why people stop taking it
    • Avoid grapefruit juice with atorvastatin and simvastatin
    • Tell your provider straight away if you become pregnant or are planning to
    • Diet and activity still matter — the drug supports them, it does not replace them
    • Report yellowing of the eyes or skin, or unusual fatigue
    Special populations
    • Pregnancy: stopped in pregnancy — cholesterol is required for fetal development. Confirm pregnancy status and teach prompt reporting in any patient of childbearing potential.
    • Older adults: higher risk of muscle symptoms, more likely to be on interacting drugs, and muscle weakness translates directly into falls — ask about muscle symptoms and gait at every visit.
    • Renal impairment: increases myopathy risk, and rhabdomyolysis would worsen existing injury; doses are adjusted for some agents.
    • Hypothyroidism: an independent cause of myopathy — untreated, it compounds statin muscle risk; thyroid status should be known.
    • On fibrates, amiodarone, or certain antibiotics and antifungals: raised statin levels and substantially higher rhabdomyolysis risk — a combination worth flagging to the prescriber.
    • Heavy alcohol use or liver disease: additive hepatic risk; liver function must be followed.
    Antiplateletsaspirin · clopidogrel · ticagrelor
    Example drugsaspirin · clopidogrel · ticagrelor
    Mechanism of action
    • Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX-1 → no thromboxane A₂ → platelets cannot aggregate, for the platelet’s whole 7–10 day life
    • Clopidogrel and ticagrelor block the P2Y12 ADP receptor, a different aggregation pathway
    • Act on the platelet plug — the arterial, high-flow side of clotting
    • Clopidogrel is a prodrug needing CYP2C19 activation, so some patients respond poorly
    Therapeutic uses
    • Secondary prevention after MI or ischemic stroke
    • Coronary stents — dual antiplatelet therapy
    • Peripheral arterial disease
    • Acute coronary syndrome
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: bruising, minor bleeding, GI upset, prolonged bleeding from small cuts
    • Serious: GI bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage, severe bleeding; aspirin also — tinnitus at toxic levels, and bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthma
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Skin and mucous membranes for bruising, petechiae, and gum or nose bleeding
    • Ask about stool and emesis colour directly — black tarry stool or coffee-ground emesis are the findings that matter, and patients will not volunteer them
    • Review the MAR for other bleeding-risk drugs: anticoagulants, NSAIDs, SSRIs, corticosteroids
    • Ask about OTC products — many contain aspirin or NSAIDs without the patient realising
    • History of GI ulcer or bleed
    • Upcoming surgery or dental work — these drugs are often held in advance, and that decision belongs to the prescriber
    2Vitals
    • HR and BP — tachycardia with hypotension suggests significant blood loss, often before bleeding is visible
    • Orthostatic vitals if dizziness or weakness is reported
    • Temperature if infection is a concern alongside bruising
    3Labs
    • CBC — hemoglobin, hematocrit and platelets; a falling hemoglobin is occult bleeding
    • PT/INR and aPTT are not used to monitor antiplatelets — these drugs affect platelet function, which routine coagulation studies do not measure
    • Renal and hepatic function
    • Stool for occult blood if bleeding is suspected
    4Patient education
    • Do not add aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen or other anti-inflammatories without checking — they multiply bleeding risk and many OTC products contain them
    • Report black tarry stools, vomit that looks like coffee grounds, or a sudden severe headache — these are emergencies, not minor bleeding
    • Expect to bruise more easily and to bleed longer from small cuts; use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor
    • Tell every dentist and surgeon that you take this before any procedure
    • Do not stop it on your own — stopping after a stent can cause the stent to clot
    • Carry a card or wear identification saying you take an antiplatelet
    Special populations
    • Patients with coronary stents: stopping antiplatelet therapy early can cause acute stent thrombosis, which is frequently fatal — never hold a dose without the prescriber, and this is one of the strongest teaching points in the class.
    • History of GI ulcer or bleed: substantially higher risk; a proton pump inhibitor is often added, and stool and hemoglobin are followed.
    • Older adults: higher GI and intracranial bleeding risk, often on multiple bleeding-risk drugs, and a fall becomes far more dangerous — review the whole medication list and fall risk together.
    • Children and teenagers with viral illness: aspirin is avoided because of Reye syndrome — acute encephalopathy and liver failure.
    • Aspirin-sensitive asthma or nasal polyps: aspirin can precipitate severe bronchospasm.
    • On an anticoagulant as well: antiplatelet plus anticoagulant is a deliberate, high-risk combination — bleeding assessment becomes a shift-by-shift priority.
    Heparinsheparin · enoxaparin
    Example drugsheparin · enoxaparin
    Mechanism of action
    • Bind antithrombin and dramatically accelerate its inactivation of clotting factors
    • Unfractionated heparin inhibits thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa; enoxaparin (LMWH) acts mainly on Xa
    • Prevents clot formation and extension — it does not dissolve existing clot
    • Heparin is monitored by aPTT or anti-Xa; enoxaparin’s response is predictable enough that routine aPTT is not used
    Therapeutic uses
    • Prevention and treatment of DVT and PE
    • Acute coronary syndrome
    • Anticoagulation during dialysis, surgery and line maintenance
    • Bridging therapy when warfarin is started
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: bruising, injection-site tenderness, minor bleeding
    • Serious: major bleeding; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — a prothrombotic complication; hyperkalemia; osteoporosis with prolonged use
    • Reversal: protamine sulfate for major bleeding — full reversal for unfractionated heparin, only partial for enoxaparin
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Baseline and serial platelet counts — a fall of roughly 50% or below 150,000, typically 5–10 days in, raises concern for HIT
    • Assess for NEW clot, not just bleeding, when platelets drop — unilateral leg pain and swelling, chest pain, dyspnea; HIT causes thrombosis
    • Full bleeding survey: skin, gums, stool, emesis, urine, neurologic status
    • Verify the concentration and the dose against the order and an independent second nurse — heparin is a high-alert drug and concentrations differ dramatically between vials
    • Renal function before enoxaparin — it accumulates when kidneys decline
    • Review all other bleeding-risk drugs
    2Vitals
    • HR and BP — tachycardia and hypotension are early signs of significant blood loss
    • Neurologic checks — a change in level of consciousness may be intracranial bleeding
    • Injection sites and any invasive line for oozing or hematoma
    3Labs
    • Platelets — the defining lab for heparin safety, at baseline and serially
    • aPTT or anti-Xa per protocol for unfractionated heparin; no routine aPTT for enoxaparin
    • Hemoglobin and hematocrit to detect occult bleeding
    • Creatinine — especially before and during enoxaparin
    • Potassium — heparin can cause hyperkalemia through aldosterone suppression
    4Patient education
    • Report any unusual bleeding — nosebleeds that will not stop, bleeding gums, blood in urine or stool, or a sudden severe headache
    • Enoxaparin at home: inject into the abdomen at least 2 inches from the navel, rotate sites, do not expel the air bubble from the prefilled syringe, and do not rub afterwards — rubbing causes bruising
    • Bruising at the injection site is expected; a hard painful lump or spreading bruise is not
    • Use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor; avoid contact sports
    • Tell every provider and dentist you are on an anticoagulant
    • Do not take aspirin or anti-inflammatories unless your provider says to
    • Dispose of syringes in a sharps container
    Special populations
    • Any patient on heparin for 5–10 days: the classic window for HIT — platelets must be followed, and a drop demands assessment for new thrombosis, not just bleeding. If HIT is suspected, all heparin stops, including line flushes, and a non-heparin anticoagulant is started. Giving platelets is the wrong reflex.
    • Renal impairment: enoxaparin accumulates and bleeding risk climbs — dose reduction is required, and unfractionated heparin is often preferred because it is not renally cleared.
    • Older adults and low body weight: higher bleeding risk at standard doses; falls become far more consequential.
    • Pregnancy: heparins do not cross the placenta and are the anticoagulants of choice — unlike warfarin, which is teratogenic.
    • Epidural or spinal anaesthesia: risk of spinal hematoma with paralysis — strict timing rules govern dosing around catheter placement and removal, and new back pain or leg weakness must be reported immediately.
    • Recent surgery, active bleeding, or severe thrombocytopenia: contraindicated or requires specific risk assessment.
    Vitamin K antagonistwarfarin
    Example drugssingle-agent class warfarin
    Mechanism of action
    • Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase → the liver cannot recycle vitamin K → reduced production of factors II, VII, IX and X
    • Because it reduces production rather than blocking existing factors, the full effect takes several days — which is why heparin bridges the start
    • Narrow therapeutic index with wide individual variation, so it is dosed to the INR, not to weight
    Therapeutic uses
    • Atrial fibrillation — stroke prevention
    • Treatment and prevention of DVT and PE
    • Mechanical heart valves, where DOACs are not used
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: bruising, minor bleeding
    • Serious: major bleeding — GI, intracranial; extensive food and drug interactions; rarely, skin necrosis early in therapy
    • Reversal: vitamin K (phytonadione); prothrombin complex concentrate or fresh frozen plasma when reversal must be immediate
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • INR and the date it was drawn — before giving the dose; warfarin is one of the few drugs where a lab value directly determines today’s dose
    • Full bleeding survey: gums, nose, skin, stool, emesis, urine, neurologic status
    • Take a complete medication and supplement history at every encounter — antibiotics, amiodarone, NSAIDs and many herbals shift the INR substantially
    • Dietary pattern: is vitamin K intake consistent, not whether they eat greens
    • Alcohol use — both acute and chronic use alter warfarin effect
    • Falls risk, and ability to manage a variable dosing schedule
    2Vitals
    • HR and BP — tachycardia with hypotension suggests blood loss
    • Neurologic assessment — sudden severe headache or confusion may be intracranial bleeding
    • No routine vital-sign hold parameter; the INR governs dosing
    3Labs
    • PT / INR — the entire safety system for this drug; frequency set by stability
    • Hemoglobin and hematocrit for occult bleeding
    • Liver function — hepatic impairment amplifies the effect
    • Note: INR applies to warfarin only, not to DOACs
    4Patient education
    • Keep vitamin K intake consistent — do not stop eating greens, just keep the amount steady week to week. What destabilises your INR is change, not vegetables
    • Never double a missed dose — call for instructions
    • Check before taking anything new, including over-the-counter drugs, antibiotics and herbal supplements. Ibuprofen is not safe just because it is sold without a prescription
    • Keep every INR appointment, even when you feel well
    • Report black tarry stools, coffee-ground vomit, blood in urine, or a sudden severe headache
    • Use a soft toothbrush and electric razor; tell your dentist before any procedure
    • Tell your provider immediately if you become pregnant
    • Carry identification stating you take warfarin
    Special populations
    • Pregnancy: contraindicated. Warfarin crosses the placenta and is teratogenic — heparin or LMWH is used instead, because they do not cross. This is a defining difference between the anticoagulants.
    • Older adults: more sensitive at lower doses, higher bleeding and fall risk, and often on interacting drugs — lower starting doses and closer INR monitoring.
    • Patients starting or stopping any antibiotic: antibiotics disturb gut flora that produce vitamin K and interfere with metabolism — INR can swing sharply, so a check is usually needed.
    • Liver disease: clotting factors are made in the liver, so impairment amplifies the effect unpredictably.
    • Unstable diet, alcohol use disorder, or food insecurity: consistency is the whole strategy — if intake cannot be kept steady, warfarin may be the wrong drug and that is worth raising.
    • Mechanical heart valves: warfarin is required — DOACs are not an acceptable substitute here.
    Direct oral anticoagulants
    DOACsapixaban · rivaroxaban · dabigatran
    Example drugsapixaban · rivaroxaban · dabigatran
    Mechanism of action
    • Directly inhibit a single clotting factor — apixaban and rivaroxaban block factor Xa; dabigatran blocks thrombin
    • Effect is immediate and predictable, so no routine INR titration
    • Short half-life — protection fades quickly when a dose is missed
    • Largely renally cleared, so kidney function drives dosing
    Therapeutic uses
    • Stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation
    • Treatment and prevention of DVT and PE
    • VTE prophylaxis after hip or knee replacement
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: bruising, minor bleeding
    • Serious: major bleeding — GI and intracranial; higher GI bleeding risk than warfarin with some agents
    • Reversal: specific agents exist — andexanet alfa for apixaban and rivaroxaban, idarucizumab for dabigatran. Vitamin K does not reverse a DOAC
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Renal function before starting and periodically — dosing depends on it and these drugs accumulate as kidneys decline
    • Assess adherence honestly and specifically — with a short half-life, a couple of missed doses leaves the patient unprotected within a day; ask how many doses were missed this week, not whether they take it
    • Full bleeding survey
    • Weight and age — both feed dose selection for apixaban
    • Upcoming procedures — these are held on a defined schedule before surgery
    • Review other bleeding-risk drugs
    2Vitals
    • HR and BP for signs of blood loss
    • Neurologic status — sudden severe headache or confusion
    • No vital-sign-based hold parameter
    3Labs
    • Creatinine and creatinine clearance — the lab that governs dosing
    • Hemoglobin and hematocrit for occult bleeding
    • Routine INR is NOT used and must not be interpreted as a measure of effect — a normal INR in a DOAC patient means nothing about their anticoagulation
    • Liver function periodically
    4Patient education
    • Take it exactly as prescribed, at the same times — missing doses removes your protection within about a day, much faster than older blood thinners
    • Rivaroxaban is usually taken with food; apixaban may be taken with or without
    • Tell every clinician and dentist before any procedure — this is usually stopped a few days beforehand
    • Report unusual bleeding, black tarry stools, coffee-ground vomit, or a sudden severe headache
    • Do not stop it on your own — stopping abruptly raises stroke risk
    • You will not need regular INR blood tests, but you do need kidney function checked
    • Carry identification stating you take an anticoagulant
    Special populations
    • Renal impairment: the central safety issue — these are renally cleared, so declining function raises drug levels and bleeding risk; doses are reduced and creatinine followed. Severe impairment may make a DOAC inappropriate.
    • Mechanical heart valves or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis: contraindicated — warfarin is required; DOACs performed worse in trials.
    • Older adults with low body weight: apixaban dosing is reduced when age, weight and creatinine criteria are met — verify the dose matches the patient rather than assuming.
    • Poor adherence or unstable housing: the short half-life makes missed doses more dangerous than with warfarin — a patient who struggles with daily dosing may be safer on a monitored drug.
    • Pregnancy: not recommended — safety is not established; LMWH is used instead.
    • Patients expecting an INR: reassure them that no INR is needed — and make sure the care team does not misread a normal INR as inadequate anticoagulation.
    Thrombolytics
    fibrinolyticsalteplase · tenecteplase
    Example drugsalteplase · tenecteplase
    Mechanism of action
    • Convert plasminogen to plasmin, which digests the fibrin mesh of a clot that already exists
    • This is the only class that dissolves clot — anticoagulants merely prevent formation and extension
    • Cannot distinguish a pathological clot from one sealing a wound or vessel, which is the source of the bleeding risk
    • Very short half-life; effect is immediate and time-critical
    Therapeutic uses
    • Selected acute ischemic stroke within the treatment window
    • Massive or high-risk pulmonary embolism
    • STEMI where percutaneous intervention is unavailable
    • Occluded central venous catheters (low dose)
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: minor bleeding, oozing from puncture sites
    • Serious: major bleeding — above all intracranial hemorrhage; angioedema; reperfusion dysrhythmias
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Complete the eligibility screen before administration — recent surgery, recent bleeding, prior intracranial hemorrhage, uncontrolled hypertension, and the time of symptom onset
    • Confirm the stroke is ischemic, not hemorrhagic, by imaging — giving this into a brain bleed is catastrophic
    • Establish last known well time — the therapy is time-limited and this single fact decides eligibility
    • Baseline neurologic assessment for comparison
    • Minimise punctures, injections and invasive lines before and during therapy
    • Identify every other anticoagulant or antiplatelet the patient has had
    2Vitals
    • Frequent neurologic checks on a defined schedule — a decline may be intracranial bleeding
    • BP on a strict protocol — uncontrolled hypertension sharply raises hemorrhage risk and must be treated before and during
    • HR and rhythm — reperfusion dysrhythmias
    • Puncture sites, gums and urine for bleeding
    3Labs
    • Type and crossmatch, hemoglobin and hematocrit before administration
    • Platelets and coagulation studies as part of eligibility
    • Glucose — hypoglycemia can mimic stroke and must be excluded
    • Renal function before contrast imaging
    4Patient education
    • This medicine dissolves the clot causing the stroke, and its main risk is bleeding — including into the brain
    • Tell us immediately about any sudden headache, new weakness, confusion, or nausea and vomiting
    • You will be checked very frequently for several hours; that is expected
    • Stay in bed and do not get up without help
    • Report bleeding from the gums, nose or any puncture site
    • For family: time matters enormously — note when the person was last seen normal, because that determines what treatment is possible
    Special populations
    • Hemorrhagic stroke: absolute contraindication — imaging must exclude it first. This is the single most important screening step.
    • Recent surgery, trauma, or active internal bleeding: contraindicated — the drug dissolves protective clot as readily as pathological clot.
    • Uncontrolled hypertension: greatly increases intracranial hemorrhage risk; BP must be brought within protocol limits before administration.
    • Older adults: higher intracranial hemorrhage risk, though benefit may still outweigh it — age alone is not an automatic exclusion, and the decision belongs to the team.
    • Outside the treatment window: benefit falls and hemorrhage risk rises — this is why last-known-well time is the pivotal assessment.
    • On an anticoagulant already: recent DOAC or warfarin use with a raised INR usually excludes the patient.
    Iron supplementsferrous sulfate · ferrous gluconate
    Example drugsferrous sulfate · ferrous gluconate
    Mechanism of action
    • Supplies the iron required to synthesise hemoglobin
    • Absorbed in the duodenum; absorption is better on an empty stomach and in an acidic environment
    • Vitamin C enhances absorption; calcium, antacids, dairy, tea and coffee reduce it
    • Unabsorbed iron in the gut is what darkens stool
    Therapeutic uses
    • Iron-deficiency anemia
    • Pregnancy supplementation
    • Chronic blood loss — heavy menstruation, GI bleeding
    • Supporting erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, which cannot work without iron
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: dark or greenish-black stools, constipation, nausea, metallic taste, abdominal discomfort
    • Serious: severe constipation or impaction; acute iron overdose is a leading cause of poisoning death in young children; tooth staining with liquid forms
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Distinguish expected dark stool from melena — ask about consistency, smell, and above all about symptoms: dizziness, weakness, pallor. Formed dark stool in a well patient is the drug; black tarry foul stool with dizziness is bleeding
    • Establish why the patient is iron deficient — in an adult, unexplained iron deficiency may be occult GI blood loss, and replacing iron without finding the cause treats the number rather than the patient
    • Bowel pattern before and during therapy
    • Ability to tolerate the dose; GI upset is the main reason patients stop
    • Review calcium supplements, antacids and dairy timing
    • Storage safety if there are children in the home
    2Vitals
    • No specific vital-sign parameter
    • HR and BP — tachycardia and orthostatic change suggest ongoing blood loss rather than simple deficiency
    • Assess fatigue and activity tolerance as the clinical response
    3Labs
    • Hemoglobin and hematocrit — a rise takes weeks; reticulocytes rise within about a week and are the earliest sign it is working
    • Ferritin, serum iron, transferrin saturation — ferritin reflects stores, which take months to refill
    • Stool for occult blood where GI loss is suspected
    • CBC indices — iron deficiency gives small, pale cells, unlike the large cells of B12 or folate deficiency
    4Patient education
    • Dark stools are expected and not a cause for alarm — but call if stools become black and tarry and you feel dizzy, weak or short of breath
    • Constipation is common — increase fluids and fibre, stay active, and ask about a stool softener rather than stopping the iron
    • Take it with orange juice or a vitamin C source to absorb more; separate it from antacids, calcium, dairy, tea and coffee by about two hours
    • If it upsets your stomach, taking it with food helps — you absorb a little less, but a dose you can tolerate beats one you stop
    • Liquid iron stains teeth — dilute it and drink through a straw, then rinse
    • Keep it locked away from children — the tablets look like sweets and an overdose can kill a small child
    • It takes weeks to feel better and months to refill your stores — keep taking it as prescribed
    Special populations
    • Young children in the home: accidental iron ingestion is a leading cause of poisoning death in children under 6 — child-resistant container, stored out of sight and reach. Teach this to every household, not only to parents of patients.
    • Older adults: constipation is more severe and can progress to impaction; polypharmacy with calcium and antacids reduces absorption — review timing and start a bowel plan proactively.
    • Adults with unexplained iron deficiency: think occult GI blood loss — including from the aspirin or anticoagulant on their own medication list. Iron alone would mask the picture.
    • Pregnancy: requirements rise substantially and supplementation is routine; constipation is already common, so the bowel plan matters more.
    • Patients on epoetin: erythropoiesis cannot proceed without iron — iron status is monitored alongside hemoglobin.
    • Inflammatory bowel disease or after gastric surgery: oral absorption may be inadequate and IV iron may be required.
    Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents
    plus B12 and folateepoetin alfa · cyanocobalamin (B12) · folic acid
    Example drugsepoetin alfa · cyanocobalamin (B12) · folic acid
    Mechanism of action
    • Epoetin alfa replaces the erythropoietin that failing kidneys no longer produce → stimulates marrow red cell production
    • Vitamin B12 and folic acid are required for DNA synthesis in developing red cells; deficiency of either causes megaloblastic anemia with large, immature cells
    • Only B12 is also required for myelin — which is why only B12 deficiency causes neurologic damage
    • Epoetin cannot work without adequate iron
    Therapeutic uses
    • Epoetin: anemia of chronic kidney disease; chemotherapy-associated anemia
    • B12: pernicious anemia, malabsorption, after gastric surgery, strict vegan diet
    • Folate: deficiency states, alcohol use disorder, pregnancy (neural tube defect prevention)
    Side & adverse effects
    • Epoetin — common: hypertension, headache, injection-site reactions, flu-like symptoms
    • Epoetin — serious: thrombosis, MI, stroke and death if hemoglobin rises too high or too fast; seizures; tumour progression in some cancers
    • B12 and folate: generally well tolerated; hypokalemia can occur early in treatment as potassium is consumed by rapid cell production
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Establish the cause of the anemia before treating it — iron, B12, folate and erythropoietin deficiency look similar on a hemoglobin value and are not interchangeable
    • Assess for neurologic signs before giving folate: numbness, tingling, balance problems, confusion. Folate will correct the blood count of a B12-deficient patient while neurologic injury continues and becomes permanent
    • Blood pressure before each epoetin dose — hypertension is the most common adverse effect and a reason to hold
    • Iron status before and during epoetin — the drug fails without it
    • Ask about diet, alcohol use, gastric surgery and vegan diet as deficiency clues
    • Assess fatigue, dyspnea and activity tolerance as the clinical endpoint
    2Vitals
    • Blood pressure before every epoetin dose and between doses — report a rising trend
    • HR and respiratory status as measures of anemia severity
    • Assess for signs of thrombosis: unilateral leg pain or swelling, chest pain, dyspnea, new neurologic deficit
    3Labs
    • Hemoglobin and hematocrit — watching the rate of rise, not just the value; too fast is the danger
    • Iron studies — ferritin and transferrin saturation — before and during epoetin
    • Serum B12 and folate to identify which deficiency is present
    • Potassium early in B12 replacement — rapid erythropoiesis can drop it
    • Reticulocyte count as the earliest evidence of response
    4Patient education
    • This will not work overnight — it takes weeks to see a change, and stopping early because you feel no different is the commonest mistake
    • The goal is a safe hemoglobin, not the highest possible one — pushing it too high causes strokes and blood clots
    • Have your blood pressure checked regularly and report headaches
    • Report leg pain or swelling, chest pain, shortness of breath, or new weakness or trouble speaking — these can mean a clot
    • Keep taking your iron — your body cannot make red cells without it
    • B12 by injection is usually lifelong if your body cannot absorb it from food — the problem is absorption, so tablets will not fix it
    • Report numbness, tingling or unsteadiness
    Special populations
    • B12 deficiency treated with folate alone: the anemia improves while neurologic damage progresses silently and can become irreversible — always establish which deficiency is present before treating. This is the highest-stakes distinction in the section.
    • Pernicious anemia or after gastric surgery: intrinsic factor is absent, so oral B12 cannot be absorbed — parenteral replacement is required, usually for life.
    • Epoetin in cancer: associated with shortened survival and tumour progression in some malignancies — used only in defined situations and not to normalise hemoglobin.
    • Uncontrolled hypertension: epoetin raises BP and is contraindicated until BP is controlled; seizures have occurred with rapid rises.
    • Iron-deficient patients: epoetin cannot work without iron and will appear to fail — iron status must be corrected alongside.
    • Pregnancy: folic acid supplementation before and during early pregnancy reduces neural tube defects — a public-health-level teaching point, not just a treatment.
    • Alcohol use disorder: a common cause of folate deficiency, and nutritional assessment matters as much as the supplement.

    Read the bleeding classes together. Open antiplatelets, heparins, warfarin and DOACs and compare only the labs rows: platelets, INR, renal function, and “no routine lab.” Four drugs that all cause bleeding, monitored four different ways — which is exactly what makes “blood thinner” a dangerous shorthand.

    Sources. Karch’s Focus on Nursing Pharmacology, 10th ed. (Tucker), Ch 45–49; Dr. Kaur’s NURS-11 Week 6 Day 2 deck and her cited references (NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN® test plan, DailyMed prescribing information); AGS Beers Criteria® for the older-adult notes. No commercial study sites were used.

    Ch 53 · Wk 8 slides 3–9

    1The respiratory system — and the one line that links it to the autonomic unit

    Her objectives open with structure and function because every drug in this unit either opens the airway or calms the inflammation. Knowing where each acts tells you what to assess.

    RegionStructuresWhat it doesWhy it matters for drugs
    Upper tractNose, mouth, pharynx, larynxWarms, filters and humidifies airTarget of decongestants, antihistamines, nasal steroids, antitussives
    Conducting airwaysTrachea → bronchi → bronchiolesMove air; cleared by the mucociliary escalator — cilia and mucus togetherWhere expectorants and mucolytics work, and where bronchodilators relax smooth muscle
    AlveoliAlveolar sacs, pulmonary capillariesThe functional unit — site of gas exchange. Needs surfactant to reduce surface tensionTarget of surfactant replacement; where failure shows as hypoxemia
    Control of ventilationDetail
    DriveControlled by the medulla and pons
    SensorsChemoreceptors respond to CO₂ and pH — not primarily to oxygen
    SympatheticBronchodilation — the airway opens
    ParasympatheticBronchoconstriction — the airway narrows

    This is the autonomic unit again, applied to the lung. Sympathetic → bronchodilation is why β2 agonists open airways. Parasympathetic → bronchoconstriction is why anticholinergics also open them — by blocking the constricting signal rather than sending a dilating one. Two drug classes, two different routes to the same result, and both derivable from α1 β1 β2 M rather than memorised. It also explains why a cholinergic drug is risky in asthma and why a nonselective beta blocker can cause bronchospasm.

    The mucociliary escalator explains two drug decisions. Cilia sweep mucus upward so it can be coughed out. That is why a productive cough is usually left alone and an expectorant is given to thin secretions — and why suppressing a cough that is clearing something is the wrong move. Her nursing slide puts it first: assess the infection before suppressing the cough.

    Ch 53 · Wk 8 slides 10–12

    2Oxygenation, hypoxia and the disorders behind the drugs

    Her objective is to recognise early and late signs of hypoxia. The early signs are the ones that get missed, because they look like anxiety rather than suffocation.

    MeasureValueWhat it tells you
    SpO₂Normal 95–100%; goal ≥ 92% in illnessOxygen saturation of hemoglobin — a bedside screen, not a ventilation measure
    ABG — PaO₂Arterial oxygenOxygenation
    ABG — PaCO₂Arterial carbon dioxideVentilation — how well air is moving, which SpO₂ cannot show
    Early hypoxiaLate hypoxia
    Restlessness · anxiety · tachycardia · pallor
    the body compensating — and the stage where intervention works    		Cyanosis · confusion · bradycardia · respiratory distress
    compensation failing — bradycardia here is a pre-arrest sign
