    The trap worth rehearsing. Early hypoxia looks like agitation. A restless, anxious patient with a rising heart rate is reaching for air, and the instinct to reassure or sedate is exactly wrong. Equally, a patient who becomes quiet, drowsy and bradycardic has not settled — they have deteriorated. Rising calm in a breathless patient is an emergency, not an improvement.

    TermMeaning
    HypoxiaLow oxygen in the tissues
    HypoxemiaLow oxygen in arterial blood
    DisorderWhat goes wrongDrug relevance
    AtelectasisAlveolar collapseMucolytics for mucus plugging; incentive spirometry
    AsthmaReversible inflammation and bronchospasmRescue bronchodilator + inhaled steroid control
    COPDChronic, progressive obstruction — emphysema plus chronic bronchitisLAMA maintenance; bronchodilators; the word chronic is the contrast with asthma
    Cystic fibrosisThick secretions, recurrent infectionDornase alfa and acetylcysteine
    ARDSSevere inflammation, falling lung complianceSupportive; surfactant damage is the mechanism
    Neonatal RDSSurfactant deficiencySurfactant replacement — beractant, calfactant

    Her memory connection, worth keeping: low surfactant → alveolar collapse → impaired gas exchange; surfactant replacement → improved alveolar stability. The same chain explains why ARDS is so hard to treat — the surfactant is damaged rather than simply absent.

    Ch 54 · Wk 8 slides 13–21, 38

    3Upper respiratory drugs — five classes, five different jobs

    Her five classes, in her order. The common student error is treating them as interchangeable cold remedies; each does something specific, and two of them work against each other.

    ClassExamplesActionSignature nursing point
    Antitussivesdextromethorphan · codeine · benzonatateSuppress the cough centre in the medulla, or anaesthetise airway stretch receptorsOnly for dry, unproductive cough. Avoid when airway clearance is needed
    Decongestantspseudoephedrine · oxymetazolineVasoconstriction → shrink swollen nasal tissueCheck BP and HR — caution in hypertension. Topical overuse → rebound congestion
    Antihistaminesdiphenhydramine · loratadine · cetirizine · fexofenadineBlock histamine → less sneezing, itching, watery eyes, rhinorrheaFirst generation sedates and is anticholinergic; avoid alcohol and driving
    ExpectorantsguaifenesinThin mucus so a cough can move itIncrease fluid intake; avoid long-term use
    Mucolyticsacetylcysteine · dornase alfaBreak down thick mucus directlyGiven by inhalation; may trigger bronchospasm — monitor respiratory response
    Intranasal corticosteroidsfluticasone · budesonide · triamcinoloneReduce nasal inflammation and mucosal swellingWorks only with consistent daily use; aim away from the septum; watch for epistaxis

    Expectorant versus mucolytic — her two mucus drugs do different things. Guaifenesin is oral and makes secretions thinner so the patient’s own cough clears them, which is why fluids matter. Acetylcysteine is inhaled and chemically breaks the mucus apart, which is why it is used in cystic fibrosis and mucus plugging — and why it can irritate the airway into bronchospasm. One assists a cough; the other dissolves the problem.

    Two decongestant traps. Pseudoephedrine is a sympathomimetic — it constricts vessels everywhere, not just the nose, so blood pressure and heart rate can rise. In a hypertensive patient that is the finding to act on. Oxymetazoline is topical and causes rebound congestion when used beyond about three days: the patient feels blocked, sprays more, and gets worse. Ask how long a nasal spray has been in use.

    Nasal steroid versus topical decongestant — her stated key point. The steroid is anti-inflammatory therapy that builds over days; it is not the immediate relief a decongestant gives. A patient who expects instant unblocking will declare it useless and stop. Set the expectation when you teach it.

    Her nursing focus tableAssess / concernKey teaching
    BenzonatateIs cough suppression appropriate?Swallow whole
    PseudoephedrineBP and HRCaution with hypertension
    DiphenhydramineSedation, anticholinergic effectsAvoid alcohol and driving
    GuaifenesinAbility to clear mucusFluids if appropriate
    AcetylcysteineBronchospasmMonitor respiratory response

    Why benzonatate must be swallowed whole. It works by anaesthetising stretch receptors in the airway. Chewed or sucked, it numbs the mouth and throat instead — causing loss of the gag reflex, choking, and in children severe toxicity. It is on her slide as a teaching point and appears in her own practice question; the reason is what makes it stick.

    Her nursing considerations, condensed. Assess for infection before suppressing a cough · monitor BP and HR with decongestants · avoid stacking combination OTC products, which duplicate ingredients · encourage fluids for mucus clearance · teach correct spray and inhaler technique · and warn about driving on sedating antihistamines.

    Ch 55 · Wk 8 slides 25–28

    4Bronchodilators — three ways to open an airway

    Her three bronchodilator groups. Two of them come straight out of the autonomic unit; the third is the one with a narrow therapeutic index.

    GroupDrugsHow it opens the airwayRole
    β2 agonists — SABA
    short-acting    		albuterolStimulates β2 → smooth muscle relaxesRapid relief / rescue — acute bronchospasm
    β2 agonists — LABA
    long-acting    		salmeterol · formoterolSame receptor, longer durationMaintenance only. In asthma, used as part of an ICS-containing plan
    Anticholinergic — SAMAipratropiumBlocks muscarinic → removes the constricting signalShort-acting; COPD; adjunct during acute exacerbations
    Anticholinergic — LAMAtiotropiumSame mechanism, long-actingMaintenance — especially important in COPD
    Xanthinestheophylline · aminophyllineRelaxes smooth muscle directlyAsthma and COPD — rarely first-line; requires level monitoring

    Two mechanisms, one result — and it is the ANS unit again. Sympathetic stimulation dilates the airway, so a β2 agonist pushes the accelerator. Parasympathetic activity constricts it, so an anticholinergic releases the brake. That is why the two classes are combined in COPD: they open the airway by different routes, and their effects add. It also explains their side effects — β2 agonists give tremor and tachycardia, anticholinergics give dry mouth.

    Theophylline — the one to respectDetail
    Therapeutic range10–20 mcg/mL — a narrow therapeutic index; monitor serum levels when ordered
    Early toxicityNausea and vomiting · restlessness · tachycardia — the stage where it is still reversible
    Serious toxicityTachyarrhythmias · seizures
    TeachingAvoid excess caffeine — it is chemically related and the effects add. Changes in smoking or nicotine use alter metabolism and drug levels

    The smoking detail is a real exam point. Smoking induces the enzymes that clear theophylline, so a smoker needs a higher dose to stay in range. If that patient stops smoking — during an admission, for instance — clearance falls and the same dose can become toxic. A change in smoking status is a reason to recheck a level, not a reason to relax.

    Rescue versus maintenance, her stated key point. Albuterol relieves; salmeterol, formoterol and tiotropium prevent. Reaching for a long-acting inhaler during an attack wastes the minutes that matter. And frequent rescue-inhaler use is itself a finding — it signals poor control and the need for reassessment, not simply a refill.

    Ch 55 · Wk 8 slides 29–32

    5Controllers — inflammation is the other half of the disease

    Bronchodilators relax the muscle. These reduce the inflammation, edema, mucus and hyperresponsiveness underneath it. Her summary line for the whole unit: relax the airway and reduce inflammation.

    Inhaled corticosteroidsDetail
    Examplesfluticasone · budesonide · beclomethasone
    ActionReduce airway inflammation, edema, mucus and hyperresponsiveness
    UseLong-term control — NOT for immediate relief. Acute bronchospasm needs rapid bronchodilation, not an extra steroid dose
    Local effectsOral candidiasis · hoarseness · throat irritation
    TeachingUse consistently; rinse the mouth and spit after each dose; correct inhaler technique
    Evidence it worksFewer symptoms and exacerbations, and less rescue-medication use

    Why rinse and spit, and why it is not optional. Inhaled steroid that settles in the mouth suppresses local immunity, letting Candida overgrow — the white patches and hoarseness on her slide. Rinsing removes the residue; spitting rather than swallowing avoids the swallowed fraction. It takes five seconds and prevents the commonest reason patients abandon a controller.

    Montelukast — leukotriene modifierDetail
    ActionBlocks leukotriene effects → less inflammation, bronchoconstriction, mucus and edema
    RoleMaintenance and prevention — NOT a rescue medication
    Critical safety teachingReport new or worsening agitation, unusual dreams, mood changes, depression, behavioural changes, or suicidal thoughts

    Her clinical-judgement line, and it is the one to carry into the exam: a new neuropsychiatric change deserves priority follow-up even if the patient also reports minor expected medication effects. Put plainly — when a montelukast patient reports a headache, dry mouth, a mild tremor and new agitation or disturbing dreams, the mood change is the answer. The other findings are real but expected; this one carries a boxed warning.

    Recognition level onlyRoleWhat she wants you to know
    Biologics
    omalizumab · dupilumab    		Target specific immune pathways in severe asthma; add-on when control fails on standard therapyClass, general role, injection route, hypersensitivity risk. Not rescue. Her instruction: do not over-focus on immune pathways
    CromolynMast-cell stabiliser — prevents release of inflammatory mediatorsPreventive; rarely used today
    Surfactants
    beractant · calfactant    		Reduce alveolar surface tension, keeping alveoli openNeonatal RDS

    These three are flagged recognition level on her own slides — know the class, the role and the route, and spend your study time on albuterol, the inhaled steroids, montelukast and theophylline instead.

    Ch 55 · Wk 8 slides 33–37, 39

    6Matching drug to moment — and getting the inhaler right

    Her clinical shortcut for the whole unit: is the patient having symptoms NOW, or are we preventing future symptoms? Almost every respiratory question resolves to that one distinction.

    The needThe therapyWhy not the others
    Acute symptoms nowRapid bronchodilator — albuterolA steroid or a LABA takes too long; using one here costs time the patient does not have
    Daily inflammation controlICS-containing therapyA rescue inhaler treats symptoms without touching the inflammation causing them
    Persistent symptomsAdd long-acting controller therapyEscalating rescue use is a control failure, not a dosing solution
    Severe / uncontrolledSpecialist-directed add-on or biologicReserved for disease that fails standard therapy
    StepInhaler sequenceWhy
    01Bronchodilator first, when separate inhalers are prescribed and bronchodilation is indicatedOpening the airway lets the second drug reach deeper lung
    02Follow the prescribed, device-specific intervalHer explicit caution: avoid teaching one universal wait time. Devices differ — follow the instructions for the one the patient has
    03Then the inhaled corticosteroidThe controller reaches an airway that is already open
    04Rinse the mouth and spit after the ICSReduces oral candidiasis and irritation
    05Use a spacer when prescribedImproves delivery; follow device-specific instructions
    Drug / classAssessExpectedRed flagTeaching
    AlbuterolHR, RR, lung sounds, work of breathingTremor, mild tachycardiaWorsening distress or poor air movementRescue medication
    Inhaled steroidMouth, voice, symptomsHoarsenessThrushRinse and spit
    TheophyllineSymptoms and levels—Vomiting, arrhythmia, seizureAvoid excess caffeine
    MontelukastMood and behaviourHeadacheNeuropsychiatric changeMaintenance, not rescue
    AnticholinergicsLung sounds, dry mouthDry mouthIncorrect rescue use; eye exposureSAMA vs LAMA

    The most dangerous reassessment finding in this unit. Fifteen minutes after albuterol, a rising heart rate and a hand tremor are expected. Wheezing that persists while air movement improves is progress. But increasing drowsiness with diminished breath sounds is the one to act on — a quiet chest in an asthmatic means too little air is moving to make a wheeze, and the drowsiness is late hypoxia with rising CO₂. The silent chest is the emergency.

    Her one-line recap: RELAX the airway + REDUCE inflammation. Every drug in the lower-tract list does one or the other, and knowing which tells you whether it belongs in an emergency or on a daily schedule.

    Ch 53–55 · med chart

    Medication chart — respiratory drugs

    Eleven classes in the same rubric format: example drugs, mechanism, uses, effects, nursing considerations in the four required parts — assessment vitals labs education — and specific special populations.

    Beta-2 agonists — SABA
    rescuealbuterol · levalbuterol
    Example drugsalbuterol · levalbuterol
    Mechanism of action
    • Stimulate β2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle → the airway relaxes and opens
    • Rapid onset — relief within minutes
    • Also drives potassium into cells, so serum K⁺ can fall
    • Sympathetic stimulation dilates the airway: this is the autonomic unit applied to the lung
    Therapeutic uses
    • Acute bronchospasm — the rescue drug
    • Exercise-induced bronchospasm
    • Acute COPD exacerbation
    • Adjunct in hyperkalemia
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: tremor, tachycardia, palpitations, jitteriness, headache
    • Serious: paradoxical bronchospasm, dysrhythmia, hypokalemia, chest pain
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Lung sounds, respiratory rate, work of breathing and ability to speak in full sentences — before and after every dose
    • Count how often the rescue inhaler is being used — more than about twice a week signals poor control and needs reassessment, not a refill
    • Check inhaler technique and whether a spacer is prescribed
    • Peak flow before and after where ordered
    • After treatment, reassess for the silent chest — drowsiness with diminished breath sounds means too little air is moving to wheeze
    2Vitals
    • RR and SpO2 before and 15–20 minutes after — the goal is measurable improvement in air movement
    • HR before and after; a modest rise is expected, report a jump above 120 or new irregularity
    • BP for a rise at higher doses
    3Labs
    • Serum potassium — β2 agonists shift K⁺ intracellularly, which matters if the patient is also on a diuretic
    • Blood glucose in diabetes — may rise
    • ABG in a severe exacerbation — PaCO2 shows ventilation, which SpO2 cannot
    • Theophylline level if co-prescribed
    4Patient education
    • This is your rescue inhaler — it is the one you reach for when you cannot breathe
    • Shakiness and a fast heartbeat are expected and usually settle; they mean the drug is working, not harming you
    • If you need it more often than usual, call — do not just keep using it. Needing it more means the asthma is getting worse
    • Rinse your mouth afterwards and prime a new inhaler before first use
    • Track your doses so you never find it empty during an attack
    • Carry it with you at all times
    Special populations
    • Older adults: higher risk of tachydysrhythmia and of tremor that interferes with holding and firing the device — assess grip strength and consider a spacer or nebuliser.
    • Cardiac disease: tachycardia raises myocardial oxygen demand and can provoke angina; levalbuterol has fewer cardiac effects.
    • Diabetes: may raise blood glucose during frequent dosing.
    • Pregnancy: treatment continues — uncontrolled asthma causes fetal hypoxia, which is the greater risk.
    • Patients on diuretics: additive potassium loss — check K⁺ before repeated dosing.
    • Anyone relying on it daily: frequent rescue use is a disease-control finding and must be escalated rather than accommodated.
    Beta-2 agonists — LABA
    maintenancesalmeterol · formoterol
    Example drugssalmeterol · formoterol
    Mechanism of action
    • Same β2 receptor as albuterol, but a long duration of action
    • Provides sustained bronchodilation rather than rapid relief
    • Onset is too slow to treat an attack
    Therapeutic uses
    • Maintenance bronchodilation in asthma — as part of an ICS-containing plan
    • COPD maintenance therapy
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: tremor, tachycardia, headache, throat irritation
    • Serious: dysrhythmia; in asthma, use without an inhaled corticosteroid has been associated with serious outcomes, which is why it is never a lone asthma therapy
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Confirm an inhaled corticosteroid is also prescribed when the indication is asthma — a LABA alone is the error to catch
    • Confirm the patient knows this is not the rescue inhaler and can say which device they would use in an attack
    • Baseline lung sounds, symptom frequency and night-time waking
    • Inhaler technique and adherence to a scheduled regimen
    • Rescue inhaler use frequency — rising use means the controller is not holding
    2Vitals
    • RR, SpO2 and lung sounds at routine assessment
    • HR for tachycardia, particularly if a SABA is also being used often
    • Symptom and exacerbation frequency over time rather than minute-to-minute response
    3Labs
    • Potassium if also on a diuretic or using frequent SABA
    • Blood glucose in diabetes
    • No routine drug level
    4Patient education
    • This is a scheduled, every-day medicine — it will not help an attack
    • Keep using your rescue inhaler for sudden symptoms; this one does not replace it
    • Take it even on days you feel well; stopping is how control is lost
    • In asthma this works alongside your steroid inhaler — do not use it on its own
    • Report increasing need for your rescue inhaler
    • Rinse the mouth after use
    Special populations
    • Asthma without a concurrent inhaled corticosteroid: do not give. LABA monotherapy in asthma is the specific combination to question — her slide states it must be part of an ICS-containing plan.
    • Any patient who believes this is a rescue inhaler: a dangerous misunderstanding — verify by asking which inhaler they would use if they could not breathe.
    • Older adults: tachydysrhythmia risk and device-handling difficulty.
    • Cardiac disease: added myocardial oxygen demand.
    • COPD: used as maintenance and the ICS requirement differs from asthma — follow the prescribed regimen.
    • Poor adherence: a scheduled controller that is taken erratically gives neither prevention nor rescue.
    Anticholinergic bronchodilators
    SAMA & LAMAipratropium · tiotropium
    Example drugsipratropium · tiotropium
    Mechanism of action
    • Block muscarinic receptors → removes the parasympathetic constricting signal → airway widens
    • A different route to the same result as a β2 agonist, which is why the two combine well
    • Ipratropium is short-acting (SAMA); tiotropium is long-acting (LAMA)
    • Also dries airway secretions
    Therapeutic uses
    • COPD — tiotropium for maintenance
    • Ipratropium as an adjunct during acute exacerbations
    • Asthma in selected patients
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: dry mouth, throat irritation, cough, bad taste
    • Serious: urinary retention, worsening narrow-angle glaucoma if sprayed into the eye, paradoxical bronchospasm
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Confirm which device is which — the most common error is a patient reaching for tiotropium during an acute attack
    • Lung sounds, respiratory effort and baseline exercise tolerance
    • Ask about urinary symptoms and glaucoma — the anticholinergic cautions from the autonomic unit apply here too
    • Mouth and throat for dryness and irritation
    • Inhaler or handling device technique — capsule-based devices are frequently used wrongly
    2Vitals
    • RR, SpO2 and lung sounds before and after
    • HR — less affected than with β2 agonists but worth noting
    • No specific hold parameter
    3Labs
    • Renal function — tiotropium is renally cleared
    • No routine drug level
    • Electrolytes only as part of broader care
    4Patient education
    • This one is for every day, not for an attack — keep your rescue inhaler for sudden symptoms
    • Do not let the spray get into your eyes — it can blur vision and raise eye pressure
    • Dry mouth is common — sip water, use sugar-free gum, keep up dental care
    • Rinse your mouth after using it
    • Report difficulty passing urine, or eye pain with halos around lights
    • If it is a capsule device, the capsule is inhaled, never swallowed
    Special populations
    • Benign prostatic hyperplasia: anticholinergic effect can precipitate urinary retention — ask about voiding before and during therapy.
    • Narrow-angle glaucoma: eye exposure can trigger an acute attack — teach to avoid spraying toward the eyes and to report eye pain, halos or sudden vision change immediately.
    • Older adults: more susceptible to dry mouth, urinary retention and confusion, and more likely to be on other anticholinergics — review the total anticholinergic burden.
    • COPD: tiotropium is a cornerstone of maintenance therapy — adherence matters more than in intermittent disease.
    • Renal impairment: tiotropium accumulates; monitor for increased anticholinergic effects.
    • Anyone who may confuse the devices: label them clearly — using a LAMA as a rescue inhaler delays effective treatment.
    Inhaled corticosteroids
    controllerfluticasone · budesonide · beclomethasone
    Example drugsfluticasone · budesonide · beclomethasone
    Mechanism of action
    • Reduce airway inflammation, edema, mucus production and hyperresponsiveness
    • Acts on the disease underneath the bronchospasm rather than the spasm itself
    • Takes days to weeks to reach full effect — no immediate bronchodilation
    • Inhaled delivery limits systemic exposure but deposits drug in the mouth
    Therapeutic uses
    • Long-term asthma control
    • COPD in selected patients, usually combined with a long-acting bronchodilator
    • Reducing exacerbation frequency
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and local: oral candidiasis (thrush), hoarseness, throat irritation, cough
    • Serious: with high doses or long-term use — adrenal suppression, growth velocity effects in children, reduced bone density, cataracts
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Inspect the mouth and throat for white patches and ask about voice change at every encounter — thrush is the reason patients quietly stop
    • Confirm the patient knows this is not the rescue inhaler and would not reach for it in an attack
    • Confirm they rinse and spit — ask them to describe what they do, not whether they do it
    • Symptom frequency, night waking and rescue-inhaler use as evidence of control
    • Inhaler technique and spacer use
    • Adherence — a controller taken intermittently does not control
    2Vitals
    • RR, SpO2 and lung sounds at routine assessment
    • Growth measurement in children on long-term therapy
    • No dose is withheld on a vital sign — this is scheduled therapy
    3Labs
    • Usually none routinely for inhaled therapy
    • Blood glucose if high-dose or systemic steroid is added
    • Bone density with prolonged high-dose use
    4Patient education
    • Use it every day, even when you feel completely well — it prevents attacks rather than treating them
    • Rinse your mouth and spit after every dose — this prevents a mouth infection and hoarseness
    • This is not your rescue inhaler. If you cannot breathe, use the rapid one
    • Report white patches in the mouth or a hoarse voice that does not settle
    • You may not feel it working — the benefit shows as fewer attacks and less rescue-inhaler use
    • Do not stop because you have been well for a few days; that is the drug working
    Special populations
    • Anyone who thinks it provides immediate relief: the single most dangerous misunderstanding — her slide states acute bronchospasm needs rapid bronchodilation, not an extra steroid dose.
    • Children: monitor growth velocity on long-term therapy; use the lowest effective dose with a spacer.
    • Older adults: higher risk of oral candidiasis from dry mouth and of cataracts with prolonged use; dexterity may require a spacer.
    • Patients with diabetes: glucose can rise, particularly at higher doses or if oral steroid is added.
    • Anyone with poor technique: the dose lands in the mouth instead of the lung — this produces both treatment failure and thrush, so technique is checked rather than assumed.
    • Immunosuppressed patients: greater risk of oral and respiratory infection.
    Leukotriene receptor antagonistmontelukast
    Example drugssingle-agent class montelukast
    Mechanism of action
    • Blocks leukotriene receptors → reduces inflammation, bronchoconstriction, mucus and edema
    • Oral tablet rather than inhaled — useful where inhaler technique is a barrier
    • Maintenance and prevention only — no rescue effect
    Therapeutic uses
    • Long-term asthma control, often as add-on therapy
    • Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction
    • Allergic rhinitis
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: headache, abdominal pain, cough
    • Serious — boxed warning: neuropsychiatric events — agitation, unusual or disturbing dreams, mood change, depression, behavioural change, and suicidal thinking
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Ask directly about mood, sleep, dreams and behaviour at every encounter — patients and families rarely connect a mood change to an asthma tablet
    • In children and teenagers, ask the parent as well — behavioural change is often noticed by someone else first
    • Establish a baseline for mood and behaviour before starting, so a change is detectable
    • Confirm the patient understands this does not treat an attack
    • Symptom frequency and rescue-inhaler use as evidence it is working
    • Any history of depression or anxiety before therapy begins
    2Vitals
    • RR, SpO2 and lung sounds at routine assessment
    • No vital-sign hold parameter — the monitoring here is behavioural rather than haemodynamic
    3Labs
    • No routine drug level or lab monitoring
    • Liver enzymes only if symptoms suggest hepatic involvement
    4Patient education
    • Report any new agitation, unusual or disturbing dreams, low mood, changes in behaviour, or thoughts of harming yourself — straight away
    • This is a daily preventive tablet. It will not stop an attack — keep using your rescue inhaler for that
    • Take it in the evening as prescribed, consistently
    • Parents: tell us about changes in your child’s mood, sleep or behaviour, even if they seem small
    • Do not stop it abruptly without speaking to the prescriber
    • Keep taking it when you feel well — that is the point of it
    Special populations
    • Children and adolescents: the group in whom neuropsychiatric effects are most often reported and least often volunteered — ask the parent directly about mood, sleep and behaviour at every visit.
    • Any patient with a history of depression, anxiety or suicidal ideation: the prescriber must know before it is started, and monitoring is closer.
    • Anyone treating it as a rescue drug: delays effective treatment in an attack — verify understanding.
    • Patients reporting several symptoms at once: her clinical-judgement point — a new mood or behaviour change takes priority over a headache or a mild tremor, even though all are reported together.
    • Older adults: a new neuropsychiatric change may be misattributed to ageing or dementia; review the medication list.
    • Pregnancy: continued when asthma control requires it, since uncontrolled asthma harms the fetus.
    Xanthinestheophylline · aminophylline
    Example drugstheophylline · aminophylline
    Mechanism of action
    • Relax bronchial smooth muscle directly → bronchodilation
    • Narrow therapeutic index: 10–20 mcg/mL
    • Hepatically metabolised, so anything that changes those enzymes changes the level
    • Rarely first-line in current practice
    Therapeutic uses
    • Asthma and COPD when other therapy is insufficient
    • Chronic maintenance in selected patients
    Side & adverse effects
    • Early toxicity: nausea and vomiting, restlessness, tachycardia — the reversible stage
    • Serious toxicity: tachyarrhythmias and seizures
    • Common: insomnia, headache, GI upset
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Ask about nausea, vomiting, restlessness and palpitations at every encounter — these are early toxicity, not a stomach upset
    • Ask about smoking and any recent change in it — stopping smoking slows clearance and can push a stable patient into toxicity on an unchanged dose
    • Ask about caffeine intake — chemically related, and the effects add
    • Review the medication list for drugs that alter hepatic metabolism
    • Serum level when ordered, with the timing documented
    • Baseline and ongoing respiratory status
    2Vitals
    • HR and rhythm — tachycardia is an early sign and tachyarrhythmia a late one
    • RR, SpO2 and lung sounds
    • Neurological status — restlessness precedes seizure
    3Labs
    • Serum theophylline level — therapeutic 10–20 mcg/mL; the defining safety lab
    • Recheck after any dose change, any change in smoking status, or any new interacting drug
    • Liver function — impairment reduces clearance
    • Electrolytes if vomiting is significant
    4Patient education
    • Report nausea, vomiting, restlessness or a racing heart — these are early warning signs, not an upset stomach
    • Avoid excess caffeine — coffee, tea, cola and energy drinks add to the drug’s effect
    • Tell your provider if you start or stop smoking, or change how much you smoke or vape — it changes how fast your body clears this drug
    • Keep every blood-test appointment; the level is how we keep this drug safe
    • Take it at the same times each day
    • Check before starting any new medicine, including over-the-counter ones
    Special populations
    • Anyone who stops smoking while taking it: the sharpest risk — smoking induces clearance, so quitting raises the level on an unchanged dose and can produce toxicity. Common during a hospital admission, when smoking stops abruptly.
    • Older adults: reduced hepatic clearance and higher sensitivity; toxicity may present as confusion or restlessness rather than classic symptoms.
    • Hepatic impairment or heart failure: clearance falls and levels rise — doses are reduced.
    • High caffeine intake: additive stimulation; ask specifically about energy drinks in younger patients.
    • Patients on interacting drugs (some antibiotics and antifungals among them): levels can rise sharply — a level check is warranted.
    • Seizure history: toxicity lowers the threshold further; the margin for error is smaller.
    Antitussivesbenzonatate · dextromethorphan · codeine
    Example drugsbenzonatate · dextromethorphan · codeine
    Mechanism of action
    • Benzonatate anaesthetises stretch receptors in the airway
    • Dextromethorphan and codeine suppress the cough centre in the medulla
    • Reduce the urge to cough rather than treating its cause
    Therapeutic uses
    • Dry, unproductive cough that is disrupting sleep or exhausting the patient
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: drowsiness, dizziness, nausea; codeine adds constipation
    • Serious: suppression of a cough that was clearing secretions; respiratory depression with codeine; if benzonatate capsules are chewed or sucked — oropharyngeal numbness, loss of the gag reflex and choking
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Decide first whether the cough should be suppressed at all — her stated nursing focus. A productive cough is clearing something
    • Assess for infection before suppressing: fever, sputum colour and volume, lung sounds
    • Characterise the cough — dry or productive, duration, what triggers it, whether it disturbs sleep
    • Confirm the patient will swallow benzonatate capsules whole
    • Review the medication list for other sedating drugs and for duplicate OTC cough products
    2Vitals
    • RR and SpO2, particularly with codeine
    • Level of consciousness and sedation score
    • Lung sounds before and during therapy
    3Labs
    • No routine level
    • Consider sputum culture if infection is suspected
    4Patient education
    • Swallow benzonatate capsules whole — never chew, suck or break them. They numb the mouth and throat and you could choke
    • Keep this medication away from children — it is dangerous in small doses for them
    • Seek evaluation if the cough lasts or gets worse — a suppressed cough is not a treated cause
    • This may make you drowsy; avoid driving until you know how it affects you
    • Do not combine with other cough or cold products without checking
    • Tell us if you start bringing up coloured or increasing sputum
    Special populations
    • Children: benzonatate is dangerous in accidental ingestion — even one or two capsules can be fatal in a small child; storage teaching is mandatory.
    • Any patient with a productive cough or pneumonia: suppressing the cough traps secretions — the assessment comes before the drug.
    • COPD, cystic fibrosis or any condition needing airway clearance: cough suppression is generally avoided.
    • Older adults: sedation adds to fall risk, and codeine adds constipation and respiratory depression.
    • Patients on other CNS depressants or opioids: additive sedation and respiratory depression with codeine.
    • Anyone with difficulty swallowing: benzonatate is unsuitable if the capsule cannot be swallowed intact.
    Decongestantspseudoephedrine · oxymetazoline · phenylephrine
    Example drugspseudoephedrine · oxymetazoline · phenylephrine
    Mechanism of action
    • Sympathomimetic — stimulate α1 receptors → vasoconstriction in the nasal mucosa → swelling shrinks
    • Pseudoephedrine is systemic, so the vasoconstriction is not confined to the nose
    • Oxymetazoline is topical, acting locally and quickly
    Therapeutic uses
    • Nasal congestion from colds, allergic rhinitis and sinusitis
    • Short-term symptom relief
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: nervousness, insomnia, dry nasal passages, headache
    • Serious: raised blood pressure and heart rate, palpitations, dysrhythmia, urinary retention
    • Topical agents: rebound congestion with use beyond about three days
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Blood pressure and heart rate — her stated assessment, and the reason this drug is cautioned in hypertension
    • Ask how many days a nasal spray has been used — beyond about three days, worsening congestion is probably rebound, not worsening illness
    • Cardiac history, thyroid disease, glaucoma, prostatic enlargement
    • Ask about combination OTC products — her slide warns against stacking them, and duplicate decongestant is a common hidden overdose
    • Sleep disturbance, since these are stimulating
    2Vitals
    • BP and HR before and during therapy — a rising pressure is the finding that changes management
    • Report a systolic rise or new palpitations
    • Temperature if infection is suspected
    3Labs
    • No routine drug level
    • Blood glucose in diabetes — sympathomimetics can raise it
    • Renal function in older adults
    4Patient education
    • Check your blood pressure if you have been told it runs high, and tell us if it climbs
    • Do not use a nasal spray for more than about three days — longer use makes the blockage worse, not better
    • Do not take several cold products at once; many contain the same ingredient
    • Avoid taking it near bedtime — it can keep you awake
    • Report a pounding heartbeat, chest discomfort or severe headache
    • Tell your provider you take this before any new prescription
    Special populations
    • Hypertension: the central caution — systemic vasoconstriction raises blood pressure, and in a patient already hypertensive a markedly elevated reading is the priority finding, outranking the congestion being treated.
    • Cardiac disease or dysrhythmia: increased myocardial oxygen demand and risk of palpitations.
    • Benign prostatic hyperplasia: α1 stimulation at the bladder neck can precipitate urinary retention.
    • Narrow-angle glaucoma and hyperthyroidism: both are worsened by sympathomimetic stimulation.
    • Older adults: more sensitive to BP rise, insomnia and retention, and more likely to be taking a duplicate OTC product unknowingly.
    • Anyone using a topical spray beyond three days: rebound congestion drives escalating use — the fix is stopping the spray, not increasing it.
    Antihistaminesdiphenhydramine · loratadine · cetirizine · fexofenadine
    Example drugsdiphenhydramine · loratadine · cetirizine · fexofenadine
    Mechanism of action
    • Block histamine at H₁ receptors → less sneezing, itching, watery eyes and rhinorrhea
    • First generation (diphenhydramine) crosses into the brain → sedation, and has anticholinergic activity
    • Second generation (loratadine, cetirizine, fexofenadine) crosses far less → generally less sedating
    Therapeutic uses
    • Allergic rhinitis and allergic symptoms
    • Urticaria and pruritus
    • First-generation agents also used for motion sickness and as sleep aids
    Side & adverse effects
    • First generation: sedation, and anticholinergic effects — dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision
    • Second generation: generally mild; headache, occasional drowsiness with cetirizine
    • Serious: confusion and falls in older adults; additive CNS depression with alcohol
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Establish whether daytime alertness is required — driving, operating machinery, caring for children, studying
    • Assess for anticholinergic effects with first-generation agents: dry mouth, constipation, voiding difficulty, blurred vision, new confusion
    • Review the whole medication list for anticholinergic burden — several mild agents together produce a strong effect
    • Ask about alcohol use
    • In older adults, baseline cognition, continence and fall risk
    2Vitals
    • No specific vital-sign parameter
    • HR may rise modestly with anticholinergic effect
    • Assess sedation level and gait before ambulating an older adult
    3Labs
    • No routine laboratory monitoring
    • Renal function for cetirizine and fexofenadine, which are renally cleared
    4Patient education
    • Avoid alcohol, and do not drive or operate machinery until you know how this affects you
    • The older antihistamines make most people drowsy; the newer ones usually do not — ask us which yours is
    • Dry mouth is common — sip water and use sugar-free gum
    • Report difficulty passing urine, constipation, or blurred vision
    • Many cold and sleep products already contain an antihistamine — check before adding another
    • For allergy prevention, take it consistently rather than only when symptoms peak
    Special populations
    • Older adults: first-generation agents such as diphenhydramine are listed on the Beers criteria — sedation, confusion, retention, constipation and falls; a second-generation agent is preferred.
    • Benign prostatic hyperplasia: anticholinergic effect can precipitate urinary retention.
    • Narrow-angle glaucoma: pupil dilation can trigger an acute attack.
    • Anyone who must stay alert: drivers, shift workers and students — a sedating antihistamine is a safety issue, not just an inconvenience.
    • Patients on other anticholinergics or CNS depressants: additive burden; review the full list.
    • Children: may show paradoxical excitation rather than sedation with first-generation agents.
    Expectorants & mucolyticsguaifenesin · acetylcysteine · dornase alfa
    Example drugsguaifenesin · acetylcysteine · dornase alfa
    Mechanism of action
    • Guaifenesin thins mucus so the patient’s own cough can clear it — it assists the mucociliary escalator
    • Acetylcysteine chemically breaks disulphide bonds in mucus, dissolving it directly
    • Dornase alfa digests DNA in thick secretions — used in cystic fibrosis
    • Mucolytics are given by inhalation; guaifenesin is oral
    Therapeutic uses
    • Guaifenesin: productive cough with thick secretions
    • Acetylcysteine: cystic fibrosis, atelectasis from mucus plugging
    • Dornase alfa: cystic fibrosis
    • Acetylcysteine is also the antidote in acetaminophen overdose
    Side & adverse effects
    • Guaifenesin: nausea, vomiting, dizziness; generally well tolerated
    • Acetylcysteine: may trigger bronchospasm; unpleasant sulphur odour, nausea, mouth irritation
    • Dornase alfa: voice change, pharyngitis, chest discomfort
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Assess the patient’s ability to actually clear mucus — cough strength, hydration and level of consciousness; thinning secretions in someone who cannot cough creates a hazard
    • Lung sounds before and after inhaled mucolytics — acetylcysteine can precipitate bronchospasm, which is her stated concern
    • Sputum colour, volume and thickness as the measure of response
    • Hydration status — guaifenesin depends on adequate fluid
    • Whether a bronchodilator is prescribed to be given first
    2Vitals
    • RR, SpO2 and lung sounds before and after an inhaled mucolytic — report new wheeze immediately
    • Work of breathing and cough effectiveness
    • Temperature if infection is suspected
    3Labs
    • No routine drug level
    • Sputum culture where infection is suspected
    • Renal and hepatic function only in broader care
    4Patient education
    • Drink plenty of fluids — guaifenesin works by thinning mucus and needs water to do it
    • Tell us straight away if you start wheezing or feel tight during an inhaled treatment
    • Acetylcysteine has a strong sulphur smell — it is expected and not a sign of spoilage
    • Cough after the treatment; the point is to move the mucus out
    • Do not use expectorants long-term without review
    • Report fever, or sputum turning green, brown or bloody
    Special populations
    • Asthma or reactive airways: acetylcysteine can provoke bronchospasm — a bronchodilator is often given first and respiratory status monitored throughout.
    • Patients with a weak cough — frail, post-operative, neuromuscular disease or reduced consciousness: loosened secretions they cannot expel can obstruct the airway; ensure suction is available.
    • Cystic fibrosis: dornase alfa and acetylcysteine are central therapy rather than occasional symptom relief.
    • Dehydrated patients: guaifenesin is far less effective without adequate fluid intake.
    • Older adults: reduced cough strength and thirst sensation make both the clearance and the hydration harder.
    • Fluid-restricted patients (heart or renal failure): the usual ‘increase fluids’ advice must be checked against their restriction rather than given automatically.
    Intranasal corticosteroidsfluticasone · budesonide · triamcinolone
    Example drugsfluticasone · budesonide · triamcinolone
    Mechanism of action
    • Reduce nasal inflammation and mucosal swelling locally
    • Anti-inflammatory therapy — not the immediate unblocking a topical decongestant gives
    • Effect develops with consistent daily use over days
    Therapeutic uses
    • Persistent allergic rhinitis
    • Chronic nasal congestion from inflammation
    • Nasal polyps in selected patients
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common: nasal dryness and irritation, sore throat, unpleasant taste
    • Serious: epistaxis; with prolonged misdirected use, septal irritation and rarely perforation
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Watch the patient use the spray — technique determines both benefit and side effects
    • Confirm they aim away from the nasal septum, which is her stated teaching point
    • Inspect for nasal dryness, crusting and bleeding
    • Establish the patient’s expectation — someone expecting instant relief will stop within days
    • Ask how long they have used any topical decongestant alongside it
    2Vitals
    • No vital-sign parameter
    • Assess nasal airflow and symptom score over weeks rather than minutes
    3Labs
    • No routine laboratory monitoring
    • Growth measurement in children on long-term therapy
    4Patient education
    • Use it every day, even when your nose feels clear — it builds up over days and only works if used consistently
    • Aim the spray toward the outer wall of your nostril, away from the middle wall — this prevents bleeding and soreness
    • This is not a fast unblocking spray. It treats the inflammation underneath, so give it time
    • Report nosebleeds, persistent dryness or crusting
    • Blow your nose gently before using it
    • Do not share the device with anyone
    Special populations
    • Anyone expecting immediate relief: her stated key point — this is anti-inflammatory therapy, not the rapid unblocking of a topical decongestant, and the mismatch is the usual reason it is abandoned.
    • Patients with recurrent epistaxis or recent nasal surgery: higher bleeding risk; technique and inspection matter more.
    • Children: monitor growth velocity on prolonged therapy and supervise technique.
    • Anyone also using a topical decongestant: ask how long — rebound congestion from the decongestant will be blamed on the steroid failing.
    • Older adults: drier nasal mucosa increases irritation and bleeding.
    • Immunosuppressed patients: greater risk of local infection.

    Read the two β2 entries side by side. SABA and LABA act on the same receptor and share the same side effects — yet one is the drug you reach for when a patient cannot breathe and the other is useless in that moment. Almost every respiratory exam question turns on that distinction, so it is worth seeing the two charts open together.

    Sources. Karch’s Focus on Nursing Pharmacology, 10th ed. (Tucker), Ch 53–55; Dr. Kaur’s NURS-11 Week 8 respiratory deck, built from the complete 47-slide set rather than the highlighted text alone; AGS Beers Criteria® for the older-adult notes. No commercial study sites were used.

    Ch 15 · Wk 9 slides 5–8

    1Non-opioid analgesics — and the hidden-dose problem

    Her framework for every drug this week: WHY → ASSESS → ACT → REASSESS and TEACH. Non-opioids are foundational for mild to moderate pain; the danger is not the drug but the total the patient is taking.

    DrugMost useful forPriority nursing concern
    AcetaminophenPain and fever — no anti-inflammatory actionLiver toxicity. Review every combination product the patient takes
    Ibuprofen
    NSAID    		Pain, fever and inflammationGI bleeding · renal injury · BP and fluid effects
    Ketorolac
    NSAID    		Short-term moderate–severe acute painBleeding, kidney injury — total use ≤ 5 days

    Her first teaching line: check the active ingredients, not the brand name. Acetaminophen hides inside combination opioids, cold remedies and sleep aids. The adult FDA maximum is 4,000 mg/day across all products — and many orders use a lower limit. The trap is that a patient taking a prescription hydrocodone/APAP, a cold medicine and an extra Tylenol can cross that line without exceeding any single label. Overdose may be initially silent, which is exactly why you add up the 24-hour total before giving rather than waiting for symptoms.

    Acetaminophen — assess beforeNSAIDs — assess before
    Liver disease or impaired liver function · alcohol use · other hepatotoxic drugs · nutritional status · total daily APAP exposureHistory of GI bleeding or ulcer · renal function, hydration, BP · anticoagulants or other NSAIDs · pregnancy-related cautions
    NSAID monitoring and teachingWhy
    Black stools, vomiting bloodGI bleeding — report immediately, do not wait for the next visit
    Reduced urine outputRenal injury — NSAIDs reduce the prostaglandins that maintain renal perfusion
    Take ibuprofen with food if upsetReduces gastric irritation
    Never combine two NSAIDsHer line: do not combine ketorolac with another NSAID — the risks add without added benefit
    Ketorolac ≤ 5 days totalA hard ceiling across all routes, because of bleeding and renal risk

    Why these two are not interchangeable. Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever but has no anti-inflammatory effect — so it does nothing for the inflammation behind, say, an arthritic joint. NSAIDs do both, but at the cost of GI, renal and bleeding risk. That is the reasoning behind multimodal therapy on her slide: combining agents that work differently gives better relief at lower doses of each. And she asks you to reassess pain and function — a number alone does not tell you whether the patient can now move, cough or sleep.

    Ch 26 · Wk 9 slides 9–10

    2Opioids and naloxone — sedation precedes respiratory depression

    Opioids may be entirely appropriate for severe pain. The nursing question is not whether to give them but what you watch afterwards.

    Assess BEFOREMonitor AFTER
    Pain severity and prior opioid exposure · sedation level, respiratory rate and quality · blood pressure · concurrent sedativesOversedation or slowed, ineffective breathing · hypotension and fall risk · constipation, urinary retention, nausea · document pain, function and reassessment

    Her explicit caution: do not rely on one respiratory-rate cutoff. Follow the order, local policy and the overall assessment. A rate of 10 in a comfortable, rousable patient is different from a rate of 12 that is shallow and ineffective in someone you can barely wake. Rate alone misses the patient who is moving too little air. This is the same principle as the beta-blocker hold parameters — assess the patient, not a remembered number.

    The sequence that makes opioid monitoring work. Sedation increases before respiration falls. A patient who is becoming hard to rouse is showing you the warning before the respiratory rate drops — which is why level of consciousness is assessed at every check rather than only the number on the monitor. Waiting for a low rate means waiting until the margin is gone.

    NaloxoneDetail
    FirstAirway and breathing support remain the priority. Activate the emergency response; support ventilation and begin CPR as indicated
    GiveBy the available route per emergency protocol
    Expect to repeatThe opioid can outlast the naloxone — repeat doses may be needed
    Keep watchingMonitor closely for recurrent respiratory depression and for withdrawal

    Her slide title says it: reversal does not end the emergency. Naloxone has a shorter duration than most opioids, so a patient who wakes up can sink again once it wears off — which is why they stay monitored rather than being left to sleep it off. Expect abrupt withdrawal too: pain returns at full force, with agitation, nausea and sweating. Both facts argue the same way — you stay with the patient.

    Ch 23 & 26 · Wk 9 slide 11

    3Neuropathic pain — two drugs borrowed from other classes

    Nerve pain responds poorly to ordinary analgesics, so the drugs used come from the antiseizure and antidepressant shelves.

    GabapentinDuloxetine SNRI
    Used forNeuropathic pain; also focal seizuresDepression, anxiety and neuropathic pain
    WatchDizziness, somnolence, ataxia → fallsBP, mood and suicidality
    SafetyAdjust to renal function; do not stop abruptly in epilepsySerotonin syndrome; avoid abrupt discontinuation

    Why duloxetine shows up twice this week. It is an antidepressant and a neuropathic pain drug, which means a patient may be taking it for either reason — and the monitoring is the same either way: blood pressure, mood, and the serotonin-syndrome risk if another serotonergic drug is added. If you see it on a medication list, find out which indication it is treating before you teach about it.

    Neither is stopped abruptly. Gabapentin taken for epilepsy can precipitate seizures on sudden withdrawal; duloxetine produces a discontinuation syndrome — dizziness, electric-shock sensations, irritability. In both cases the teaching is the same: any change goes through the prescriber and is tapered.

    Ch 20 · Wk 9 slides 14–16

    4Benzodiazepines and zolpidem — one class, several jobs

    All the benzodiazepines enhance GABA activity, the brain’s main inhibitory signal. That single mechanism explains every use and every danger.

    DrugUsed forParticular concern
    LorazepamAnxiety, agitation; also acute seizure managementSedation and respiratory depression
    AlprazolamAnxiety and panicDependence and withdrawal
    DiazepamAnxiety, muscle spasm, seizure rescue, withdrawalLong duration; accumulation in older adults
    Zolpidem
    hypnotic, not an anxiolytic    		Insomnia only — give just before intended sleepBoxed warning: complex sleep behaviours

    The combination that kills: opioid + benzodiazepine. Her slide says avoid combining with opioids or alcohol unless clinically justified and closely monitored. Both depress the CNS by different mechanisms, so the respiratory depression is more than additive. This is her Case 2 and it is worth rehearsing: a patient given oxycodone 45 minutes ago who is now difficult to arouse does not get the PRN lorazepam — you assess airway and breathing, withhold the sedative, and escalate.

    Before giving a benzodiazepinePatient education
    Respiratory status, alertness, falls risk · other opioids, alcohol or sedatives · the indication and medication historyTake as prescribed; do not share · do not stop abruptly after regular use · avoid unsafe combinations and driving if sedated · older adults: delirium and falls

    Zolpidem is not a benzodiazepine and not an anxiolytic — her slide title makes the point. It is for insomnia, taken immediately before bed, with enough time allowed for sleep (often 7–8 hours depending on the formulation). The FDA boxed warning covers complex sleep behaviours — sleep-walking, sleep-driving, preparing food while not fully awake. Any prior such behaviour is a contraindication; if one occurs, the drug is stopped and the prescriber contacted. In older adults, non-drug sleep strategies and fall precautions come first.

    Ch 21 · Wk 9 slides 19–21

    5Antidepressants — four classes and two emergencies

    Her framing: therapeutic response takes weeks, but new suicidality or serotonin syndrome requires action now. That gap between slow benefit and fast danger is the whole nursing problem.

    ClassExemplarCommon concernTeaching priority
    SSRIfluoxetine · sertralineGI effects, sexual dysfunction, serotonin syndromeDaily adherence; monitor mood and suicidality
    SNRIduloxetineBP changes; withdrawal on abrupt stopBP and mood checks; tapered discontinuation
    TCAamitriptylineOrthostasis, anticholinergic effects, cardiac toxicity — danger in overdoseFalls and overdose precautions
    MAOIphenelzineHypertensive crisis; major food and drug interactionsAvoid high-tyramine foods; verify all medications

    Why suicidality can rise before mood improves. Antidepressants often restore energy and initiative before they lift mood — so a severely depressed patient who previously lacked the drive to act may gain it while still feeling hopeless. That is why monitoring is closest in the first weeks and after any dose change, and why “it takes a few weeks to work” is never the whole teaching.

    Serotonin syndromeMAOI hypertensive crisis
    Agitation · clonus and hyperreflexia · sweating · fever · diarrhea
    often follows adding a serotonergic drug or an interaction
    Hold the suspected medication; seek immediate evaluation    		Severe headache · marked hypertension · chest pain · neurologic symptoms
    triggered by tyramine-containing food or an interacting sympathomimetic
    Emergency evaluation

    Telling the two apart. Both are emergencies, both can involve headache and autonomic upset — but serotonin syndrome brings hyperreflexia and clonus (the neuromuscular signature) and usually follows a new serotonergic drug. Hypertensive crisis brings a severe headache with a markedly high blood pressure and follows an MAOI plus tyramine — aged cheese, cured meats, draught beer, fermented foods. Ask what changed: a new drug points one way, a meal points the other.

    Compare with NMS, which you met in the adverse-reactions chapter. Serotonin syndrome gives hyperreflexia and clonus; neuroleptic malignant syndrome gives lead-pipe rigidity. Both have fever and altered mental status. The muscles tell you which — twitchy and overreactive versus stiff and rigid.

    Ch 22 · Wk 9 slides 22–24

    6Lithium and antipsychotics — the narrow index and the two movement emergencies

    Lithium is this unit’s digoxin: a narrow therapeutic index drug where an ordinary physiological change tips the patient into toxicity.

    Lithium — the safety triadDetail
    LevelsNarrow therapeutic index — check correctly timed levels per order
    Salt and fluidMaintain consistent salt and fluid intake; dehydration increases toxicity
    OrgansMonitor kidney and thyroid function
    ToxicityWorsening tremor · vomiting and diarrhea · ataxia · confusion → hold and escalate
    InteractionsNSAIDs and some diuretics raise lithium levels

    Why sodium and fluid decide lithium safety. The kidney handles lithium much as it handles sodium. When sodium falls or the patient becomes dehydrated — vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, a low-salt diet, a new diuretic — the kidney reabsorbs more lithium and the level climbs on an unchanged dose. That is the mechanism behind her “consistent salt and fluid” teaching, and it is why NSAIDs matter too: they reduce renal perfusion and raise levels. The vicious part is that early toxicity causes vomiting and diarrhea, which dehydrates the patient further and drives the level higher still.

    Fine tremor versus coarse tremor. A fine hand tremor can be an expected lithium effect. A coarse tremor with ataxia, vomiting and confusion is toxicity — her Case 3 exactly. The action is to hold the dose, assess, and notify urgently for a level and renal function. Giving the dose or adding salt tablets without assessment both act on a guess.

    Haloperidol typicalRisperidone / olanzapine atypical
    Dopamine D2 blockade
    Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS), dystonia
    QT prolongation · NMS    		Lower EPS risk than high-potency typicals — but not zero
    Metabolic effects: weight, glucose, lipids
    Sedation, orthostasis; monitor movement disorders
    EPSNMS — emergency
    Dystonia — spasms of neck, eyes, tongue
    Akathisia — inner restlessness
    Parkinsonism; later tardive dyskinesia    		High fever and severe rigidity
    Altered mental status and autonomic instability
    Stop the antipsychotic; urgent emergency treatment

    Her slide says it plainly: do not confuse EPS with NMS. EPS is a movement problem — distressing, sometimes treated with benztropine, not usually life-threatening. NMS adds fever, rigidity, altered consciousness and autonomic instability, and it kills. The discriminator is systemic: is the patient febrile and unstable, or just moving abnormally? Akathisia is the one most often mistaken for anxiety — a patient who cannot sit still may be having a drug effect, not a psychiatric one, and giving more antipsychotic makes it worse.

    Ch 23 · Wk 9 slides 27–28

    7Antiseizure medications — each one has a different red flag

    Her governing rule first: most long-term antiseizure medications should not be stopped abruptly. Sudden withdrawal can precipitate status epilepticus.

    DrugKey adverse effectNursing response
    PhenytoinNystagmus, ataxia; gingival hyperplasia; severe rash; many interactionsAssess levels, neurologic status, rash
    LevetiracetamBehaviour or mood changes; sedation; renal dosingAsk about depression, agitation, self-harm
    LamotrigineNew rash or mucosal lesions — serious cutaneous reaction, especially earlyStop pending urgent evaluation per prescribing advice
    Diazepam
    rescue    		Respiratory depressionAirway readiness and close monitoring after the dose

    Lamotrigine and rash — the one that cannot wait. This drug can cause life-threatening skin reactions, and the risk is highest early in treatment and when titration is rushed — which is why the dose is increased slowly. Mucosal involvement is the major red flag: a rash with mouth sores is not an ordinary drug rash. Her Case 4 is exactly this: three weeks in, new rash with mouth sores → withhold and seek urgent evaluation. Not an antihistamine, not “reassess tomorrow.”

    Phenytoin’s signs are neurological and visible. Nystagmus and ataxia are the classic early toxicity findings — you can see them at the bedside before a level comes back. Gingival hyperplasia is the long-term effect patients notice, and it makes meticulous oral hygiene and dental review part of the teaching rather than an afterthought.

    Levetiracetam’s red flag is psychiatric, not physical. Mood and behaviour change — irritability, agitation, depression, suicidal thinking — is the effect to ask about directly, because patients rarely connect it to a seizure medicine and families often notice first. This is her Case 6: a patient on levetiracetam with new suicidal thoughts outranks mild nausea, improved pain or dry mouth for urgency.

    Ch 24–25 · Wk 9 slides 29–30

    8Parkinson’s, drug-induced movement problems and spasticity

    Three groups that all affect movement — but one replaces dopamine, one blocks acetylcholine, and one works on muscle tone.

    Carbidopa / levodopaDetail
    How it worksLevodopa becomes dopamine in the brain; carbidopa limits peripheral conversion so more reaches the CNS and there is less nausea
    TimingGive ON TIME — assess wearing-off, mobility and dyskinesias
    WatchOrthostatic hypotension · hallucinations · nausea
    FoodHigh-protein meals can reduce the response in some patients — individualise timing
    Vitamin B6B6 supplements are compatible with the combination product

    Why “on time” is a safety instruction, not a courtesy. Parkinson’s symptom control tracks the drug level closely. A dose given an hour late can leave a patient unable to move, swallow or speak until it takes effect — so this is one of the few oral medications where the scheduled time genuinely cannot slide for ward convenience.

    The vitamin B6 point is worth understanding, because the old rule was the opposite. With levodopa alone, B6 speeds its breakdown in the periphery and reduces the amount reaching the brain — hence the historic “avoid B6” teaching. Carbidopa blocks that peripheral conversion, so with the combination product the interaction is no longer significant. Her slide reflects current practice; if you have seen the older rule elsewhere, this is why they differ.

    High protein competes for absorption. Levodopa is an amino acid and uses the same transporter as dietary protein, so a large protein meal can blunt the dose. The answer is individualised timing, not a protein-free diet — patients need the protein.

    BenztropineBaclofen & cyclobenzaprine
    Anticholinergic for drug-induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia
    Dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, overheating
    Older adults: confusion and delirium risk    		Baclofen — neurologic spasticity; withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium
    Cyclobenzaprine — short-term musculoskeletal spasm
    Both: sedation, dizziness, falls

    Benztropine is the autonomic unit reappearing. It treats drug-induced movement problems by blocking acetylcholine — restoring the dopamine–acetylcholine balance that an antipsychotic disturbed. So it carries the full anticholinergic profile you already know: dry, dilated, retained, confused, plus impaired sweating and heat intolerance. In an older adult that confusion can be mistaken for worsening illness.

    Baclofen is not stopped abruptly. Sudden withdrawal — particularly from intrathecal therapy — can cause seizures, delirium, rebound spasticity and hyperthermia. Cyclobenzaprine is for short-term use and is structurally related to the tricyclics, which is why it sedates and carries anticholinergic effects of its own.

    Ch 26–28 · Wk 9 slides 31–32

    9Migraine therapy — and two critical-care drugs at recognition level

    SumatriptanDetail
    Class and actionTriptan — 5-HT1B/1D agonist with cranial vasoconstrictive effects
    RoleAcute treatment — not prevention
    Avoid inCoronary artery disease · prior stroke or TIA · uncontrolled hypertension
    Her warningEvaluate new or severe chest symptoms rather than calling them “expected”

    Why the cardiac history matters before a migraine drug. Triptans relieve migraine partly by constricting cranial vessels — but that vasoconstriction is not perfectly selective, and in a patient with coronary disease it can provoke myocardial ischemia. Triptans do commonly cause a benign tightness in the chest, throat or jaw, which is exactly what makes her warning important: the expected sensation and a real ischemic event feel similar, so new or severe chest symptoms get evaluated rather than dismissed.

    Serotonergic, like the antidepressants. A triptan added to an SSRI or SNRI raises serotonin-syndrome risk — so check the full medication list, and keep the agitation-clonus-fever picture in mind in a patient taking both.

    Recognition level for Semester 1What to know
    Propofol
    sedative / anaesthetic    		Can produce apnea and hypotension. Needs trained personnel, airway readiness and monitoring. Check product-specific allergy precautions
    Succinylcholine
    paralytic    		Paralysis is not sedation or analgesia — requires ventilation and an appropriate sedation plan. Hyperkalemia; malignant hyperthermia → dantrolene

    The sentence on her slide worth memorising exactly: paralysis ≠ sedation or analgesia. A paralysed patient can be fully awake and in pain while unable to move, breathe or signal distress. That is why a neuromuscular blocker is never given without ventilation and a sedation plan. These two drugs are recognition level — know the class, the danger and the antidote pairing, and spend your study time on the drugs you will actually administer.

    Wk 9 slides 4, 39–40 · integration

    10Her ten must-know connections — the exam blueprint

    Slide 39 is titled “Exam 2: the 10 must-know connections.” That is as close to a blueprint as you will get. Each row below is her pairing, with the reasoning that makes it answerable rather than memorised.

    #Her connectionWhat it means at the bedside
    01Acetaminophen → liverAdd up every product containing it. Max 4,000 mg/day in adults, often lower. Overdose can be silent at first
    02NSAIDs → GI & kidneyAsk about black stools and reduced urine output. Never two NSAIDs together. Ketorolac ≤ 5 days
    03Opioid + benzo → breathingSedation rises before the respiratory rate falls. A hard-to-rouse patient does not get the second sedative
    04Naloxone → it wears offIt wears off before the opioid does. Airway and breathing stay the priority; keep monitoring
    05SSRI / MAOI → serotoninSerotonin syndrome — agitation, clonus, fever. MAOI + tyramine — hypertensive crisis
    06Lithium → sodium & fluidDehydration or low sodium raises the level on an unchanged dose. NSAIDs raise it too
    07Antipsychotics → EPS vs NMSMovement problem versus fever + rigidity + altered mental status. The second is an emergency
    08Phenytoin → neuro toxicityNystagmus and ataxia are visible before the level returns
    09Lamotrigine → rashRash with mucosal lesions = withhold and escalate. Risk is highest early
    10Carbidopa/levodopa → timingLate doses mean a patient who cannot move or swallow
    Her 4-step frameworkUse it on every drug family
    1 · WHYWhy is this medication ordered for this patient?
    2 · ASSESSWhich vital signs, labs, symptoms or interactions matter before giving?
    3 · ACTGive, question, hold per order and policy, or escalate
    4 · REASSESS & TEACHWhat response — or what danger — should be watched for?

    The patterns that cut across this whole unit. CNS depressants stack — opioids, benzodiazepines, zolpidem, muscle relaxants and alcohol all add, and the combination is where patients stop breathing. Narrow-index drugs need levels and context — lithium and phenytoin here, as digoxin and theophylline were earlier; in every case a physiological change (dehydration, renal decline, a stopped cigarette) moves the level without anyone changing the dose. And several of these drugs are never stopped abruptly — benzodiazepines, antiseizure drugs, antidepressants, baclofen.

    Three findings in this unit mean “act now,” not “report later.” A new rash with mucosal lesions on lamotrigine. New suicidal thinking on levetiracetam or an antidepressant. Fever with rigidity on an antipsychotic. Each appears in one of her own case questions, and in each the distractors are plausible, mild, and wrong.

    Her study prompt, worth doing out loud. For any drug: say why it is given, two assessments before administration, one serious adverse effect and what you would do, and one clear teaching sentence. If you can do that for every drug on this page, you are ready.

    Pain & CNS · med chart

    Medication chart — pain & CNS drugs

    Nineteen classes in the same rubric format: example drugs, mechanism, uses, effects, nursing considerations in the four required parts — assessment vitals labs education — and specific special populations.

    Acetaminophen
    non-opioid — the hidden-dose drugacetaminophen (APAP)
    Example drugsacetaminophen (APAP)
    Mechanism of action
    • Raises the pain threshold centrally and acts on the hypothalamic heat-regulating centre
    • Little anti-inflammatory effect — this is what separates it from an NSAID
    • No antiplatelet effect, so it does not add bleeding risk
    • Metabolised by the liver; a minor pathway produces a toxic metabolite normally neutralised by glutathione. Overwhelm that reserve and hepatocytes die
    Therapeutic uses
    • Mild to moderate pain
    • Fever
    • First-line where NSAIDs are unsafe — GI bleeding risk, anticoagulation, kidney disease
    • Part of a multimodal plan to reduce opioid requirement
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: generally well tolerated at correct doses — which is exactly why the danger is invisible
    • Serious: hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure. Her slide: “overdose may be initially silent → urgent evaluation”
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Add up every product containing acetaminophen — prescriptions, OTC cold and flu remedies, combination opioids. Check the active ingredients, not the brand name
    • Adult FDA maximum 4,000 mg/day across all products; many orders and products set a lower ceiling — follow the lower one
    • Liver disease or impaired liver function
    • Alcohol use, and other hepatotoxic medications
    • Nutritional status — malnutrition and fasting deplete the glutathione that detoxifies the metabolite
    2Vitals
    • Temperature, to judge whether an antipyretic worked
    • Pain score and function before and after, not pain alone
    • Vitals are not where acetaminophen toxicity shows — the cumulative dose is
    3Labs
    • LFTs (AST, ALT, bilirubin) in liver disease, alcohol use or suspected excess
    • INR — rises as liver synthetic function fails
    • Acetaminophen level and time of ingestion if overdose is suspected
    4Education
    • Read every label for “acetaminophen” or “APAP” before taking anything extra — this one habit prevents most accidental overdoses
    • Never take two products containing it at once
    • Seek care promptly after a suspected excess even while feeling well
    • Report nausea, right-upper-quadrant pain, dark urine, yellowing of skin or eyes
    • Limit alcohol
    Special populations
    • Chronic alcohol use: induces the enzyme that makes the toxic metabolite and depletes glutathione — toxicity at doses a healthy liver would tolerate.
    • Liver disease: reduced capacity to clear the drug; the daily ceiling is lowered.
    • Malnourished or fasting patients: low glutathione reserve, same mechanism.
    • Older adults: often take several OTC products and are the group most likely to double up unknowingly.
    • Children: dosed by weight with different concentrations between formulations — a frequent source of error.
    • Patients on warfarin: regular high-dose use can raise INR; still preferred over an NSAID, which adds direct bleeding risk.
    NSAIDs
    anti-inflammatory — GI, renal and bleeding riskibuprofen · ketorolac
    Example drugsibuprofen · ketorolac
    Mechanism of action
    • Block cyclo-oxygenase, reducing prostaglandin production → less pain, fever and inflammation
    • But those same prostaglandins protect the gastric lining and maintain renal blood flow — which is why the therapeutic action and the adverse effects are the same mechanism
    • Also inhibit platelet aggregation → bleeding risk
    • Promote sodium and water retention → blood pressure rises and heart failure can worsen
    Therapeutic uses
    • Pain, fever and inflammation — the inflammatory component is what acetaminophen cannot treat
    • Ketorolac: short-term moderate to severe acute pain, often postoperative
    • Multimodal analgesia to spare opioids
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: dyspepsia, nausea, heartburn, dizziness, fluid retention
    • Serious: GI bleeding and ulceration, acute kidney injury, raised blood pressure, worsening heart failure, bleeding, cardiovascular events
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • History of GI bleeding or ulcers — a prior ulcer changes the risk category
    • Renal function and hydration — a dehydrated kidney depends on prostaglandins for perfusion, so an NSAID can tip it into injury
    • Anticoagulants, antiplatelets, corticosteroids, other NSAIDs — additive bleeding risk. Her slide: do not combine ketorolac with another NSAID
    • Ketorolac: maximum 5 days total, every route counted
    • Monitor for black stools, vomiting blood, and reduced urine output
    2Vitals
    • Blood pressure — sodium and water retention raises it and can destabilise treated hypertension
    • Heart rate and signs of fluid overload — new weight gain, oedema, crackles
    • Pain score and function before and after
    3Labs
    • Hemoglobin and hematocrit — a slow GI bleed shows as a falling Hgb before anything is visible
    • BUN and creatinine at baseline and during therapy
    • Platelets and coagulation studies where bleeding risk is a concern
    • Potassium — can rise as renal function falls
    4Education
    • Take with food or milk if GI upset occurs
    • Report black or tarry stools, vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, and reduced urine output
    • Avoid alcohol — additive gastric injury
    • Do not combine OTC NSAIDs with a prescribed one; check labels for ibuprofen, naproxen and aspirin
    • Maintain fluid intake
    • Report new swelling or rapid weight gain
    Special populations
    • Older adults: highest GI bleeding and renal risk, often with reduced baseline renal function — NSAIDs appear on the Beers criteria for this reason.
    • Patients on anticoagulants: two bleeding mechanisms at once — platelet inhibition plus anticoagulation.
    • Chronic kidney disease or dehydration: the prostaglandin-dependent kidney loses its last compensation.
    • Heart failure or hypertension: fluid retention worsens both.
    • History of peptic ulcer: re-bleeding risk; a protective agent may be required or an NSAID avoided.
    • Pregnancy: avoided in the third trimester — prostaglandin inhibition closes the ductus arteriosus.
    • Asthma with nasal polyps: a subgroup develops severe NSAID-induced bronchospasm.
    Opioid agonists
    severe pain — watch sedation before ratemorphine · oxycodone · hydrocodone/APAP
    Example drugsmorphine · oxycodone · hydrocodone/APAP
    Mechanism of action
    • Bind mu receptors in the brain and spinal cord, reducing pain transmission and altering the perception of pain
    • The same receptors in the brainstem reduce the drive to breathe and blunt the response to rising CO₂
    • Slow GI motility → constipation, which does not improve with time
    • Cause histamine release → itching, flushing, hypotension
    Therapeutic uses
    • Moderate to severe pain where non-opioids are insufficient
    • Postoperative and procedural pain
    • Cancer and palliative pain
    • Morphine also reduces preload and anxiety in acute pulmonary oedema
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: sedation, nausea, constipation, itching, urinary retention, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension
    • Serious: respiratory depression, over-sedation, hypotension, falls, dependence. Her slide: do not rely on one respiratory-rate cutoff — follow orders, policy and the overall assessment
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Sedation level — this is the earliest warning. Her ten-connection list is explicit: sedation rises before the respiratory rate falls, so a drowsy, hard-to-rouse patient is the finding to act on
    • Respiratory rate and quality — shallow or irregular breathing at a normal rate is still respiratory depression
    • Concurrent sedatives: benzodiazepines, alcohol, sleep aids, muscle relaxants — the combination is more than additive
    • Pain severity, prior opioid exposure and tolerance
    • Bowel function from the first dose
    • Fall risk — sedation plus orthostasis
    • Confirm naloxone and an airway are available
    2Vitals
    • Respiratory rate, depth and SpO2 before and after — and sedation scored alongside them
    • Blood pressure — hypotension and orthostasis, particularly after the first dose or an increase
    • Heart rate
    • End-tidal CO₂ where monitored — it rises before saturation falls
    3Labs
    • No routine level; assessment is the monitor
    • Renal and hepatic function — impaired clearance means accumulation with repeat dosing
    • For combination products, the acetaminophen total is the lab-equivalent number to track
    4Education
    • Report drowsiness that makes it hard to stay awake — do not wait for breathing to feel difficult
    • Start a bowel regimen with the first dose; constipation is expected, not optional
    • No alcohol, and no sedating medicines without checking
    • Rise slowly — orthostatic hypotension and falls
    • Do not drive or operate machinery while sedated
    • Store securely and never share; dispose of unused doses properly
    • Take as prescribed and report inadequate relief rather than self-escalating
    Special populations
    • Older adults: more sensitive at any dose, with slower clearance, higher fall risk and a tendency to delirium — start low.
    • Patients also receiving benzodiazepines: her flagged high-risk pair — two different respiratory depressant mechanisms together.
    • Obstructive sleep apnoea or obesity: an already compromised airway plus blunted ventilatory drive.
    • Opioid-naïve patients: no tolerance, so the standard dose produces far more depression.
