    • Renal or hepatic impairment: morphine metabolites accumulate and prolong the effect.
    • Head injury: sedation masks neurological deterioration and CO₂ retention raises intracranial pressure.
    • Pregnancy and breastfeeding: neonatal withdrawal and sedation risk.
    Opioid antagonist
    reversal does not end the emergencynaloxone
    Example drugsnaloxone
    Mechanism of action
    • Competitively displaces opioids from mu receptors, restoring respiratory drive within minutes
    • Its duration is shorter than most opioids — the single most important fact about it
    • Reverses analgesia along with everything else, and precipitates acute withdrawal in a dependent patient
    Therapeutic uses
    • Suspected opioid overdose with respiratory depression
    • Reversal of procedural over-sedation
    • Take-home kits for patients and families where overdose risk exists
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: acute withdrawal — agitation, sweating, nausea and vomiting, pain returning abruptly
    • Serious: recurrent respiratory depression once it wears off, hypertension, tachycardia, dysrhythmia, pulmonary oedema, seizures
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Airway and breathing remain the priority — activate the emergency response and support ventilation or begin CPR as indicated; naloxone is given alongside that, not instead of it
    • Monitor closely for returning sedation. Her slide: repeat doses may be needed because the opioid effect can outlast naloxone — so a patient who wakes up is not a patient who is safe
    • Level of consciousness, pupils and respiratory effort continuously
    • Have suction, oxygen and a bag-valve mask at hand
    • Reassess pain once stable — analgesia was reversed too
    2Vitals
    • Respiratory rate, depth and SpO2 continuously, not intermittently
    • Blood pressure and heart rate — both can rise sharply with abrupt reversal
    • Temperature and level of consciousness
    3Labs
    • No level guides the dose — titrate to breathing
    • ABG where available, for CO₂ retention
    • Glucose and a broader workup if the cause of unresponsiveness is uncertain
    4Education
    • For families with a kit: call emergency services first, then give naloxone — and stay, because it can wear off
    • Expect withdrawal symptoms if the person is dependent
    • Anyone who receives naloxone needs continued observation in a monitored setting
    • Never leave the person alone or let them “sleep it off” after a reversal
    Special populations
    • Opioid-dependent patients: abrupt full reversal precipitates severe withdrawal — titrate to adequate breathing rather than full alertness.
    • Patients on long-acting or sustained-release opioids: the drug outlasts naloxone by many hours; repeat dosing or an infusion is expected.
    • Neonates of opioid-dependent mothers: risk of precipitated withdrawal and seizures.
    • Cardiac disease: the catecholamine surge from abrupt reversal can provoke ischemia or dysrhythmia.
    • Patients with chronic pain: reversal returns severe pain — plan how it will be managed once breathing is secure.
    Neuropathic pain adjuvants
    nerve pain — not ordinary analgesicsgabapentin · duloxetine
    Example drugsgabapentin · duloxetine
    Mechanism of action
    • Gabapentin: binds a calcium-channel subunit on overactive neurons, reducing excitatory neurotransmitter release — it calms abnormal nerve firing rather than blocking a pain signal
    • Duloxetine (SNRI): raises serotonin and norepinephrine in descending inhibitory pathways, strengthening the body’s own pain suppression
    • Neither is an opioid and neither works on acute injury pain — which is why a patient expecting immediate relief stops them early
    Therapeutic uses
    • Neuropathic pain — diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia
    • Gabapentin: also focal seizures
    • Duloxetine: depression, anxiety and neuropathic pain — one drug, three indications
    • Opioid-sparing in chronic pain
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: gabapentin: dizziness, somnolence, ataxia, peripheral oedema. Duloxetine: nausea, dry mouth, insomnia, raised blood pressure
    • Serious: gabapentin: falls, respiratory depression with opioids, withdrawal seizures if stopped abruptly in epilepsy. Duloxetine: serotonin syndrome, hepatotoxicity, new suicidality, discontinuation syndrome
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Gabapentin: falls risk — dizziness, somnolence and ataxia together, especially while the dose is being titrated
    • Gabapentin dose is adjusted to renal function — the kidney clears it unchanged, so impaired function means accumulation and sedation
    • Never stop either abruptly — gabapentin in epilepsy risks withdrawal seizures; duloxetine causes a discontinuation syndrome
    • Duloxetine: mood and suicidality, and all other serotonergic drugs on the list
    • Reassess neuropathic pain over weeks, not hours
    2Vitals
    • Duloxetine: blood pressure at baseline and during therapy — the norepinephrine effect can raise it
    • Orthostatic blood pressure for both — fall risk
    • Respiratory status if gabapentin is combined with an opioid
    3Labs
    • Gabapentin: BUN and creatinine to set and adjust the dose
    • Duloxetine: LFTs; avoided in significant hepatic impairment
    • Sodium — SNRIs can cause hyponatremia, particularly in older adults
    4Education
    • Full benefit takes weeks — keep taking it even when nothing has changed yet
    • Do not stop suddenly; a taper is required
    • Change position slowly and report dizziness or unsteadiness
    • Avoid alcohol and other sedatives
    • Duloxetine: report fever with agitation, sweating and twitching — serotonin syndrome
    • Report worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm immediately
    Special populations
    • Older adults: gabapentin sedation and ataxia cause falls; duloxetine adds hyponatremia risk.
    • Renal impairment: gabapentin accumulates — the dose must be reduced to the clearance.
    • Patients on opioids: gabapentin adds to respiratory depression — a combination now carrying a specific warning.
    • Patients on other serotonergic drugs: duloxetine plus an SSRI, a triptan or tramadol risks serotonin syndrome.
    • Hepatic impairment or heavy alcohol use: duloxetine is avoided.
    • Patients with epilepsy: abrupt gabapentin withdrawal can precipitate seizures.
    Benzodiazepines
    one class, several different useslorazepam · alprazolam · diazepam
    Example drugslorazepam · alprazolam · diazepam
    Mechanism of action
    • Enhance GABA, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter — the whole CNS is dampened
    • That single mechanism explains every use and every risk: anxiolysis, sedation, muscle relaxation, seizure termination — and impaired alertness and breathing
    • Tolerance and physical dependence develop with regular use
    Therapeutic uses
    • Lorazepam: anxiety, agitation, and acute seizure management
    • Alprazolam: anxiety and panic — with prominent dependence and withdrawal concerns
    • Diazepam: anxiety, muscle spasm, seizure rescue, alcohol withdrawal
    • Procedural sedation
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: drowsiness, dizziness, unsteadiness, confusion, impaired coordination and memory
    • Serious: respiratory depression — greatly amplified with opioids or alcohol, falls, paradoxical agitation, dependence, and a withdrawal syndrome that can include seizures
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Respiratory status, alertness and falls risk before giving — her three pre-administration checks
    • Screen for opioids, alcohol and other sedatives. Her slide: avoid combining unless clinically justified and closely monitored — so a PRN benzodiazepine due soon after an opioid is a question, not a task
    • The indication and the medication history — how long has it been taken, and at what dose
    • Never stop abruptly after regular use — withdrawal can cause seizures
    • For seizure rescue: airway readiness and close monitoring afterwards
    2Vitals
    • Respiratory rate, depth and SpO2 before and after — with sedation level
    • Blood pressure, including orthostatic — hypotension plus sedation is the fall combination
    • Heart rate; continuous monitoring during procedural sedation
    3Labs
    • No routine level
    • Hepatic function — most are liver-metabolised and accumulate when it is impaired
    • Consider a toxicology screen when unexplained sedation appears
    4Education
    • Take exactly as prescribed and never share
    • Do not stop abruptly after regular use — a taper is required
    • Avoid alcohol and other sedating medicines
    • Do not drive while sedated
    • Rise slowly; remove home trip hazards
    • Report increasing need for the drug rather than taking extra
    • For a family given a rescue dose: give it, then call for help and watch the breathing
    Special populations
    • Older adults: her named risks — delirium and falls. Benzodiazepines are a core Beers criteria class; non-drug measures come first.
    • Patients on opioids: the high-risk pair — respiratory depression beyond the sum of the parts.
    • Alcohol use: additive CNS and respiratory depression; also the group most likely to need them for withdrawal, under monitoring.
    • Respiratory disease or sleep apnoea: less reserve when ventilatory drive is reduced.
    • Hepatic impairment: prolonged effect; lorazepam is often preferred for its simpler metabolism.
    • Pregnancy: neonatal sedation and withdrawal.
    • History of substance use disorder: dependence risk shapes whether the class is used at all.
    Non-benzodiazepine hypnotic
    hypnotic, not an anxiolyticzolpidem
    Example drugszolpidem
    Mechanism of action
    • Acts at a subtype of the GABA receptor that produces sleep without much anxiolytic or muscle-relaxant effect
    • Short-acting by design — intended to cover a night, not a day
    • Can produce behaviour during sleep that the person has no memory of
    Therapeutic uses
    • Insomnia only. Her slide title makes the distinction the point: it is a hypnotic, not an anxiolytic — giving it for daytime anxiety is a misuse of the drug
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: daytime drowsiness, dizziness, headache, a drugged feeling the next morning
    • Serious: FDA boxed warning: complex sleep behaviours including sleep-driving, sleep-walking and sleep-eating; falls, respiratory depression with other CNS depressants, dependence
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Give immediately before intended sleep, with the patient already in bed
    • Allow sufficient sleep time for the formulation — often 7–8 hours. Taken too late, the effect carries into waking hours
    • Ask directly about any prior complex sleep behaviour — a previous episode is a contraindication
    • If one occurs: stop the drug and contact the prescriber. This is not a timing problem to adjust around
    • Falls precautions — call bell within reach, bed low, path clear
    • Screen for other CNS depressants
    2Vitals
    • Respiratory rate and SpO2 if combined with another CNS depressant
    • Orthostatic blood pressure — night-time waking plus sedation is a fall
    • Document sleep achieved and next-day alertness
    3Labs
    • No routine level
    • Hepatic function — impairment prolongs the effect and lowers the dose
    4Education
    • Take it in bed, right before sleep — never earlier in the evening
    • Allow a full night before driving or anything requiring alertness
    • Report any episode of doing things while asleep with no memory of it — and stop the drug
    • No alcohol and no other sedatives
    • Do not take a second dose in the same night
    • Use non-drug sleep measures alongside it: consistent schedule, dark quiet room, no screens or caffeine late
    • Do not stop abruptly after long regular use
    Special populations
    • Older adults: her explicit direction — prioritise non-drug sleep strategies and fall precautions. Night-time falls and delirium are the dominant risks, and women and older adults clear the drug more slowly.
    • Patients on opioids or benzodiazepines: additive respiratory depression.
    • Anyone with a prior complex sleep behaviour: contraindicated, not merely cautioned.
    • Hospitalised patients: unfamiliar room, IV lines and urgency to reach a bathroom turn sedation into a fall.
    • Hepatic impairment: prolonged sedation into the next day.
    • Sleep apnoea or respiratory disease: reduced ventilatory reserve.
    SSRIs and SNRI
    weeks to work — watch early suicidalityfluoxetine · sertraline · duloxetine
    Example drugsfluoxetine · sertraline · duloxetine
    Mechanism of action
    • SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline): block serotonin reuptake → more serotonin signalling
    • SNRI (duloxetine): blocks serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake
    • The receptor effect is immediate but the clinical response takes weeks — the brain has to adapt downstream
    • Too much serotonergic activity produces serotonin syndrome
    Therapeutic uses
    • Depression, anxiety disorders, panic, OCD, PTSD
    • Duloxetine: also neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia
    • Generally first-line, because they are far safer in overdose than TCAs or MAOIs
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: nausea and GI upset early, headache, insomnia or sedation, sexual dysfunction, weight change
    • Serious: new or worsening suicidality, serotonin syndrome, hyponatremia, bleeding risk with NSAIDs or anticoagulants, discontinuation syndrome, duloxetine: raised blood pressure and hepatotoxicity
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Monitor mood and suicidality, especially in the first weeks — energy and initiative often return before mood lifts, which is when risk peaks
    • Teach that full response takes weeks; the most common reason patients stop is expecting it sooner
    • Review every other serotonergic drug — triptans, tramadol, linezolid, St John’s wort, another antidepressant
    • Serotonin syndrome: agitation, clonus and hyperreflexia, sweating, fever, diarrhea — hold the suspected drug and seek immediate evaluation
    • Never stop abruptly — a taper is required
    • Daily adherence
    2Vitals
    • Duloxetine and venlafaxine: blood pressure at baseline and during therapy
    • Orthostatic blood pressure
    • Temperature and heart rate if serotonin syndrome is suspected — fever and tachycardia are part of it
    • Weight at intervals
    3Labs
    • Sodium — SIADH-type hyponatremia, most often in older adults in the first weeks
    • Duloxetine: LFTs
    • Platelets or Hgb if combined with an NSAID or anticoagulant
    • No therapeutic drug level
    4Education
    • Keep taking it — full benefit may take several weeks
    • Report any thoughts of self-harm at once
    • Do not stop suddenly; ask for a taper
    • Report fever with agitation, sweating and twitching — serotonin syndrome
    • Check every new medicine, including OTC and herbal, for serotonin interactions
    • Early nausea usually settles; take with food
    • Sexual side effects are common and treatable — raise them rather than stopping the drug
    Special populations
    • Children, adolescents and young adults: boxed warning for increased suicidal thinking — close early monitoring.
    • Older adults: hyponatremia, falls and bleeding risk; fluoxetine’s long half-life makes it harder to adjust.
    • Patients on triptans, tramadol or another serotonergic drug: serotonin syndrome risk — the combination that produced her case.
    • Patients on NSAIDs or anticoagulants: serotonin is involved in platelet function, so GI bleeding risk rises.
    • Pregnancy: individualised — untreated depression carries its own risk.
    • Bipolar disorder: an antidepressant alone can precipitate mania — screen before starting.
    • Hepatic impairment or heavy alcohol use: duloxetine avoided.
    Tricyclic antidepressant
    anticholinergic, sedating, dangerous in overdoseamitriptyline
    Example drugsamitriptyline
    Mechanism of action
    • Blocks serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake — but also blocks muscarinic, histamine and alpha-1 receptors
    • Those extra blockades are the whole side-effect profile: anticholinergic effects, sedation, orthostatic hypotension
    • Cardiac sodium-channel effects make overdose lethal — a limited quantity may be dispensed to a patient at risk
    Therapeutic uses
    • Depression — now largely second-line
    • Neuropathic pain and migraine prophylaxis at lower doses
    • Insomnia associated with chronic pain
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, sedation, weight gain, orthostatic hypotension
    • Serious: cardiac toxicity and dysrhythmia in overdose, falls from orthostasis, confusion and delirium in older adults, QT prolongation, new suicidality, serotonin syndrome in combination
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Falls and overdose precautions — her two named teaching priorities for this class
    • Anticholinergic burden: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, confusion — and every other anticholinergic the patient takes
    • Cardiac history and ECG before starting in older adults or known heart disease
    • Mood and suicidality — made more serious by how dangerous an overdose is
    • Bowel and bladder function
    • Give at bedtime to use the sedation rather than fight it
    2Vitals
    • Orthostatic blood pressure — lying and standing, the measurement that predicts the fall
    • Heart rate and rhythm; ECG for QT where indicated
    • Weight
    3Labs
    • Electrolytes — potassium and magnesium, which affect QT
    • No routine level in ordinary practice; levels are used in overdose
    • Hepatic function
    4Education
    • Rise slowly from lying or sitting — dizziness on standing is the main injury risk
    • Dry mouth: sugar-free gum, sips of water, good dental care
    • Increase fluid and fibre for constipation; report inability to pass urine
    • Keep only the quantity dispensed and store it securely — overdose is dangerous
    • Full effect takes weeks
    • Avoid alcohol
    • Do not stop abruptly
    • Report palpitations, fainting or confusion
    Special populations
    • Older adults: a Beers criteria drug — anticholinergic effects, orthostasis, falls and delirium all converge.
    • Cardiac disease or conduction abnormality: sodium-channel effects risk dysrhythmia.
    • Patients at risk of suicide: lethality in overdose shapes prescribing and quantity dispensed.
    • Benign prostatic hyperplasia: anticholinergic effect can cause acute urinary retention.
    • Narrow-angle glaucoma: pupil dilation can precipitate an acute attack.
    • Patients on other anticholinergics: additive burden — benztropine, antihistamines, oxybutynin.
    • Dementia: anticholinergic drugs worsen cognition.
    MAOI
    the food and drug interaction classphenelzine
    Example drugsphenelzine
    Mechanism of action
    • Irreversibly inhibits monoamine oxidase, the enzyme that breaks down serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine — and dietary tyramine
    • With the enzyme gone, absorbed tyramine releases a surge of norepinephrine → hypertensive crisis
    • Because inhibition is irreversible, the effect persists about two weeks after stopping — washout periods are mandatory
    Therapeutic uses
    • Treatment-resistant depression
    • Atypical depression, after safer options have failed
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: orthostatic hypotension, insomnia, weight gain, dizziness, dry mouth, sexual dysfunction
    • Serious: hypertensive crisis from tyramine or sympathomimetics; serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs — which can be fatal
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Verify ALL medications — prescription, OTC, herbal. Her slide says to check all of them, because so many interact
    • Hypertensive crisis: severe headache, marked hypertension, chest pain, neurological symptoms → emergency evaluation
    • Avoid high-tyramine foods — aged cheeses, cured and fermented meats, draught beer, soy products, overripe fruit
    • No sympathomimetics — OTC decongestants, stimulants
    • No serotonergic drugs — SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, tramadol, meperidine, dextromethorphan
    • Observe the washout period when switching to or from another antidepressant
    2Vitals
    • Blood pressure at every opportunity, lying and standing — this class runs both low and dangerously high
    • Heart rate
    • Temperature if serotonin syndrome is suspected
    3Labs
    • No routine level
    • Hepatic function
    • Electrolytes if vomiting accompanies a crisis
    4Education
    • Carry a list of foods to avoid and keep it with you — the restriction is absolute, not approximate
    • Report severe headache immediately — it is the first sign of a hypertensive crisis
    • Ask the pharmacist before any new medicine, including cold remedies
    • Rise slowly — orthostatic hypotension is common
    • Wear or carry medical identification
    • The food restriction continues about two weeks after stopping
    • Do not stop abruptly
    Special populations
    • Older adults: orthostatic hypotension and falls; interacting medications accumulate with polypharmacy.
    • Patients on any serotonergic drug: contraindicated — a washout is required in both directions.
    • Patients who cannot follow a strict diet: adherence is a safety requirement, not a preference, so the class may be unsuitable.
    • Surgical patients: interactions with anesthetic agents and meperidine — the team must know.
    • Cardiovascular disease: a crisis is far more dangerous.
    • Pheochromocytoma: contraindicated.
    Mood stabiliser
    the safety triad — narrow indexlithium
    Example drugslithium
    Mechanism of action
    • Alters sodium transport and several second-messenger systems in neurons, stabilising mood
    • The kidney handles lithium much as it handles sodium — so sodium loss or dehydration means more lithium is reabsorbed and the level rises on an unchanged dose
    • A narrow therapeutic index: the effective level sits close to the toxic one
    Therapeutic uses
    • Bipolar disorder — acute mania and long-term maintenance
    • Reduces suicide risk in bipolar illness
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: fine hand tremor, increased thirst and urination, nausea, weight gain, metallic taste
    • Serious: toxicity — worsening or coarse tremor, vomiting and diarrhea, ataxia, confusion, progressing to seizures and arrhythmia; hypothyroidism; nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and chronic kidney injury
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Her safety triad. (1) Narrow therapeutic index — correctly timed levels, usually about 12 hours after the last dose. (2) Consistent salt and fluid intake — dehydration increases toxicity. (3) Monitor kidney and thyroid function
    • Toxicity: worsening tremor, vomiting or diarrhea, ataxia, confusion → hold and escalate. A fine tremor can be expected; a coarse tremor with ataxia is not
    • Review interacting drugs — especially NSAIDs and some diuretics, both of which raise the level
    • Any cause of fluid loss is a lithium problem: vomiting, diarrhea, fever, heavy sweating, hot weather, strenuous exercise — and toxicity itself causes vomiting and diarrhea, which worsens the dehydration
    • Baseline and periodic assessment of mood, cognition and gait
    2Vitals
    • Temperature — fever means fluid loss means a rising level
    • Blood pressure, heart rate and rhythm
    • Intake, output and daily weight where fluid balance is uncertain
    • Neurological status and gait
    3Labs
    • Lithium level — timed correctly, and whenever toxicity is suspected or the clinical picture changes
    • Renal function — BUN, creatinine, urinalysis
    • Thyroid function — TSH
    • Sodium — a low sodium drives the level up
    • Calcium; ECG in older adults or cardiac disease
    • Pregnancy test where relevant
    4Education
    • Keep salt and fluid intake steady day to day — do not start a low-sodium diet or a new fluid regimen without telling the prescriber
    • Report vomiting, diarrhea, fever or heavy sweating — these raise the level
    • Report a worsening or coarse tremor, unsteadiness, confusion or slurred speech at once
    • No NSAIDs without checking — use acetaminophen instead unless told otherwise
    • Attend every level and blood test, and know when the last dose was taken
    • Take extra care in hot weather and with exercise
    • Do not stop on your own
    Special populations
    • Older adults: reduced renal clearance, less thirst sensation and more polypharmacy — toxicity at standard doses.
    • Patients on NSAIDs or thiazide diuretics: both reduce lithium clearance and raise the level.
    • Patients with vomiting, diarrhea or any dehydrating illness: the mechanism behind her case — fluid loss raises the level while symptoms mimic toxicity.
    • Renal impairment: lithium is cleared only by the kidney — often a contraindication.
    • Pregnancy: teratogenic risk including cardiac defects — needs careful discussion.
    • Thyroid disease: lithium causes hypothyroidism and can worsen existing disease.
    • Patients on a low-sodium diet or taking salt tablets: either change shifts the level — consistency is what matters.
    Typical antipsychotic
    EPS is movement · NMS is systemichaloperidol
    Example drugshaloperidol
    Mechanism of action
    • Strong dopamine D2 blockade — reduces psychotic symptoms
    • But dopamine also controls movement, so blocking it produces extrapyramidal symptoms
    • Blocks D2 in the chemoreceptor trigger zone too, which is why it also treats nausea
    • Affects cardiac conduction → QT prolongation
    Therapeutic uses
    • Schizophrenia and psychotic disorders
    • Acute agitation and delirium with psychosis
    • Nausea and vomiting, and Tourette syndrome
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: EPS, sedation, dry mouth, orthostatic hypotension
    • Serious: neuroleptic malignant syndrome, QT prolongation and dysrhythmia, acute dystonia, tardive dyskinesia, agranulocytosis (rare)
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • EPS — the movement effects. Dystonia: spasms of neck, eyes or tongue, which can threaten the airway and needs treatment now. Akathisia: inner restlessness driving constant movement — often mistaken for worsening agitation, and raising the dose makes it worse. Parkinsonism: tremor, rigidity, shuffling gait. Tardive dyskinesia: late, involuntary face and tongue movements that may be permanent
    • NMS is the emergency: high fever, severe lead-pipe rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability → stop the antipsychotic and get urgent treatment
    • The distinction to hold onto: EPS is movement; NMS is systemic — fever and rigidity together move it from a side effect to an emergency
    • Use a standard movement-disorder scale at intervals
    • Review every QT-prolonging drug and swallowing safety
    2Vitals
    • Temperature — the vital sign that separates NMS from EPS
    • Blood pressure, lying and standing, and heart rate — autonomic instability means both swing
    • Respiratory rate and level of consciousness
    • ECG for QT at baseline and with dose changes
    3Labs
    • Potassium and magnesium — low levels worsen QT prolongation
    • CK (creatine kinase) — markedly raised in NMS from muscle breakdown
    • WBC with differential
    • Renal function — myoglobin from NMS injures the kidney
    4Education
    • Report any new muscle stiffness, restlessness, or abnormal movements of face, tongue or neck
    • Report fever with stiffness immediately — this is an emergency
    • Rise slowly; orthostatic hypotension is common early
    • Avoid alcohol and other sedatives
    • Take as prescribed; stopping abruptly risks relapse
    • Avoid overheating — temperature regulation is impaired
    • Keep follow-up appointments for movement and ECG monitoring
    Special populations
    • Older adults with dementia: boxed warning for increased mortality — antipsychotics are not first-line for behavioural symptoms.
    • Older adults generally: higher EPS, falls, orthostasis and anticholinergic sensitivity.
    • Patients with cardiac disease or QT prolongation: additive conduction risk, especially IV.
    • Patients on other QT-prolonging drugs: many antiemetics, antibiotics and antidepressants qualify.
    • Parkinson’s disease: D2 blockade worsens the disease directly.
    • Dehydrated, restrained or agitated patients: recognised risk factors for NMS.
    • Patients with low potassium or magnesium: correct before dosing.
    Atypical antipsychotics
    lower EPS, metabolic costrisperidone · olanzapine
    Example drugsrisperidone · olanzapine
    Mechanism of action
    • Block D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors — the serotonin component is why EPS risk is lower
    • Lower EPS risk than high-potency typicals, but not zero — risperidone at higher doses behaves more like a typical
    • Also block histamine and other receptors, driving weight gain and metabolic effects
    Therapeutic uses
    • Schizophrenia and psychotic disorders
    • Bipolar disorder — mania and maintenance
    • Adjunct in treatment-resistant depression
    • Acute agitation
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: weight gain, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, constipation, raised prolactin with risperidone
    • Serious: metabolic syndrome — weight, glucose and lipids; new or worsened diabetes; EPS and tardive dyskinesia (lower risk, not absent); NMS; QT prolongation; increased mortality in elderly dementia
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Metabolic effects are the monitoring priority for this class: weight, glucose, lipids
    • Still monitor movement disorders — lower risk is not no risk, and tardive dyskinesia can still develop
    • Sedation and orthostasis — falls risk, especially early and after dose increases
    • NMS remains possible — the same fever-plus-rigidity picture
    • Adherence, and prolactin symptoms with risperidone
    2Vitals
    • Weight and waist circumference at baseline and regular intervals — the vital sign of this class
    • Blood pressure, lying and standing
    • Heart rate; ECG where QT is a concern
    • Temperature if NMS is suspected
    3Labs
    • Fasting glucose or HbA1c at baseline and periodically
    • Lipid panel at baseline and periodically
    • Prolactin if symptomatic — galactorrhea, menstrual change, sexual dysfunction
    • CBC, LFTs, electrolytes including potassium and magnesium
    4Education
    • Expect weight monitoring and act early — diet and activity from the start, not after 15 kg
    • Report increased thirst, urination, hunger or fatigue — possible new diabetes
    • Rise slowly
    • Report new stiffness, restlessness or abnormal movements
    • Report fever with rigidity immediately
    • Keep laboratory follow-up appointments
    • Do not stop abruptly; avoid alcohol
    Special populations
    • Older adults with dementia: boxed warning for increased mortality.
    • Patients with diabetes, obesity or metabolic syndrome: olanzapine has the strongest metabolic effect — drug choice matters.
    • Adolescents: more weight gain and prolactin elevation than adults.
    • Older adults generally: orthostasis, sedation and falls.
    • Parkinson’s disease: D2 blockade worsens motor symptoms, though these are preferred over haloperidol if one is needed.
    • Cardiac disease: QT and orthostatic effects.
    Antiseizure medications
    each has its own red flagphenytoin · levetiracetam · lamotrigine
    Example drugsphenytoin · levetiracetam · lamotrigine
    Mechanism of action
    • Phenytoin: stabilises neuronal sodium channels. Narrow therapeutic index with many interactions
    • Levetiracetam: binds a synaptic vesicle protein; few interactions, renally dosed
    • Lamotrigine: sodium-channel action; requires slow titration to reduce rash risk
    • None of the long-term agents should be stopped abruptly — withdrawal can precipitate seizures or status epilepticus
    Therapeutic uses
    • Epilepsy — agent chosen by seizure type
    • Lamotrigine: also bipolar maintenance
    • Phenytoin: status epilepticus after benzodiazepine rescue
    • Some are also used for neuropathic pain
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: phenytoin: gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, sedation. Levetiracetam: sedation, dizziness, irritability. Lamotrigine: headache, dizziness, nausea
    • Serious: phenytoin: nystagmus and ataxia (early toxicity), severe rash, cardiovascular collapse with rapid IV. Levetiracetam: mood and behaviour change including suicidality. Lamotrigine: Stevens-Johnson syndrome — serious rash, especially early
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Phenytoin: nystagmus and ataxia are the classic early toxicity signs — visible at the bedside before a level returns. Assess levels, neurological status and skin
    • Levetiracetam: ask directly about depression, agitation and self-harm. Patients rarely connect a mood change to a seizure medicine, so the question has to be asked
    • Lamotrigine: a new rash — especially with mucosal lesions — means stop pending urgent evaluation. Risk is highest early and with too-rapid titration
    • Diazepam rescue: airway readiness and close monitoring after the dose — respiratory depression is the risk
    • Never stop abruptly
    • Phenytoin: review interactions — it induces hepatic enzymes and alters many drugs including warfarin and oral contraceptives
    • Seizure precautions, and a record of seizure frequency and type
    2Vitals
    • Neurological assessment — gait, eye movements, speech, level of consciousness
    • IV phenytoin: continuous cardiac monitoring and blood pressure — rapid infusion causes hypotension and dysrhythmia
    • Respiratory rate and SpO2 after any benzodiazepine rescue dose
    • Temperature with any serious rash
    3Labs
    • Phenytoin level — narrow therapeutic index; also albumin, since only free drug is active
    • Levetiracetam: renal function to set the dose
    • CBC and LFTs for phenytoin and lamotrigine
    • Electrolytes including sodium
    • Vitamin D and calcium with long-term phenytoin — it affects bone metabolism
    4Education
    • Never stop suddenly — stopping can cause a seizure worse than any before
    • Report any new rash immediately, especially with mouth or eye sores
    • Report any change in mood, new irritability, depression or thoughts of self-harm
    • Phenytoin: meticulous oral hygiene and regular dental care for gum overgrowth; report unsteadiness or double vision
    • Attend level checks and know the last dose time
    • Avoid alcohol
    • Phenytoin reduces oral contraceptive effectiveness — discuss alternatives
    • Carry medical identification; follow local driving rules
    Special populations
    • Pregnancy: several agents are teratogenic — phenytoin and valproate notably. Needs planning, folic acid and specialist input; uncontrolled seizures are also harmful.
    • Older adults: sedation, ataxia and falls; low albumin raises free phenytoin at a “normal” total level.
    • Renal impairment: levetiracetam requires dose reduction.
    • Patients starting lamotrigine: the titration schedule is a safety measure — skipping ahead raises SJS risk.
    • Patients with depression: levetiracetam can worsen mood — monitor closely or choose another agent.
    • Patients on warfarin or oral contraceptives: phenytoin’s enzyme induction changes their effect.
    • Children: weight-based dosing and behavioural effects that may be missed as “school problems”.
    Antiparkinson — dopamine replacement
    give it on timecarbidopa/levodopa
    Example drugscarbidopa/levodopa
    Mechanism of action
    • Levodopa crosses into the brain and becomes dopamine; dopamine itself cannot cross
    • Carbidopa blocks that conversion in the periphery, so more levodopa reaches the brain and there is less peripheral nausea and hypotension
    • Benefit tracks the drug level closely, which is why timing dominates everything else
    • The vitamin B6 nuance: B6 accelerates peripheral conversion, so the old advice to avoid it applied to levodopa alone. With carbidopa blocking that pathway, B6 supplements are compatible with carbidopa/levodopa — her slide says so explicitly
    Therapeutic uses
    • Parkinson’s disease — the most effective symptomatic treatment
    • Drug-induced parkinsonism in some cases
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: nausea, orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, dyskinesias, vivid dreams, dark sweat and urine
    • Serious: hallucinations and psychosis, severe orthostatic hypotension and falls, wearing-off and on–off fluctuations, impulse-control behaviours; abrupt withdrawal can cause a syndrome resembling NMS
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Give ON TIME. A late dose can leave a patient unable to move, speak or swallow until it takes effect — so a dose delayed for an off-ward appointment is a real harm, not an administrative detail
    • Assess wearing-off, mobility and dyskinesias — her three assessment targets. Document what the patient can actually do, and when
    • Watch orthostatic hypotension, hallucinations and nausea
    • High-protein meals can reduce the response in some patients — individualise the timing; dietary amino acids compete with levodopa for transport
    • Falls risk — the disease and the drug both contribute
    • Swallowing safety
    • Never stop abruptly
    2Vitals
    • Orthostatic blood pressure — lying and standing, at baseline and with dose changes
    • Heart rate
    • Document mobility and gait at peak and trough — the pattern tells you about wearing-off
    • Weight — Parkinson’s disease carries nutritional risk
    3Labs
    • No routine therapeutic level
    • CBC, LFTs and renal function periodically
    • Glucose, and a mental-status assessment where psychosis is suspected
    4Education
    • Take it at the same times every day, and take it on time — even in hospital. Ask for home-time dosing
    • Rise slowly — dizziness on standing is common early
    • Report hallucinations, confusion or new compulsive behaviours (gambling, shopping, eating)
    • Dark sweat or urine is harmless
    • Nausea often settles; a small non-protein snack can help
    • Discuss meal timing if the response seems weaker after high-protein meals
    • Never stop suddenly
    • Vitamin B6 supplements are compatible with this combination
    Special populations
    • Older adults: higher risk of hallucinations, confusion, orthostasis and falls.
    • Hospitalised patients: the group most harmed by timing — missed and standardised dose times cause avoidable immobility.
    • Patients on antipsychotics: D2 blockade works directly against this drug; haloperidol is particularly problematic.
    • Patients on an MAOI: risk of hypertensive crisis.
    • High-protein diets: competition for absorption and transport may need meal-timing changes.
    • Patients with psychiatric history: higher risk of drug-induced psychosis.
    • Narrow-angle glaucoma and melanoma history: specific cautions.
    Anticholinergic for movement effects
    drug-induced parkinsonism & dystoniabenztropine
    Example drugsbenztropine
    Mechanism of action
    • Blocks muscarinic receptors in the basal ganglia, restoring the acetylcholine–dopamine balance that D2 blockade disturbed
    • This is why it treats drug-induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia rather than the disease itself
    • The same blockade everywhere else produces the classic anticholinergic effects
    Therapeutic uses
    • Drug-induced parkinsonism from antipsychotics
    • Acute dystonia — given urgently, since laryngeal spasm threatens the airway
    • Adjunct in Parkinson’s disease, mainly for tremor
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, blurred vision, overheating — her four named effects plus impaired sweating
    • Serious: confusion and delirium, especially in older adults; acute urinary retention; heat stroke from impaired sweating; acute angle-closure glaucoma; tachycardia
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Anticholinergic effects are the assessment: dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, overheating
    • Older adults: confusion and delirium risk — her specific caution. A new confusion after this drug is started is a drug effect, not progression of the illness
    • Bladder function — ask about difficulty passing urine and palpate for retention
    • Bowel pattern
    • Add up the total anticholinergic burden — antihistamines, TCAs, oxybutynin all stack
    • Distinguish akathisia, which this drug does not help, from parkinsonism and dystonia, which it does
    2Vitals
    • Temperature, and the ability to sweat — impaired sweating means heat intolerance
    • Heart rate — tachycardia from vagal blockade
    • Blood pressure
    • Intake and output; bladder scan if retention is suspected
    3Labs
    • No routine level
    • Renal function if retention is prolonged
    • Electrolytes if intake is poor
    4Education
    • Avoid heat — hot weather, hot baths, heavy exercise. You cannot sweat normally, so you can overheat quickly
    • Report inability to pass urine
    • Dry mouth: sugar-free gum, sips of water, dental care
    • Increase fluid and fibre for constipation
    • Report new confusion — particularly in an older adult
    • Rise slowly; do not drive if vision is blurred
    • Do not stop abruptly
    Special populations
    • Older adults: her named risk — confusion and delirium. A Beers criteria drug; anticholinergic effects worsen cognition.
    • Benign prostatic hyperplasia: can precipitate acute urinary retention.
    • Narrow-angle glaucoma: contraindicated — pupil dilation can trigger an acute attack.
    • Dementia: cognition worsens measurably.
    • Hot climates or outdoor work: impaired sweating causes heat illness.
    • Patients on other anticholinergics: cumulative burden — delirium, retention and constipation.
    • Patients with tardive dyskinesia: can worsen it — it is not the treatment for that.
    Muscle relaxants
    two drugs, two different jobsbaclofen · cyclobenzaprine
    Example drugsbaclofen · cyclobenzaprine
    Mechanism of action
    • Baclofen: a GABA-B agonist acting in the spinal cord to reduce reflex activity — used for neurologic spasticity
    • Cyclobenzaprine: acts centrally on the brainstem for short-term musculoskeletal spasm; structurally related to the TCAs, which is why it is anticholinergic and sedating
    • Both: sedation, dizziness and falls — her shared warning
    • Neither is an analgesic, and neither treats the cause of the spasm
    Therapeutic uses
    • Baclofen: spasticity from multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury or cerebral palsy — oral or intrathecal
    • Cyclobenzaprine: acute musculoskeletal spasm, short-term use — typically 2–3 weeks
    • Adjuncts, alongside physical therapy and positioning
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: sedation, dizziness, weakness; cyclobenzaprine: dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation
    • Serious: baclofen: abrupt withdrawal can cause seizures, delirium, hyperthermia and severe rebound spasticity — especially intrathecal. Falls; respiratory depression with other CNS depressants; cyclobenzaprine: serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs, cardiac effects
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Baclofen withdrawal is the headline risk — her slide: withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium. If a patient on home baclofen is admitted and it is missing from the orders, that is a problem to raise before the next dose is due
    • Falls risk from sedation, dizziness and weakness — and note that reducing spasticity can itself reduce the tone a patient was using to stand or transfer
    • Baseline spasticity and function, so the effect can be judged
    • Screen for other CNS depressants
    • Cyclobenzaprine: confirm the intended short course and the anticholinergic burden; check for serotonergic drugs
    2Vitals
    • Orthostatic blood pressure and heart rate
    • Respiratory rate if combined with an opioid or benzodiazepine
    • Temperature with suspected baclofen withdrawal — hyperthermia is part of it
    • Document function and tone, not just comfort
    3Labs
    • No routine level
    • Renal function — baclofen is renally cleared and accumulates when it is impaired
    • LFTs with prolonged use
    4Education
    • Never stop baclofen suddenly — it must be tapered, and an intrathecal pump problem is an emergency
    • Tell any admitting team you take baclofen so doses are not missed
    • Expect drowsiness and dizziness; do not drive until you know the effect
    • Avoid alcohol and other sedatives
    • Rise slowly and use the mobility aids provided
    • Cyclobenzaprine is for short-term use only
    • Keep up physical therapy — the drug supports it rather than replacing it
    Special populations
    • Older adults: cyclobenzaprine is a Beers criteria drug — sedation, anticholinergic effects and falls; often poorly tolerated.
    • Patients on home baclofen who are admitted: the withdrawal scenario — a missed home medication becomes seizures and delirium.
    • Intrathecal baclofen patients: pump failure or catheter problems cause life-threatening withdrawal — an emergency.
    • Renal impairment: baclofen accumulates; the dose must be reduced.
    • Patients on opioids or benzodiazepines: additive sedation and respiratory depression.
    • Patients who rely on spasticity to stand or transfer: reducing tone can reduce function — assess mobility, not tone alone.
    • Patients on serotonergic drugs: cyclobenzaprine adds serotonin syndrome risk.
    Triptan
    acute migraine — not preventionsumatriptan
    Example drugssumatriptan
    Mechanism of action
    • 5-HT1B/1D agonist — constricts dilated cranial vessels and reduces neurogenic inflammation and pain transmission
    • That vasoconstriction is not perfectly selective, which is the entire basis of its cardiac contraindications
    • Acute treatment, not prevention — her first line on the slide. It is taken when a migraine starts, not daily
    Therapeutic uses
    • Acute migraine, ideally taken early in the attack
    • Cluster headache (subcutaneous)
    • Not for prophylaxis — and not for ordinary tension headache
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: flushing, tingling, a sensation of chest or throat tightness, dizziness, drowsiness, injection-site reaction
    • Serious: coronary vasospasm and myocardial ischemia or infarction, dysrhythmia, stroke, raised blood pressure, serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs, medication-overuse headache
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Avoid in coronary artery disease, prior stroke or TIA, and uncontrolled hypertension — her three contraindications. A cardiac history turns this order into one to clarify
    • Evaluate new or severe chest symptoms rather than calling them “expected”. Mild transient tightness is described with triptans, but chest pain in a patient with cardiac risk gets worked up, not dismissed
    • Review all serotonergic drugs — SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol: serotonin syndrome risk, and the pairing behind her case
    • No MAOI within two weeks, and no ergot within 24 hours
    • Headache pattern and frequency — frequent use causes medication-overuse headache
    • Confirm the diagnosis is migraine; a sudden worst-ever headache needs evaluation first
    2Vitals
    • Blood pressure before and after — it can rise
    • Heart rate and rhythm; ECG where cardiac risk exists
    • Document headache relief, function and whether a second dose was needed
    3Labs
    • No routine level
    • Lipids, glucose and cardiac risk assessment in patients with risk factors
    • Pregnancy test where relevant
    4Education
    • Take it as early in the attack as possible — it works far better early than late
    • Report chest pain, pressure, jaw or arm pain, or shortness of breath — do not dismiss it
    • This treats an attack; it does not prevent migraines — frequent attacks need a preventive plan instead
    • Do not exceed the prescribed doses in 24 hours
    • Tell the prescriber about all antidepressants and other serotonergic drugs
    • Keep a headache diary — frequency, triggers, what worked
    • Rest in a dark quiet room alongside the medication
    • Report using it more than about twice a week
    Special populations
    • Coronary artery disease, prior MI, or Prinzmetal angina: contraindicated — vasoconstriction in a narrowed coronary artery.
    • Prior stroke or TIA: contraindicated.
    • Uncontrolled hypertension: contraindicated until controlled.
    • Patients with cardiac risk factors — older age, smoking, diabetes, strong family history — may need evaluation before a first dose.
    • Patients on SSRIs or SNRIs: serotonin syndrome risk — usable with monitoring and teaching, not automatically.
    • Patients on MAOIs: contraindicated.
    • Pregnancy: individualised; some triptans have more reassuring data.
    • Hemiplegic or basilar migraine: contraindicated.
    Critical-care agents
    recognition level only for Semester 1propofol · succinylcholine
    Example drugspropofol · succinylcholine
    Mechanism of action
    • Propofol: a short-acting IV sedative/anesthetic — profound CNS depression with rapid onset and offset
    • Succinylcholine: a depolarising neuromuscular blocker — it paralyses skeletal muscle, including the diaphragm
    • “Paralysis ≠ sedation or analgesia.” Her line, and the single most important idea here: a paralysed patient can be fully aware and in pain while unable to move, breathe or signal
    Therapeutic uses
    • Propofol: procedural sedation, induction of anesthesia, sedation of a ventilated patient
    • Succinylcholine: rapid-sequence intubation and short procedures requiring paralysis
    • Both are administered in settings with trained personnel and airway support — never on a general ward by a first-semester nurse
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: propofol: hypotension, injection-site pain, apnoea. Succinylcholine: muscle fasciculations then paralysis, post-procedure muscle pain
    • Serious: propofol: apnoea and hypotension, bradycardia, propofol infusion syndrome. Succinylcholine: hyperkalemia, malignant hyperthermia → dantrolene, prolonged paralysis, bradycardia
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Her framing: these are recognition-level medications for Semester 1. Know what they do and why they are dangerous — you are not expected to manage them, and an exam item will not ask you to administer one
    • Propofol: needs trained personnel, airway readiness and monitoring, because it can produce apnoea and hypotension
    • Propofol: check exact product allergy precautions before use
    • Succinylcholine: requires ventilation and an appropriate sedation plan. Paralysis provides no sedation and no pain relief
    • Succinylcholine: hyperkalemia, and malignant hyperthermia treated with dantrolene
    • Recognise the setting: continuous monitoring, immediate airway equipment, a provider able to intubate
    2Vitals
    • Continuous respiratory rate, SpO2 and end-tidal CO₂
    • Continuous blood pressure — propofol drops it
    • Continuous ECG and heart rate
    • Temperature — a sharp rise suggests malignant hyperthermia
    3Labs
    • Potassium — succinylcholine releases it from cells, a danger in burns, crush injury, prolonged immobility or renal failure
    • ABG, lactate and CK
    • Triglycerides with prolonged propofol infusion — it is delivered in a lipid emulsion
    4Education
    • For a patient or family before a procedure: the medication works quickly, breathing will be supported and monitoring is continuous
    • Afterwards: grogginess and muscle aching are expected
    • Report any history of a problem with anesthesia, including a family history of malignant hyperthermia — this matters before, not after
    • For the student: recognise the names, the dangers and the setting; the testable idea is that paralysis is not sedation
    Special populations
    • Burns, crush injury, prolonged immobility, spinal cord injury or renal failure: succinylcholine can release enough potassium to cause cardiac arrest.
    • Personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia: succinylcholine is contraindicated — dantrolene must be available where it is used.
    • Hypovolemic or hypotensive patients: propofol drops blood pressure further.
    • Older adults: more sensitive — lower doses, more hypotension.
    • Egg or soy allergy: the reason for checking the specific product precautions.
    • Children: higher risk of succinylcholine complications, so its use is restricted.
    • Any paralysed patient: requires sedation and analgesia alongside, plus eye care and positioning — they cannot tell you anything.
    Ch 35 · slides 3–9

    1How the endocrine system is wired — and why that wiring is a drug-safety rule

    The objective is to identify the major glands and their hormones. The part worth more than memorising the list is the loop: almost every nursing caution in this unit falls out of negative feedback.

    PrincipleWhat it meansWhy it matters at the bedside
    Hormones as messengersProduced in small amounts, secreted into the bloodstream, bind specific receptors, then modify cell activityTiny dose changes produce large effects — which is why endocrine drugs are titrated slowly and monitored by lab, not by feel
    Works with the nervous systemThe two control systems together maintain homeostasis — nerves act in milliseconds, hormones over minutes to daysExplains why endocrine problems present as gradual, whole-body change rather than one sharp symptom
    Negative feedbackLow hormone → more stimulation. High hormone → less stimulation. The loop holds the level steadyThis single rule explains most of this unit — including why a hormone given as a drug shuts down the gland that makes it
    HypothalamusMonitors homeostasis and releases both stimulating and inhibiting hormones to the pituitaryThe top of the chain — a problem here looks identical at the bedside to a problem in the gland itself
    Pituitary lobeHormonesThe drug connection in this unit
    AnteriorGH · ACTH · FSH/LH · Prolactin · TSHGH → somatropin and octreotide · ACTH → the corticosteroids · FSH/LH → leuprolide and cetrorelix · TSH → the thyroid agents
    PosteriorADH (vasopressin) · OxytocinADH → desmopressin. The posterior lobe stores and releases; it does not manufacture
    DirectionNameWhere the fault can sit
    Too little hormoneHypofunctionThe gland, the pituitary, or the hypothalamus — three possible levels, one presentation
    Too much hormoneHyperfunctionSame three levels. Treatment is either replacement or suppression, and which one depends on the direction, not the level

    The idea that unlocks the rest of the unit. Negative feedback is not just a diagram — it is a safety rule. Give a hormone from outside and the body reads the level as high, so it stops its own production and the gland shrinks. Stop that drug suddenly and there is nothing left to take over. That is the entire reason corticosteroids are tapered rather than discontinued, and it is the same loop that makes a thyroid or adrenal axis slow to recover. Every time you meet a hormone replacement in this unit, ask what the body stopped doing while the drug was on board.

    Three levels, one picture. Low cortisol can mean a failing adrenal gland, a pituitary making no ACTH, or a hypothalamus making no releasing hormone. The patient looks the same in all three. This is why endocrine workups measure the stimulating hormone alongside the target hormone — a low cortisol with a high ACTH points at the gland, while a low cortisol with a low ACTH points upstream.

    Ch 36 · slides 11–21, 29

    2Hypothalamic and pituitary agents — five prototypes, three axes

    Growth hormone, posterior pituitary (ADH), and the GnRH axis. Each axis has a drug that turns it up and one that turns it down, which is the cleanest way to hold five drugs in mind.

    Drug · classMechanismIndicationsContraindications
    somatropinGH agonist — stimulates growth through GH receptorsGH deficiency · Turner syndromeClosed epiphyses · acute illness
    octreotideGH antagonist — inhibits GH releaseAcromegalyGallbladder disease · caution in diabetes
    desmopressinSynthetic ADH → ↑ water reabsorption at the kidneyDiabetes insipidus · nocturnal enuresisRenal failure · hyponatremia
    leuprolideGnRH agonist → continuous stimulation ultimately suppresses LH and FSHProstate cancer · endometriosisPregnancy
    cetrorelixGnRH antagonist — blocks the receptor directly, with no initial surgeControlled ovarian stimulationPregnancy · ovarian cysts
    DrugAdverse effectsNursing care
    somatropinEdema · joint pain · hyperglycemiaMonitor growth plates, glucose and thyroid levels; rotate injection sites
    octreotideGI upset · gallstones · bradycardiaMonitor glucose, liver function and ECG
    desmopressinHyponatremia · headache · fluid retentionMonitor intake and output, sodium, daily weight
    leuprolideHot flashes · mood changes · bone lossMonitor bone density; teach about the flare reaction
    cetrorelixInjection-site pain · ovarian hyperstimulationMonitor for abdominal pain and ascites

    Agonist and antagonist on the same axis — read the goal, not the word. Somatropin and octreotide both act on growth hormone and do opposite things; leuprolide and cetrorelix both act on GnRH. The trap is assuming “agonist” always means “more”. Leuprolide is an agonist that ends in suppression: the GnRH receptor needs pulses to keep working, so continuous stimulation exhausts it. That is also why there is an initial flare — symptoms or tumour activity briefly worsen before they improve. A patient with prostate cancer whose bone pain increases in the first two weeks has not failed treatment, and telling them so in advance is the teaching point.

    Desmopressin is a water drug, not a urine drug. It makes the kidney hold water, so every adverse effect is dilution: sodium falls, weight rises, headache comes on. That is why the monitoring list is intake/output, sodium and daily weight rather than anything about the bladder — and why existing hyponatremia is a contraindication rather than a caution. Expect the opposite picture from the diabetes insipidus it treats: too little ADH makes dilute urine in volume, too much makes concentrated urine and dilute blood.

    Ch 37 · slides 22–28

    3Adrenocortical agents — glucocorticoid vs mineralocorticoid

    Two prototypes that are easy to blur together and behave completely differently. Separating what each hormone does makes the adverse effects and the contraindications predictable rather than memorised.

    Drug · classMechanismIndicationsContraindications
    prednisoneGlucocorticoid — anti-inflammatory, suppresses the immune responseAsthma · autoimmune disease · adrenal insufficiencyActive infection · caution in diabetes
    fludrocortisoneMineralocorticoid — ↑ sodium retention, ↑ potassium excretionAddison’s disease · adrenal insufficiencyHeart failure · hypertension
    DrugAdverse effectsNursing care
    prednisoneHyperglycemia · infection risk · mood changesDo not stop abruptly · give with food · monitor glucose
    fludrocortisoneFluid retention · hypertension · hypokalemiaMonitor BP, weight and electrolytes
    DisorderWhat is wrongDirection of treatment
    Addison’sLow cortisol and aldosteroneReplace — a glucocorticoid, often with a mineralocorticoid such as fludrocortisone
    Cushing’sExcess steroids — frequently from treatment itselfSuppress or withdraw — and the withdrawal must be gradual

    Two hormones, two different jobs — and the contraindications follow directly. A glucocorticoid works on inflammation, immunity and glucose, so its cautions are infection and diabetes. A mineralocorticoid works on sodium and water, so its cautions are heart failure and hypertension — holding sodium means holding water, and a failing heart cannot take the extra volume. You do not have to memorise either list if you can name what the hormone does.

    Why “do not stop abruptly” is the single most tested line here. Exogenous steroid suppresses ACTH by negative feedback; the adrenal cortex, unstimulated, atrophies. Stop the drug suddenly and the patient has neither the tablet nor a working gland — that is acute adrenal crisis: hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia with hyperkalemia, and vascular collapse. The same logic explains why a patient on long-term steroids needs more, not the usual dose, during surgery or serious illness: the stress response they would normally mount is not available.

    Ch 38 · slides 30–36

    4Thyroid agents — replace, block, or quiet the gland

    Three drug groups moving in two directions. Hypothyroid patients get hormone; hyperthyroid patients get synthesis blocked, or iodine when the gland must be calmed quickly.

    Drug · classMechanismIndicationsContraindications
    levothyroxineSynthetic T4 → ↑ metabolic rateHypothyroidism · myxedema comaAcute MI · thyrotoxicosis
    methimazole / PTUInhibit thyroid hormone synthesisHyperthyroidism · Graves diseasePregnancy (methimazole) · liver disease (PTU)
    Lugol’s / SSKIIodine solutions — at high dose they inhibit hormone releaseThyroid storm · pre-op thyroidectomyIodine allergy
    DrugAdverse effectsNursing care
    levothyroxineTachycardia · anxiety · heat intolerance — the picture of too much thyroidGive on an empty stomach · monitor TSH · avoid switching brands
    methimazole / PTUAgranulocytosis · liver toxicity · rashMonitor CBC and LFTs · report fever or sore throat
    Lugol’s / SSKIMetallic taste · sore gums · iodismDilute in juice, drink through a straw · monitor for swelling

    Why a sore throat is an emergency on an antithyroid drug. Agranulocytosis means the neutrophils are gone, so the patient cannot mount a normal response to infection — and the first sign is usually the most ordinary-sounding one: fever and a sore throat. That is why the teaching is to report those symptoms rather than wait them out, and why the monitoring is a CBC. A student who files “sore throat” under minor complaints will miss the one item this drug is famous for.

    The iodine paradox. Iodine is the raw material for thyroid hormone, so more iodine ought to mean more hormone — and in small amounts it does. At high doses it does the opposite and inhibits release, which is precisely why it works in thyroid storm and before a thyroidectomy, where the goal is to quiet the gland fast. The dose determines the direction. Dilution and a straw are not politeness: undiluted iodine solution stains teeth and irritates the mouth.

    Levothyroxine teaching, each point with a reason. Empty stomach — food, calcium and iron all bind it and cut absorption, so a changing breakfast means a changing dose. Same brand — small bioavailability differences matter in a narrow-window drug measured by TSH. Do not stop when feeling well — feeling well is the drug working, not the condition resolving. And the adverse effects are simply too much thyroid: tachycardia, anxiety, heat intolerance, weight loss. In an older adult or anyone with cardiac disease the dose starts low, because raising the metabolic rate raises cardiac workload — the same reason acute MI is a contraindication.

    Ch 38 · slides 37–42

    5Calcium and bone agents — which way does it move the calcium?

    Calcitriol, alendronate and calcitonin are easy to confuse because all three are “bone drugs”. Sorting them by their effect on serum calcium separates them cleanly.

    Drug · classMechanismIndicationsContraindications
    calcitriolActive vitamin D — promotes calcium absorption from the gutHypocalcemia · hypoparathyroidismHypercalcemia
    alendronateBisphosphonate — inhibits bone resorption by osteoclastsOsteoporosis · Paget’s diseaseEsophageal disorders · inability to sit upright
    calcitonin-salmonInhibits osteoclasts → lowers serum calciumPaget’s disease · hypercalcemiaFish / salmon allergy
    DrugAdverse effectsNursing care
    calcitriolHypercalcemia · weakness · bone painMonitor calcium · avoid calcium supplements unless ordered
    alendronateEsophagitis · GI upset · bone painFull glass of water, remain upright 30 minutes
    calcitonin-salmonFlushing · nausea · nasal irritationRotate injection sites · monitor calcium

    Three drugs, three directions — sort them by what happens to serum calcium. Calcitriol raises it by pulling calcium in from the gut, so its own overdose is hypercalcemia and existing hypercalcemia is the contraindication. Calcitonin lowers it by shutting down osteoclasts. Alendronate also blocks resorption, but it is prescribed to keep calcium in bone rather than to move the serum number. Ask “which way does this push the calcium?” and the indications and the contraindications both fall out.

    The alendronate rule is mechanical, not fussy. The drug is directly caustic to the esophagus, so anything that keeps it sitting there causes ulceration: a full glass of water to carry it down, upright for 30 minutes so gravity keeps it down, and taken first thing on an empty stomach because food blocks the already-poor absorption. It follows that a patient who cannot sit or stand upright — on bed rest, or unable to tolerate sitting — cannot safely take it at all. That is why “inability to sit upright” sits in the contraindication column next to actual esophageal disease.

    Ch 39 · slides 44–46

    6Insulin — replacement, and the two electrolyte consequences

    One mechanism with three predictable adverse effects. Two of them — hypoglycemia and hypokalemia — are the direct result of what insulin does to glucose and potassium.

    Prototype groupMechanismIndicationsContraindications
    regular · lisproReplaces endogenous insulin — drives glucose, and potassium, into cellsType 1 · Type 2 not controlled by oral agentsHypoglycemia
    NPH · glargineSame mechanism, longer action — intermediate and long-acting coverageBasal coverage between meals and overnightHypoglycemia
    Adverse effectWhy it happensNursing response
    HypoglycemiaThe dose exceeds the glucose available — a missed meal, extra activity, or a dose given too earlyMonitor glucose · match the dose to meals · treat promptly
    HypokalemiaInsulin moves potassium into cells along with glucose, so the serum level fallsMonitor potassium — especially on an insulin infusion or in DKA treatment
    LipodystrophyRepeated injection into the same site changes the fat under the skin, which then absorbs unpredictablyRotate sites — this is about absorption reliability, not comfort

    The potassium thread you have already met twice. Insulin pushes potassium into cells — which is exactly why it is given (with glucose) to treat hyperkalemia, and why a patient on an insulin drip needs potassium watched. You saw the same shift from the other side in the respiratory unit, where high-dose β2 agonists lower potassium, and in the cardiovascular unit, where potassium decides whether digoxin is safe. Three units, one electrolyte: it is worth knowing which drugs move it and in which direction.

    InsulinOnsetPeakDuration
    Rapid — lispro, aspart10–30 min1–2 hr3–5 hr
    Short — regular30–60 min2–4 hr5–8 hr
    Intermediate — NPH1–2 hr6–14 hr16–24 hr
    Long — glargine, detemir1–2 hrnone~24 hr
    Ultra-long — degludec~1 hrnone42+ hr

    Why the peak is the number that matters. Hypoglycemia clusters at the peak, so knowing when a given insulin peaks tells you when to watch and when a missed meal becomes dangerous. A rapid-acting insulin peaking in 1–2 hours is why the tray has to be in front of the client before the dose is given. The long and ultra-long insulins have no appreciable peak — they provide background cover, which is why they are given at the same time daily rather than with food.

    Mixing ruleDetail
    Regular + NPHThe standard mix. Draw up regular (clear) first, then NPH (cloudy) — clear before cloudy, so the longer-acting cloudy insulin can never contaminate the vial of short-acting
    Rapid + NPHLispro, aspart and glulisine may be mixed with NPH — but not with any long-acting insulin
    Glargine · detemirNever mixed with anything. Glargine is acidic, and mixing it with a neutral insulin makes it precipitate — absorption becomes unpredictable
    DegludecNever mixed. Designed for slow steady release; mixing destroys that profile
    Premixed 70/30, 75/25Already combined — the ratio cannot be adjusted, so nothing is added to them

    Clear before cloudy, and why NPH is the cloudy one. NPH contains protamine, which is what slows its absorption and makes it look cloudy — so it is rolled, never shaken, to resuspend it. Only regular and the rapid-acting analogues stay stable when combined with it. And of all these, only regular insulin can be given intravenously.

    “Match the dose to meals” carries more weight than it looks. Rapid-acting insulin given to a patient whose tray has not arrived, or who is about to go for a procedure and be kept nil by mouth, is a predictable hypoglycemia rather than bad luck. Before giving a mealtime dose the question is not only “what is the glucose?” but “is this patient actually going to eat?”

    Ch 39 · slides 47–60

    7Non-insulin agents — seven classes, sorted by hypoglycemia risk

    Seven prototypes is a lot to hold. The organising question is whether the drug forces insulin out regardless of glucose, or works with the body’s own signals — that decides who can go hypoglycemic.

    Class · prototypeMechanismIndicationKey contraindication
    Sulfonylurea — glipizideStimulates pancreatic insulin releaseType 2 with functioning beta cellsType 1 DM · sulfa allergy
    Biguanide — metformin↓ hepatic glucose production, ↑ insulin sensitivityFirst-line in type 2Renal impairment · contrast studies
    Alpha-glucosidaseAcarbose — slows carbohydrate absorption in the gutPostprandial hyperglycemiaGI disorders
    DPP-4 — sitagliptin↑ incretins → ↑ insulin, ↓ glucagonType 2 DMHistory of pancreatitis
    GLP-1 — liraglutide↑ insulin, ↓ glucagon, slows gastric emptyingType 2 DM · weight reductionThyroid tumors
    SGLT-2 — canagliflozin↑ glucose excretion in the urineType 2 with cardiovascular and renal benefitSevere renal impairment
    Meglitinide — repaglinideStimulates rapid insulin releasePost-meal glucose controlSkip the meal → skip the dose
    PrototypeAdverse effectsNursing care
    glipizideHypoglycemia · weight gainAvoid alcohol · monitor glucose
    metforminGI upset · lactic acidosis (rare)Hold for contrast dye · monitor renal labs
    acarboseGas · diarrhea · abdominal painTreat hypoglycemia with glucose, not sucrose
    sitagliptinPancreatitis · joint painMonitor abdominal pain · amylase and lipase
    liraglutideNausea · vomiting · pancreatitisMonitor GI tolerance · teach injection technique
    canagliflozinUTIs · dehydration · DKA · amputationsHydration · monitor ketones · foot care
    repaglinideHypoglycemia · weight gainDose with meals only

    Which of these can drop the glucose on their own? Only the two that make the pancreas release insulin regardless of what the glucose is doing: sulfonylureas and meglitinides. Metformin, acarbose, DPP-4, GLP-1 and SGLT-2 work with the body’s own glucose-dependent signals, so alone they rarely cause hypoglycemia — they do once a sulfonylurea or insulin is added. This single split answers most “which patient is at risk” questions in this group, and it explains why repaglinide’s rule is no meal, no dose: the drug forces insulin out whether or not food is coming.

    Acarbose and the sucrose trap. Acarbose blocks the gut enzyme that splits complex sugars into absorbable ones. Give table sugar (sucrose) for a hypoglycemic episode and the enzyme needed to break it down is the very one the drug has blocked — so it will not work fast enough. Glucose needs no splitting, which is why glucose tablets or gel are the required treatment. The mechanism dictates the antidote.

    Metformin and contrast dye. Contrast can injure the kidney; metformin is cleared by the kidney, and if it accumulates the rare complication is lactic acidosis. Holding it around the study is about preventing accumulation if renal function dips — which is also why renal impairment is the standing contraindication. Canagliflozin fails the other way: it works by dumping glucose into the urine, so it needs functioning kidneys to work at all, and the glucose-rich urine explains the UTIs, the dehydration, and the attention to foot care.

    Ch 39 · slides 61–63

    8Glucose-elevating agents — and telling a low from a high

    One drug, and the recognition skill that decides when it is needed. Knowing which direction a patient is moving matters more than knowing the number.

    DrugMechanismIndicationContraindication
    glucagonBreaks down glycogen → ↑ blood glucoseSevere hypoglycemia — when the patient cannot swallow safelyPheochromocytoma
    AspectDetailWhy
    Adverse effectsNausea · vomitingCommon enough that it shapes the positioning instruction below
    PositionTurn the patient on their sideAn unconscious patient who vomits is an aspiration risk — the side-lying position protects the airway
    TeachingTeach caregivers to give itBy definition the patient is too impaired to treat themselves, so the skill has to sit with someone else
    After it worksGive a carbohydrate once able to swallowGlucagon empties the glycogen store; without replacement the glucose falls again
    HypoglycemiaHyperglycemia
    Tremors · sweating · tachycardia · anxiety · hunger · confusion
    fast onset — this is the adrenergic alarm, the same sympathetic surge you met in the autonomic unit    		Polyuria · polydipsia · polyphagia · flushed, dry skin · fruity breath
    slow onset — dehydration and acidosis build over hours to days

    Tremor is the one to recognise. When glucose falls, the body releases catecholamines before the brain runs short — so the earliest signs are sympathetic: shakiness, sweating, a fast heart, anxiety and hunger. Flushed dry skin, a dry mouth and polyuria all point the other way, toward hyperglycemia and dehydration. The practical danger is that early hypoglycemia can be mistaken for anxiety — the same trap as early hypoxia in the respiratory unit, and the same answer: check, do not assume.

    Hypoglycemia is the faster killer. Hyperglycemia damages over hours and days; hypoglycemia can cause seizures, coma and death within minutes, because the brain has no glucose reserve. That asymmetry is why “when in doubt, treat the low” is standard practice, and why glucagon is kept where the patient is rather than in a pharmacy.

    Endocrine · synthesis

    9Thinking across the endocrine list

    Twelve connections that carry most of the reasoning in this unit. If a question seems to need a fact you cannot recall, one of these usually reaches the answer anyway.

    #ConnectionWhat it means at the bedside
    01Feedback → taperGive a hormone, the gland stops. Prednisone and levothyroxine are never stopped abruptly — for steroids the consequence is adrenal crisis
    02Replace or suppressDecide the direction first. Addison’s and hypothyroidism get replacement; Cushing’s and Graves get suppression
    03Gluco vs mineraloGlucocorticoid acts on inflammation, immunity, glucose → watch infection and diabetes. Mineralocorticoid acts on sodium and water → watch heart failure and hypertension
    04Fever + sore throatOn methimazole or PTU this is agranulocytosis until proven otherwise — report it, do not wait it out
    05Empty stomachLevothyroxine — food, calcium and iron block absorption. Same brand each time; TSH is the monitor
    06Which way for calciumCalcitriol raises serum calcium · calcitonin lowers it · alendronate keeps it in bone
    07Stay upright 30 minAlendronate is caustic to the esophagus. Full glass of water, upright afterwards — and unusable in anyone who cannot sit up
    08Who goes hypoglycemicOnly the drugs that force insulin out: sulfonylureas and meglitinides (and insulin itself). No meal → no repaglinide dose
    09Glucose, not sucroseOn acarbose, sucrose cannot be split because the drug blocks the enzyme. Use glucose tablets or gel
    10Hold for contrastMetformin — renal injury from contrast lets it accumulate, and the rare consequence is lactic acidosis
    11Insulin moves K⁺Glucose and potassium go into the cell together — the reason insulin treats hyperkalemia and the reason a drip needs potassium watched
    12Low looks like anxietyEarly hypoglycemia is a sympathetic alarm — tremor, sweating, tachycardia. Flushed, dry and polyuric points the other way

    How to use this list. Each line is a decision, not a fact to recite. Before any endocrine drug, run three questions: which direction is this moving the hormone, what did the body stop doing while the drug was on board, and what single finding would make me hold the dose and escalate? Most of this unit answers to those three.

    The threads that cross units. Potassium ties insulin here to β2 agonists in respiratory and to digoxin in cardiovascular. The “early warning looks like anxiety” trap ties hypoglycemia here to early hypoxia in respiratory. And the sympathetic signs that announce a falling glucose are the same α and β effects from the autonomic unit — a β-blocker can mask them, which is why a patient on both a beta blocker and insulin may lose their warning signs.

    Endocrine · med chart

    Medication chart — endocrine drugs

    Twenty-three classes in the same rubric format: example drugs, mechanism, uses, effects, nursing considerations in the four required parts — assessment vitals labs education — and specific special populations.

    Growth hormone agonist
    replacement for deficiencysomatropin
    Example drugssomatropin
    Mechanism of action
    • Stimulates linear growth and tissue anabolism through GH receptors
    • Acts largely by raising IGF-1, which does most of the growth work
    • Antagonises insulin — which is why glucose rises
    Therapeutic uses
    • Growth hormone deficiency in children and adults
    • Turner syndrome
    • Selected chronic renal and genetic short-stature conditions
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: injection-site reactions, edema, joint and muscle pain, headache
    • Serious: hyperglycemia and new diabetes, intracranial hypertension, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, scoliosis progression, fluid retention
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Confirm the epiphyses are still open — once they have closed the drug cannot add height and is contraindicated
    • Acute critical illness is a contraindication
    • Baseline height, weight and growth velocity, plotted at every visit
    • Ask about hip or knee pain and any limp — it can signal a slipped epiphysis
    • Watch for persistent headache or visual change
    2Vitals
    • Height and weight at each visit — the primary outcome measure
    • Blood pressure
    • Assess for peripheral edema
    3Labs
    • Glucose and HbA1c — GH opposes insulin
    • Thyroid function — therapy can unmask hypothyroidism, which then blunts the growth response
    • IGF-1 to guide dosing
    • Bone age radiographs
    4Education
