    • Rotate injection sites to protect the subcutaneous tissue
    • Give at the time prescribed, usually evening, and keep it refrigerated as directed
    • Report hip or knee pain, limping, persistent headache or vision change
    • Expect regular growth measurements — they are how the dose is set
    • Report increased thirst or urination
    Special populations
    • Children: the main population — growth velocity and bone age guide therapy, and treatment stops when epiphyses close.
    • Diabetes or prediabetes: GH raises glucose, so antidiabetic therapy may need adjusting.
    • Critically ill patients: contraindicated — associated with increased mortality in acute illness.
    • Patients with active malignancy: avoided, since GH is a growth signal.
    • Hypothyroid patients: growth will not respond until thyroid replacement is adequate.
    Growth hormone antagonist
    for excess GHoctreotide
    Example drugsoctreotide
    Mechanism of action
    • A somatostatin analogue — somatostatin is the body’s own GH-inhibiting hormone, so this suppresses GH release
    • Also suppresses insulin, glucagon, and several gut hormones
    • Slows GI motility and gallbladder emptying
    Therapeutic uses
    • Acromegaly — GH excess in adults
    • Severe diarrhea from carcinoid and VIPomas
    • Variceal bleeding in some protocols
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: GI upset — nausea, cramping, diarrhea or constipation; injection-site pain
    • Serious: gallstones and biliary sludge, bradycardia and conduction changes, hyper- or hypoglycemia, hypothyroidism
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Gallbladder disease is a contraindication — the drug slows gallbladder emptying and precipitates stones
    • Caution in diabetes: it suppresses insulin and glucagon, so glucose can move in either direction
    • Assess for right-upper-quadrant pain, especially after fatty meals
    • Baseline and periodic assessment of acromegaly symptoms — ring and shoe size, headache, soft-tissue change
    • Bowel pattern
    2Vitals
    • Heart rate — bradycardia is a recognised effect
    • ECG where cardiac disease exists
    • Blood pressure
    • Weight
    3Labs
    • Glucose — in both directions
    • Liver function and gallbladder imaging as ordered
    • Thyroid function
    • GH and IGF-1 to judge response
    • Vitamin B12 on long-term therapy
    4Education
    • Report right-upper-quadrant pain, nausea after fatty food, or yellowing of skin or eyes
    • Rotate injection sites
    • Monitor glucose more closely at the start and after dose changes
    • Report a slow or irregular pulse, dizziness or fainting
    • Keep follow-up imaging and laboratory appointments
    Special populations
    • Patients with gallbladder disease: contraindicated — the mechanism directly worsens it.
    • Diabetic patients: glucose becomes unpredictable because both insulin and glucagon are suppressed.
    • Patients with bradycardia or conduction disease: additive heart-rate slowing.
    • Older adults: higher gallstone risk and less tolerance of bradycardia.
    • Patients on cyclosporine or other narrow-index drugs: altered GI absorption changes levels.
    Posterior pituitary agent
    synthetic ADH — a water drugdesmopressin
    Example drugsdesmopressin
    Mechanism of action
    • Synthetic antidiuretic hormone → the collecting duct reabsorbs more water
    • Urine becomes concentrated and smaller in volume; plasma becomes more dilute
    • Also raises von Willebrand factor and factor VIII, which is why it has a bleeding-disorder use
    Therapeutic uses
    • Diabetes insipidus
    • Primary nocturnal enuresis
    • Mild hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: headache, nausea, flushing, fluid retention
    • Serious: hyponatremia, which can progress to confusion, seizures and coma; water intoxication; hypertension
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Hyponatremia is both the main adverse effect and a contraindication — check the sodium before and during therapy
    • Renal failure is a contraindication
    • Monitor intake and output and daily weight — a rising weight is retained water before it is anything else
    • Assess for headache, confusion, drowsiness or seizures — the neurological face of a falling sodium
    • Ask about fluid intake: drinking freely on this drug is what produces dilutional hyponatremia
    2Vitals
    • Daily weight, at the same time and in the same clothing
    • Blood pressure — can rise
    • Strict intake and output
    • Level of consciousness
    3Labs
    • Serum sodium — the critical laboratory value
    • Serum and urine osmolality
    • Urine specific gravity
    • Renal function
    4Education
    • Report headache, nausea, confusion or drowsiness promptly — these are low-sodium symptoms
    • Follow the fluid advice given; do not drink large volumes simply because you can
    • Weigh daily and report a sudden gain
    • For nasal forms, clear the nose first and use the technique demonstrated
    • Do not double a missed dose
    Special populations
    • Older adults: highest hyponatremia risk — reduced free-water clearance and often other drugs that lower sodium.
    • Children treated for enuresis: fluid must be limited in the evening; seizures from water intoxication have occurred.
    • Renal impairment: contraindicated.
    • Heart failure or hypertension: retained water worsens both.
    • Patients on SSRIs, thiazides or carbamazepine: additive hyponatremia risk.
    GnRH agonist
    stimulates, then suppressesleuprolide
    Example drugsleuprolide
    Mechanism of action
    • A GnRH agonist. The receptor normally responds to pulses, so continuous stimulation downregulates it
    • First an initial surge — the flare — then sustained suppression of LH and FSH
    • Downstream, testosterone or estrogen falls to very low levels
    Therapeutic uses
    • Advanced prostate cancer
    • Endometriosis and uterine fibroids
    • Central precocious puberty
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: hot flashes, mood changes, sweating, decreased libido, injection-site reaction
    • Serious: bone loss and osteoporosis with prolonged use, tumour flare in the first weeks, hyperglycemia, cardiovascular events, depression
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Teach about the flare reaction — symptoms, bone pain or urinary obstruction may briefly worsen in the first 1–2 weeks before improving
    • Pregnancy is a contraindication; confirm pregnancy status before starting
    • Monitor bone density on prolonged therapy
    • Assess mood — depression is common and under-reported
    • For prostate cancer, watch for worsening urinary obstruction or new neurological signs during the flare
    2Vitals
    • Blood pressure and weight
    • Assess pain, and document whether a change is flare or progression
    • Height over time, as a marker of vertebral loss
    3Labs
    • Testosterone or estradiol to confirm suppression
    • PSA in prostate cancer
    • Bone density scanning
    • Glucose and lipids
    • Calcium and vitamin D status
    4Education
    • Expect symptoms to worsen briefly before they improve — this is predictable, not treatment failure
    • Report severe bone pain, difficulty passing urine, or new weakness or numbness in the legs
    • Hot flashes are expected; discuss management rather than stopping
    • Weight-bearing exercise, calcium and vitamin D protect bone
    • Use reliable non-hormonal contraception
    • Report persistent low mood
    Special populations
    • Pregnancy: contraindicated — fetal harm.
    • Patients with spinal metastases or urinary obstruction: the flare can cause cord compression or retention — an antiandrogen may be given first to cover it.
    • Long-term users: bone loss is the dominant risk; density monitoring and bone protection are standard.
    • Children with precocious puberty: growth and pubertal staging are followed closely.
    • Patients with depression or cardiovascular disease: both can worsen.
    GnRH antagonist
    blocks immediately — no flarecetrorelix
    Example drugscetrorelix
    Mechanism of action
    • A GnRH antagonist — competitively blocks the receptor
    • Suppression is immediate, with no initial surge, which is the practical difference from leuprolide
    • Prevents the premature LH surge during controlled ovarian stimulation
    Therapeutic uses
    • Controlled ovarian stimulation in assisted reproduction
    • Other settings where rapid suppression without a flare is needed
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: injection-site pain and redness, headache, nausea
    • Serious: ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome — abdominal pain, distension, ascites, and in severe cases hemoconcentration and thrombosis
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Monitor for abdominal pain and ascites — the signs of ovarian hyperstimulation
    • Pregnancy and ovarian cysts are contraindications
    • Assess abdominal girth and comfort during stimulation cycles
    • Rotate injection sites and inspect previous ones
    • Confirm the patient understands the exact timing — these cycles are schedule-critical
    2Vitals
    • Weight and abdominal girth — rapid gain suggests third-spacing
    • Blood pressure and heart rate
    • Assess for shortness of breath, which suggests significant ascites
    3Labs
    • Estradiol, to track the response
    • Hematocrit — rises with hemoconcentration in hyperstimulation
    • Electrolytes and renal function
    • Follicle counts by ultrasound
    4Education
    • Report abdominal pain, bloating, rapid weight gain, nausea or shortness of breath
    • Take the dose at the time specified — timing drives the whole cycle
    • Mild injection-site redness is expected; rotate sites
    • Keep every monitoring appointment
    Special populations
    • Pregnancy: contraindicated.
    • Women with polycystic ovary syndrome or high follicle counts: greatest hyperstimulation risk.
    • Patients with ovarian cysts: contraindicated.
    • Patients with thrombophilia: hemoconcentration in hyperstimulation raises clot risk.
    • Severe renal or hepatic impairment: not well studied; generally avoided.
    Glucocorticoid
    anti-inflammatory · never stopped abruptlyprednisone · hydrocortisone
    Example drugsprednisone · hydrocortisone
    Mechanism of action
    • Binds intracellular receptors and alters gene transcription → broad anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effect
    • Raises blood glucose by increasing hepatic glucose production and opposing insulin
    • Causes protein catabolism and redistributes fat — the source of the long-term Cushingoid picture
    • Suppresses ACTH by negative feedback, so the adrenal cortex atrophies — the single most important fact for safety
    Therapeutic uses
    • Asthma and COPD exacerbations
    • Autoimmune and inflammatory disease
    • Adrenal insufficiency — replacement
    • Transplant rejection, allergic reactions, some malignancies
    • Adrenal crisis — parenteral hydrocortisone with IV fluids is the emergency treatment, given alongside assessment of airway, breathing and circulation
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: hyperglycemia, increased appetite and weight gain, mood changes and insomnia, fluid retention, GI irritation
    • Serious: infection masked by suppressed inflammation, adrenal crisis on abrupt withdrawal, osteoporosis, peptic ulcer, hyperglycemia and new diabetes, cataracts and glaucoma, poor wound healing, psychosis
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Do not stop abruptly — the dose is tapered so the suppressed adrenal axis can recover. Abrupt withdrawal means adrenal crisis
    • Active infection is a contraindication; steroids blunt fever and inflammation, so an infection can be well advanced before it looks like one
    • Assess for infection with a low threshold — any new malaise, cough or wound change deserves attention even without fever
    • Caution in diabetes — expect glucose to rise and the antidiabetic regimen to need adjusting
    • Give with food to limit gastric irritation
    • Ask about mood, sleep and any new agitation or confusion
    • Note that a patient on long-term therapy needs increased cover during illness, injury or surgery
    • Know the stress-dose plan and where the emergency steroid is kept — in adrenal crisis the nurse prepares parenteral hydrocortisone and IV fluids while escalating urgently
    2Vitals
    • Blood pressure — sodium and water retention raise it
    • Temperature, remembering it may be blunted
    • Weight — fluid and fat gain
    • Assess for edema
    3Labs
    • Blood glucose — the most immediate laboratory effect
    • Electrolytes: sodium rises, potassium falls
    • CBC — WBC rises on steroids without meaning infection
    • Bone density on long-term therapy
    • Lipids; consider vitamin D and calcium status
    4Education
    • Never stop this medicine on your own — it must be reduced gradually
    • Take it with food, usually in the morning, to match the body’s own rhythm and protect sleep
    • Report signs of infection promptly, even mild ones
    • Monitor glucose more closely if you are diabetic
    • Carry or wear identification saying you take steroids
    • Tell any clinician treating you for illness, injury or surgery — you may need a larger dose temporarily
    • Report black stools, severe stomach pain, or marked mood change
    Special populations
    • Patients with any active infection: contraindicated — immunosuppression plus a masked presentation is a dangerous pairing.
    • Diabetic patients: glucose rises predictably; insulin or oral agents usually need adjusting.
    • Older adults: osteoporosis, fracture, cataract and skin-tearing risk all rise.
    • Children: growth suppression with prolonged use — growth velocity is monitored.
    • Patients on long-term therapy facing surgery or illness: need increased dosing, because they cannot mount a stress response.
    • Peptic ulcer disease or concurrent NSAIDs: additive GI bleeding risk.
    • Patients with psychiatric history: steroid-induced mood change and psychosis.
    Mineralocorticoid
    sodium and water — watch the heartfludrocortisone
    Example drugsfludrocortisone
    Mechanism of action
    • Acts on the distal nephron to increase sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion
    • Sodium retention pulls water with it → plasma volume and blood pressure rise
    • Replaces aldosterone where the adrenal cortex no longer makes it
    Therapeutic uses
    • Addison’s disease and other primary adrenal insufficiency, alongside a glucocorticoid
    • Salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia
    • Severe orthostatic hypotension in selected cases
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: fluid retention, weight gain, hypertension, headache
    • Serious: hypokalemia with arrhythmia and muscle weakness, heart failure decompensation, pulmonary edema, hypernatremia, metabolic alkalosis
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Heart failure and hypertension are the contraindications, and both follow directly from retaining sodium and water
    • Monitor blood pressure, weight and electrolytes — the three measures that track the drug’s whole effect
    • Assess for edema, new shortness of breath, orthopnea or crackles — early decompensation
    • Assess for muscle weakness, cramps or palpitations, which suggest a falling potassium
    • In Addison’s, confirm the glucocorticoid is also prescribed — this drug alone does not replace cortisol
    2Vitals
    • Blood pressure, lying and standing — the therapeutic target in orthostatic use and the warning sign in everyone else
    • Daily weight — a rapid gain is retained fluid
    • Heart rate and rhythm
    • Respiratory assessment for fluid overload
    3Labs
    • Potassium — the electrolyte this drug actively wastes
    • Sodium
    • Renal function
    • Glucose, since it has some glucocorticoid activity
    • ECG where potassium is low
    4Education
    • Weigh yourself daily and report a sudden gain
    • Report swelling of the ankles, new breathlessness, or difficulty lying flat
    • Report muscle weakness, cramps or palpitations
    • Follow the dietary sodium and potassium advice you are given
    • Do not stop abruptly, and tell clinicians you take adrenal replacement
    • During illness, vomiting or heavy sweating, contact your prescriber — replacement needs may change
    Special populations
    • Heart failure: contraindicated — the added volume is exactly what a failing ventricle cannot handle.
    • Hypertension: contraindicated or used with close control.
    • Patients on potassium-wasting diuretics: additive hypokalemia.
    • Patients on digoxin: a low potassium markedly increases digoxin toxicity — the cardiovascular-unit link.
    • Older adults: less tolerance of volume expansion and higher arrhythmia risk at a low potassium.
    • Addison’s patients during illness: may need increased replacement; dehydration changes requirements quickly.
    Thyroid hormone replacement
    narrow window · empty stomachlevothyroxine
    Example drugslevothyroxine
    Mechanism of action
    • Synthetic T4, converted peripherally to the more active T3
    • Raises the basal metabolic rate in essentially every tissue — oxygen use, heat production, cardiac output, gut motility
    • Restores normal negative feedback, so a correct dose brings TSH back into range
    Therapeutic uses
    • Hypothyroidism of any cause
    • Myxedema coma — given intravenously as an emergency
    • TSH suppression after thyroid cancer
    • Congenital hypothyroidism
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: usually none at the right dose. At too high a dose: tachycardia, palpitations, anxiety, heat intolerance, insomnia, weight loss, tremor
    • Serious: angina, atrial fibrillation and myocardial infarction in cardiac disease, thyroid storm from marked overdose, bone loss with long-term over-replacement
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Acute MI and thyrotoxicosis are contraindications — raising the metabolic rate raises cardiac oxygen demand
    • Give on an empty stomach, typically 30–60 minutes before breakfast, with water
    • Separate from calcium, iron, antacids and some fibre by about four hours — all bind it and cut absorption
    • Avoid switching brands — small bioavailability differences matter in a narrow-window drug
    • Assess for chest pain, palpitations or new breathlessness, especially early and after any increase
    • Expect a slow response — weeks before full effect, and TSH is rechecked around 6–8 weeks after a change
    • Review interacting drugs: warfarin effect increases, and insulin or oral antidiabetic needs may change
    2Vitals
    • Heart rate and rhythm — the first place over-replacement shows
    • Blood pressure
    • Weight
    • Temperature and heat tolerance
    • Assess for chest pain with any dose increase
    3Labs
    • TSH — the monitor that matters; free T4 alongside it
    • Lipids, which fall as hypothyroidism is treated
    • Glucose in diabetic patients
    • INR in patients on warfarin
    4Education
    • Take it in the morning on an empty stomach, with water, and wait before eating
    • Keep to the same brand — ask the pharmacy not to substitute
    • Do not stop when you feel well; feeling well is the medicine working
    • Separate it from calcium, iron and antacids by several hours
    • Report chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, or marked anxiety and sleeplessness
    • Take a missed dose when you remember, but never double up
    • It takes weeks to feel the benefit — keep your blood-test appointments
    Special populations
    • Older adults and anyone with cardiac disease: started at a low dose and raised slowly — a full dose can precipitate angina, arrhythmia or infarction.
    • Pregnancy: requirements increase, often early; untreated hypothyroidism harms fetal neurodevelopment, so therapy continues and TSH is followed closely.
    • Patients on calcium, iron or antacids: absorption is reduced — timing has to be taught explicitly.
    • Patients on warfarin: anticoagulant effect increases as metabolism rises; INR needs watching.
    • Infants with congenital hypothyroidism: prompt treatment prevents permanent cognitive impairment.
    • Patients with adrenal insufficiency: cortisol is replaced first — thyroid hormone alone can precipitate adrenal crisis.
    Antithyroid agents
    fever or sore throat = report nowmethimazole · propylthiouracil (PTU)
    Example drugsmethimazole · propylthiouracil (PTU)
    Mechanism of action
    • Inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis by blocking the incorporation of iodine into thyroglobulin
    • PTU also blocks peripheral conversion of T4 to T3, which is why it is preferred in thyroid storm
    • Neither destroys existing stored hormone, so the effect takes weeks to appear
    Therapeutic uses
    • Hyperthyroidism and Graves disease
    • Preparation before thyroidectomy or radioactive iodine
    • Thyroid storm — PTU preferred
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: rash, itching, GI upset, arthralgia, altered taste
    • Serious: agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity (more severe with PTU), vasculitis, hypothyroidism from over-treatment
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Report fever or sore throat immediately — the classic first sign of agranulocytosis, and the single most important teaching point for this class
    • Methimazole is contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic); PTU is avoided in liver disease and carries the greater hepatotoxicity risk
    • Assess for jaundice, dark urine, right-upper-quadrant pain or unusual fatigue
    • Assess for any sign of infection, not just fever
    • Set expectations: symptom relief takes weeks because stored hormone must be used up
    • Monitor for the opposite swing — over-treatment produces hypothyroid symptoms
    2Vitals
    • Heart rate — should fall as hyperthyroidism is controlled
    • Temperature — fever is the agranulocytosis signal
    • Blood pressure
    • Weight, which should stabilise or rise
    3Labs
    • CBC with differential — baseline and whenever infection is suspected
    • Liver function tests, particularly on PTU
    • TSH and free T4 to track response
    • Consider prothrombin time with PTU
    4Education
    • Report a sore throat, fever, mouth ulcers or any sign of infection straight away — do not wait
    • Report yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, severe tiredness or right-sided abdominal pain
    • Take it at the same times each day
    • It takes several weeks to work — keep taking it even if nothing has changed
    • Do not stop on your own
    • Report increasing tiredness, cold intolerance or weight gain — signs of swinging too far the other way
    • Tell your prescriber if you are or may become pregnant
    Special populations
    • Pregnancy: methimazole is teratogenic, particularly in the first trimester; PTU is generally used then, with liver monitoring.
    • Liver disease: PTU avoided — it carries a risk of severe hepatic failure.
    • Patients with any infection: must be evaluated with a CBC rather than treated symptomatically.
    • Older adults: may present atypically; cardiac complications of untreated hyperthyroidism are more dangerous.
    • Breastfeeding: methimazole at lower doses is generally acceptable.
    • Patients before thyroidectomy: used to make the patient euthyroid first, reducing the risk of storm during surgery.
    Iodine solutions
    high dose inhibits releaseLugol's solution · SSKI
    Example drugsLugol's solution · SSKI
    Mechanism of action
    • At high doses iodine inhibits thyroid hormone release and reduces gland vascularity — the opposite of its effect in small amounts
    • Acts within hours, far faster than the thionamides
    • The effect is temporary, so it is a bridging agent rather than a long-term treatment
    Therapeutic uses
    • Thyroid storm, after a thionamide has been given
    • Before thyroidectomy, to shrink and firm the gland and reduce bleeding
    • Radiation emergencies, to block uptake
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: metallic taste, sore gums and mouth, burning mouth, stained teeth, GI upset
    • Serious: iodism — metallic taste with sore gums, salivation, coryza and rash; hypersensitivity reactions; swelling of the throat or airway
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Dilute in juice or water and give through a straw — undiluted solution irritates mucosa and stains teeth
    • Iodine allergy is a contraindication
    • Monitor for swelling of the lips, tongue or throat — a hypersensitivity emergency
    • In thyroid storm, confirm a thionamide was given first — iodine given alone can supply substrate and worsen the picture
    • Assess the mouth for soreness, ulceration or excess salivation
    • Ask about seafood and contrast reactions as part of the allergy history
    2Vitals
    • Heart rate and rhythm — should settle as storm is controlled
    • Temperature — often very high in storm
    • Blood pressure
    • Respiratory assessment for airway swelling
    3Labs
    • Thyroid function tests
    • Electrolytes, particularly with vomiting
    • Renal function
    • CBC
    4Education
    • Always dilute it and drink it through a straw, then rinse your mouth
    • Report a metallic taste, sore gums, mouth ulcers or increased saliva — these are signs of iodism
    • Report any swelling of the lips, tongue or throat immediately
    • Take it after meals to reduce stomach upset
    • Do not take extra or stop without advice
    • Mention any previous reaction to iodine, shellfish or contrast dye
    Special populations
    • Patients with iodine hypersensitivity: contraindicated.
    • Pregnancy: crosses the placenta and can cause fetal goiter and hypothyroidism — used only briefly and when necessary.
    • Patients in thyroid storm: sequence matters — thionamide first, then iodine.
    • Children: dosing is weight-based and mucosal irritation is less well tolerated.
    • Patients with hyperkalemia or on potassium-sparing drugs: SSKI is a potassium salt and adds a load.
    Vitamin D analogue
    raises serum calciumcalcitriol
    Example drugscalcitriol
    Mechanism of action
    • Active vitamin D — the form the kidney normally makes
    • Increases calcium absorption from the gut and reabsorption at the kidney
    • Also mobilises calcium from bone when parathyroid hormone is present
    • Works where plain vitamin D will not, because it needs no renal activation
    Therapeutic uses
    • Hypocalcemia
    • Hypoparathyroidism
    • Chronic kidney disease, where activation fails
    • Renal osteodystrophy
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: usually none at the right dose; early excess causes nausea, constipation, thirst and fatigue
    • Serious: hypercalcemia — weakness, bone pain, confusion, arrhythmia, renal stones and renal impairment; vascular and soft-tissue calcification
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Hypercalcemia is the contraindication and the main toxicity — the same thing at two doses
    • Do not take additional calcium supplements unless specifically ordered, and check antacids, which are often calcium carbonate
    • Assess for weakness, bone pain, constipation, increased thirst and urination, confusion
    • Ask about thiazide diuretics, which reduce calcium excretion and compound the rise
    • In a digoxin patient, remember hypercalcemia increases digoxin toxicity
    2Vitals
    • Blood pressure and heart rate; rhythm if calcium is high
    • Assess level of consciousness and muscle strength
    • Weight and hydration status
    • Intake and output
    3Labs
    • Serum calcium — the central value, checked often at first
    • Phosphate, since the calcium–phosphate product drives calcification
    • Parathyroid hormone
    • Renal function
    • Magnesium and alkaline phosphatase
    4Education
    • Do not add calcium tablets, or antacids containing calcium, without asking
    • Report weakness, bone pain, constipation, unusual thirst, frequent urination or confusion
    • Attend calcium blood tests as scheduled
    • Drink adequate fluid unless told otherwise
    • Report nausea and vomiting that does not settle
    Special populations
    • Patients with existing hypercalcemia: contraindicated.
    • Chronic kidney disease: the group that most needs it, because the kidney can no longer activate vitamin D — and the group where calcification risk is highest.
    • Patients on digoxin: a rising calcium increases digoxin toxicity.
    • Patients on thiazide diuretics: reduced calcium excretion adds to the rise.
    • Older adults: more likely to be taking calcium-containing supplements and antacids unknowingly.
    Bisphosphonate
    upright 30 minutes — it is causticalendronate
    Example drugsalendronate
    Mechanism of action
    • Inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and is incorporated into bone matrix
    • Bone formation continues while breakdown slows, so density rises over months
    • Very poorly absorbed, and food or any other drink reduces it further
    • Directly irritating to esophageal mucosa on contact
    Therapeutic uses
    • Osteoporosis — treatment and prevention
    • Paget’s disease of bone
    • Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis
    • Some malignancy-related bone disease
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: GI upset, abdominal pain, musculoskeletal and bone pain, heartburn
    • Serious: esophagitis, esophageal ulceration and stricture, osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femoral fracture, hypocalcemia, severe musculoskeletal pain
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Take first thing in the morning with a full glass of plain water — not coffee, juice, milk or mineral water
    • Remain upright for at least 30 minutes, and take nothing else by mouth during that time
    • Esophageal disorders and an inability to sit or stand upright are contraindications — not cautions
    • Assess for difficulty or pain on swallowing, heartburn or chest pain — stop and report
    • Correct hypocalcemia and vitamin D deficiency before starting
    • Ask about dental work — invasive procedures are best completed beforehand
    • Assess for new thigh or groin pain, which can precede an atypical fracture
    2Vitals
    • Height over time — loss suggests vertebral fracture
    • Assess pain, and distinguish expected musculoskeletal aching from new focal thigh or groin pain
    • Blood pressure and heart rate are not the monitor here — swallowing and posture are
    3Labs
    • Serum calcium and vitamin D before starting and periodically
    • Renal function — avoided in significant impairment
    • Phosphate and alkaline phosphatase, especially in Paget’s
    • Bone density scanning to judge response
    4Education
    • Morning, empty stomach, full glass of plain water, stay upright 30 minutes — every part of that has a reason
    • Do not lie down, and do not eat, drink or take other medicines during those 30 minutes
    • Stop and report difficulty swallowing, pain on swallowing, new heartburn or chest pain
    • Report new thigh, hip or groin pain
    • Tell your dentist you take this medicine, and keep up dental care
    • Take calcium and vitamin D as advised — but at a different time of day
    • Weight-bearing exercise helps
    Special populations
    • Patients who cannot sit or stand upright: contraindicated — including those on bed rest or with limited mobility.
    • Esophageal stricture, achalasia or significant reflux: contraindicated.
    • Patients having invasive dental work: osteonecrosis of the jaw risk — dental assessment first where possible.
    • Renal impairment: avoided below a defined clearance.
    • Patients with untreated hypocalcemia or vitamin D deficiency: correct first, or the calcium falls further.
    • Older adults: the main treatment group, and also the most likely to have swallowing difficulty or to take it lying down.
    Calcitonin
    lowers serum calciumcalcitonin-salmon
    Example drugscalcitonin-salmon
    Mechanism of action
    • Inhibits osteoclasts, reducing bone resorption and lowering serum calcium
    • Also increases renal calcium excretion
    • The salmon form is more potent than human calcitonin
    • Effect on calcium is relatively rapid but wanes with continued use
    Therapeutic uses
    • Hypercalcemia — useful early while other agents take effect
    • Paget’s disease
    • Postmenopausal osteoporosis as a second-line option
    • Some painful vertebral fractures
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: flushing, nausea, nasal irritation and dryness with the nasal spray, injection-site reaction
    • Serious: hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis, hypocalcemia with tetany, nasal ulceration, a small reported malignancy signal with long-term use
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Fish or salmon allergy is a contraindication — ask specifically, and know skin testing may be used before the first dose
    • Monitor calcium — the drug lowers it, so watch for going too far
    • Assess for tingling around the mouth or in the fingers, muscle twitching or cramps — early hypocalcemia
    • Inspect the nares regularly with the nasal spray, and alternate nostrils daily
    • Rotate injection sites
    • Give at bedtime where nausea and flushing are troublesome
    2Vitals
    • Heart rate and rhythm, since calcium affects conduction
    • Blood pressure
    • Assess for signs of hypocalcemia — including Chvostek and Trousseau signs where taught
    • Observe after the first dose for hypersensitivity
    3Labs
    • Serum calcium — before and during therapy
    • Phosphate and alkaline phosphatase in Paget’s
    • Renal function
    • Vitamin D status
    4Education
    • Tell your prescriber about any fish or seafood allergy before the first dose
    • Alternate nostrils daily with the spray, and report nosebleeds, crusting or persistent soreness
    • Rotate injection sites
    • Report tingling around the mouth or in the fingers, muscle cramps or twitching
    • Flushing and nausea often settle; taking it at bedtime can help
    • Keep calcium blood tests as scheduled
    • Take calcium and vitamin D as prescribed
    Special populations
    • Patients with fish or salmon allergy: contraindicated — anaphylaxis has occurred.
    • Patients already hypocalcemic: the drug lowers calcium further.
    • Older adults: the main osteoporosis group; nasal dryness and irritation are more troublesome.
    • Long-term users: effectiveness wanes and a malignancy signal has been reported — duration is reviewed.
    • Patients with nasal disease or recent nasal surgery: the spray may be unsuitable.
    Insulin
    replacement · moves glucose and potassiumregular · lispro · aspart · NPH · glargine · detemir
    Example drugsregular · lispro · aspart · glulisine · NPH · glargine · detemir · degludec
    Mechanism of action
    • Replaces endogenous insulin — drives glucose into muscle and fat and stops hepatic glucose output
    • Also drives potassium into cells, which is both a therapeutic use and an adverse effect
    • Suppresses ketone production
    • Onset and duration differ by preparation — rapid (lispro, aspart, glulisine), short (regular), intermediate (NPH), long (glargine, detemir), ultra-long (degludec)
    • Only regular insulin can be given intravenously
    • NPH is the only cloudy insulin — it contains protamine, which is what slows its absorption
    Therapeutic uses
    • Type 1 diabetes — always required
    • Type 2 not controlled by oral agents
    • Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar states
    • Gestational diabetes
    • Hyperkalemia, given with glucose
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: hypoglycemia, weight gain, injection-site reactions, lipodystrophy with repeated use of one site
    • Serious: severe hypoglycemia with seizures, coma and death; hypokalemia with arrhythmia; hypersensitivity; worsening heart failure with some combinations
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Match the dose to the meal — before giving a mealtime dose, confirm the food is actually coming and the patient is not nil by mouth
    • Know the onset and peak of the preparation, because that is when hypoglycemia is most likely
    • Recognise hypoglycemia early: tremor, sweating, tachycardia, anxiety, hunger, confusion
    • Rotate injection sites — lipodystrophy makes absorption erratic
    • Check the right insulin and concentration — insulin is a high-alert medication and is independently double-checked in most settings
    • Only regular insulin is given intravenously among the common preparations
    • Never mix glargine with another insulin
    2Vitals
    • Capillary glucose at the frequency ordered — the primary monitor
    • Heart rate — tachycardia can be the first sign of a falling glucose
    • Level of consciousness
    • Blood pressure; weight over time
    3Labs
    • Glucose, and HbA1c for longer-term control
    • Potassium — especially on infusions and during DKA treatment
    • Ketones where hyperglycemia is marked
    • Renal function, since insulin needs fall as clearance drops
    4Education
    • Always have fast-acting glucose within reach
    • Know your own early warning signs — shakiness, sweating, hunger, a pounding heart
    • Do not skip meals after taking insulin
    • Rotate injection sites within the same region
    • Store spare insulin in the fridge; the in-use pen as directed
    • Extra activity, alcohol, or a smaller meal all lower your glucose — plan for it
    • Check glucose before driving
    • Report repeated lows — the dose may need changing
    Special populations
    • Older adults: hypoglycemia is more dangerous and less well perceived; targets are often relaxed deliberately.
    • Patients on beta blockers: the sympathetic warning signs are blunted — sweating may be the only one left.
    • Renal impairment: insulin is cleared more slowly, so requirements fall and hypoglycemia risk rises.
    • Patients nil by mouth or going to theatre: mealtime doses must be reviewed, not given on autopilot.
    • Pregnancy: insulin is the treatment of choice; requirements change across the trimesters.
    • Patients being treated for DKA: potassium falls as insulin works — it is replaced alongside.
    • Children and anyone with erratic eating: dose timing matters more than dose size.
    Sulfonylurea
    forces insulin out — can cause lowsglipizide
    Example drugsglipizide
    Mechanism of action
    • Stimulates insulin release from pancreatic beta cells by closing potassium channels
    • Works regardless of the current glucose, which is exactly why it causes hypoglycemia
    • Requires functioning beta cells, so it is useless in type 1
    Therapeutic uses
    • Type 2 diabetes with functioning beta cells
    • Usually added when metformin alone is insufficient
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: hypoglycemia, weight gain, nausea, headache
    • Serious: prolonged severe hypoglycemia, particularly in older adults and renal impairment; hyponatremia; rarely blood dyscrasias and cholestatic jaundice
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Hypoglycemia is the defining risk of this class — and it can be prolonged, so a patient who has had one episode needs observation, not just a snack
    • Type 1 diabetes and sulfa allergy are contraindications
    • Avoid alcohol — it both worsens hypoglycemia and can cause a disulfiram-like reaction
    • Ask about meal patterns — a skipped meal on a sulfonylurea is a predictable low
    • Check renal and hepatic function, which prolong the effect when impaired
    • Review interacting drugs, including warfarin, NSAIDs and some antibiotics
    2Vitals
    • Capillary glucose
    • Heart rate — tachycardia with a falling glucose
    • Weight over time
    • Level of consciousness if a low is suspected
    3Labs
    • Glucose and HbA1c
    • Renal and hepatic function
    • Sodium, which can fall
    • CBC if symptoms suggest a dyscrasia
    4Education
    • Do not skip meals
    • Carry fast-acting glucose and know the early signs of a low
    • Avoid alcohol
    • Take it before a meal as directed
    • Check glucose when ill, exercising more, or eating less
    • Report repeated lows — the dose may be too high
    • Use sun protection; photosensitivity occurs
    Special populations
    • Older adults: highest risk of severe, prolonged hypoglycemia — longer-acting agents in this class are on the Beers criteria.
    • Renal or hepatic impairment: the drug accumulates and lows last longer.
    • Patients with sulfa allergy: contraindicated.
    • Type 1 diabetes: ineffective — there are no functioning beta cells to stimulate.
    • Patients who skip meals or fast: a structural mismatch with how the drug works.
    • Patients on beta blockers: warning signs masked.
    Biguanide
    first-line · hold for contrastmetformin
    Example drugsmetformin
    Mechanism of action
    • Decreases hepatic glucose production and increases insulin sensitivity
    • Does not stimulate insulin release, so it does not cause hypoglycemia on its own
    • Modestly reduces intestinal glucose absorption; tends to be weight-neutral or weight-reducing
    • Cleared unchanged by the kidney — accumulation is what causes the rare serious toxicity
    Therapeutic uses
    • First-line therapy in type 2 diabetes
    • Prediabetes in selected patients
    • Polycystic ovary syndrome
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: GI upset — nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, metallic taste; these usually settle
    • Serious: lactic acidosis — rare but with high mortality; vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Hold before and after iodinated contrast studies as ordered — contrast can impair renal function, the drug accumulates, and lactic acidosis follows
    • Renal impairment is the key contraindication
    • Assess for lactic acidosis: unexplained hyperventilation, muscle pain, unusual fatigue, abdominal discomfort and feeling cold — vague symptoms that are easy to dismiss
    • Take with food to limit GI effects; expect them to improve over weeks
    • Hold in any condition causing hypoxia or hypoperfusion — sepsis, dehydration, acute heart failure
    • Ask about alcohol, which raises lactic acidosis risk
    2Vitals
    • Blood pressure and heart rate
    • Respiratory rate — hyperventilation can be the clue to a metabolic acidosis
    • Weight
    • Hydration status
    3Labs
    • Renal function — before starting and at least annually
    • Glucose and HbA1c
    • Vitamin B12 on long-term therapy
    • Lactate if acidosis is suspected; LFTs
    4Education
    • Take it with food — stomach upset is common at first and usually settles
    • Tell any clinician arranging a scan with dye that you take metformin
    • Report unusual tiredness, muscle aching, trouble breathing, stomach pain or feeling unusually cold
    • Limit alcohol
    • Keep up kidney blood tests
    • Hold it and seek advice if you have vomiting, diarrhea or cannot keep fluids down
    • This medicine alone rarely causes low glucose — but that changes if insulin or a sulfonylurea is added
    Special populations
    • Renal impairment: the central contraindication — the drug is renally cleared.
    • Patients having contrast imaging: held around the procedure and restarted once renal function is confirmed.
    • Older adults: renal function may be lower than the creatinine suggests — estimate clearance.
    • Patients with heart failure, sepsis, dehydration or any hypoxic state: lactic acidosis risk rises sharply.
    • Heavy alcohol use: a significant added risk.
    • Long-term users: check B12 — deficiency can present as neuropathy and be mistaken for diabetic neuropathy.
    Alpha-glucosidase inhibitor
    treat lows with glucose, not sucroseacarbose
    Example drugsacarbose
    Mechanism of action
    • Blocks the intestinal enzyme that splits complex carbohydrates into absorbable monosaccharides
    • Carbohydrate absorption is slowed and flattened → lower post-meal glucose peaks
    • Does not stimulate insulin, so it does not cause hypoglycemia alone
    • The same enzyme block is why sucrose will not correct a low on this drug
    Therapeutic uses
    • Postprandial hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes
    • Added to other agents where the fasting glucose is acceptable but the post-meal rise is not
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: flatulence, diarrhea, abdominal pain and bloating — from unabsorbed carbohydrate fermenting in the colon
    • Serious: hepatic enzyme elevation at high doses, and failure of sucrose to treat hypoglycemia when combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Treat hypoglycemia with glucose — tablets or gel — not table sugar, juice or sweets, because the drug blocks the enzyme that would break sucrose down
    • Give with the first bite of each meal; it has nothing to act on without food
    • GI disorders are a contraindication — inflammatory bowel disease, obstruction, malabsorption
    • Set expectations about flatulence and bloating, which are the usual reason patients stop
    • Remember it cannot cause a low by itself — but it changes how a low must be treated
    2Vitals
    • Weight
    • Assess abdominal comfort and bowel pattern
    • Glucose, particularly post-meal
    • Heart rate if a low is suspected
    3Labs
    • Post-prandial glucose — the value this drug is aimed at
    • HbA1c
    • Liver enzymes on higher doses
    • Renal function
    4Education
    • If your glucose goes low, use glucose tablets or gel — ordinary sugar, juice or candy will not work quickly enough
    • Take it with the first bite of your meal; skip it if you skip the meal
    • Expect wind and bloating at first — it usually improves
    • Tell anyone treating you that ordinary sugar will not correct your low
    • Report persistent abdominal pain or diarrhea
    • Keep glucose tablets with you
    Special populations
    • Patients also on insulin or a sulfonylurea: the group who can actually go low — and for whom the glucose-not-sucrose rule becomes critical.
    • Inflammatory bowel disease, obstruction or malabsorption: contraindicated.
    • Patients with hepatic impairment: enzyme elevation at higher doses.
    • Renal impairment: avoided in significant impairment.
    • Patients who find flatulence socially unacceptable: a real adherence barrier worth raising openly.
    DPP-4 inhibitor
    incretin-based · watch the pancreassitagliptin
    Example drugssitagliptin
    Mechanism of action
    • Inhibits DPP-4, the enzyme that breaks down incretin hormones
    • More incretin → more insulin and less glucagon — but only when glucose is raised
    • Because the effect is glucose-dependent, hypoglycemia alone is uncommon
    • Weight-neutral
    Therapeutic uses
    • Type 2 diabetes, alone or with metformin
    • Useful where hypoglycemia must be avoided
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: headache, nasopharyngitis, joint pain, upper respiratory symptoms
    • Serious: pancreatitis, severe disabling arthralgia, hypersensitivity including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, bullous pemphigoid, heart-failure hospitalisation with some agents in the class
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • A history of pancreatitis is a contraindication
    • Assess for pancreatitis: severe persistent abdominal pain, often radiating to the back, with vomiting — stop the drug and escalate
    • Ask about joint pain — severe arthralgia is a recognised, reversible effect that is easily attributed to something else
    • Dose is reduced in renal impairment
    • Review other glucose-lowering drugs; a low usually means the partner drug needs reducing
    2Vitals
    • Blood pressure and heart rate
    • Assess for signs of heart failure — weight gain, edema, breathlessness
    • Weight
    • Abdominal assessment where pain is reported
    3Labs
    • Amylase and lipase if pancreatitis is suspected
    • Renal function, which sets the dose
    • Glucose and HbA1c
    • LFTs
    4Education
    • Report severe stomach pain that goes through to your back, especially with vomiting — stop the medicine and seek care
    • Report severe or disabling joint pain
    • Take it at the same time daily, with or without food
    • Report any blistering rash
    • This medicine alone rarely causes low glucose
    • Keep kidney blood tests up to date
    Special populations
    • Patients with a history of pancreatitis: contraindicated.
    • Renal impairment: dose reduction required.
    • Patients with heart failure: some drugs in this class increased heart-failure hospitalisation — agent choice matters.
    • Older adults: often chosen deliberately because hypoglycemia risk is low.
    • Patients on a sulfonylurea or insulin: the partner drug usually needs reducing.
    Thiazolidinedione (TZD)
    insulin sensitiser — watch for fluidpioglitazone
    Example drugspioglitazone
    Mechanism of action
    • Increases insulin sensitivity in muscle and fat by acting on nuclear receptors that regulate glucose and lipid metabolism
    • Does not stimulate insulin release, so it does not cause hypoglycemia on its own
    • Causes sodium and fluid retention — which is the source of every serious caution
    • Takes weeks to reach full effect, because it works by altering gene expression
    Therapeutic uses
    • Type 2 diabetes, usually added to metformin
    • Useful where insulin resistance is the dominant problem
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: fluid retention and edema, weight gain, headache, myalgia
    • Serious: new or worsening heart failure, fractures in women, macular edema, hepatotoxicity, bladder-cancer signal with long-term use
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Avoid in heart failure — fluid retention is the mechanism, and it can precipitate or worsen decompensation
    • Assess for edema, new shortness of breath, orthopnea and rapid weight gain before and during therapy
    • Baseline cardiac history — this is the question that decides whether the drug is appropriate at all
    • Assess fracture risk, particularly in postmenopausal women
    • Ask about visual change — macular edema is uncommon but reported
    • Set expectations: the glucose effect builds over weeks rather than days
    2Vitals
    • Daily weight — a rapid gain is retained fluid, not fat
    • Assess for edema and listen to the lung bases
    • Blood pressure and heart rate
    • Respiratory assessment for signs of overload
    3Labs
    • Liver function tests at baseline and periodically
    • Glucose and HbA1c
    • Lipid panel
    • Hemoglobin — a small dilutional fall is common
    4Education
    • Report swelling of the ankles or legs, sudden weight gain, or new breathlessness
    • Weigh yourself regularly and keep a record
    • Expect several weeks before the full benefit shows in your glucose
    • Report any change in vision
    • Report unusual tiredness, nausea, or yellowing of the skin or eyes
    • This medicine alone rarely causes low glucose — that changes if insulin or a sulfonylurea is added
    Special populations
    • Heart failure: avoided — fluid retention can precipitate decompensation.
    • Postmenopausal women: increased fracture risk.
    • Patients with hepatic impairment: liver function is monitored and the drug avoided in active disease.
    • Patients on insulin: fluid retention and heart-failure risk are both greater in combination.
    • Older adults: less tolerance of volume expansion; edema is often mistaken for a cardiac problem alone.
    • Patients with macular edema or visual symptoms: needs ophthalmic assessment.
    GLP-1 agonist
    slows the stomach · thyroid warningliraglutide · semaglutide · tirzepatide
    Example drugsliraglutide · semaglutide · tirzepatide
    Mechanism of action
    • GLP-1 receptor agonist — increases insulin and decreases glucagon, glucose-dependently
    • Liraglutide and semaglutide are GLP-1 receptor agonists; tirzepatide is a dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist, acting at a second incretin receptor as well
    • Slows gastric emptying and increases satiety, which drives the weight effect
    • Injected; does not cause hypoglycemia alone
    Therapeutic uses
    • Type 2 diabetes
    • Weight reduction
    • Cardiovascular risk reduction in selected patients
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, decreased appetite, injection-site reaction — GI effects are dose-related and usually improve
    • Serious: pancreatitis, thyroid C-cell tumors (boxed warning), gallbladder disease, dehydration and acute kidney injury from persistent vomiting, diabetic retinopathy complications
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • A personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2 is a contraindication
    • Assess for pancreatitis — severe persistent abdominal pain radiating to the back
    • Monitor GI tolerance: persistent vomiting causes dehydration and can injure the kidney
    • Teach injection technique and site rotation
    • Ask about a neck lump, hoarseness or difficulty swallowing
    • Remember delayed gastric emptying alters absorption of other oral drugs, and matters before procedures requiring sedation
    2Vitals
    • Weight — an intended effect here, so track it
    • Blood pressure and heart rate; a modest rise in heart rate occurs
    • Hydration status
    • Abdominal assessment where pain is reported
    3Labs
    • Glucose and HbA1c
    • Renal function, especially if vomiting has been significant
    • Amylase and lipase if pancreatitis is suspected
    • Calcitonin only if clinically indicated
    4Education
    • Nausea is common at first and usually settles — eat smaller meals, stop when full, avoid fatty food
    • Report severe stomach pain going through to your back, with vomiting
    • Report a lump in the neck, hoarseness or trouble swallowing
    • Rotate injection sites; use the technique demonstrated
    • Keep fluids up if you are vomiting, and seek advice if you cannot
    • Tell clinicians before any procedure with sedation — your stomach empties more slowly
    Special populations
    • Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2: contraindicated.
    • History of pancreatitis: used with caution or avoided.
    • Patients with gastroparesis: delayed emptying is worsened.
    • Patients having procedures under sedation: retained gastric contents raise aspiration risk.
    • Patients on insulin or a sulfonylurea: the partner drug needs reducing.
    • Patients with advanced retinopathy: rapid glucose improvement can transiently worsen it.
    SGLT-2 inhibitor
    glucose out in the urinecanagliflozin · empagliflozin
    Example drugscanagliflozin · empagliflozin
    Mechanism of action
    • Blocks glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule → glucose is excreted in the urine
    • Independent of insulin, so it works regardless of beta-cell function
    • The osmotic diuresis lowers blood pressure and weight
    • Needs working kidneys to work at all — which is why it fails in severe impairment
    Therapeutic uses
    • Type 2 diabetes
    • Cardiovascular and renal protection — often the reason it is chosen
    • Heart failure in selected patients
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: genital mycotic infections and urinary tract infections, increased urination, thirst, dehydration and dizziness
    • Serious: diabetic ketoacidosis, which can occur at near-normal glucose, volume depletion and acute kidney injury, lower-limb amputation signal, Fournier gangrene, fractures
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Assess for DKA even when the glucose looks acceptable — nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, breathlessness and fatigue. Euglycemic DKA is the trap in this class
    • Severe renal impairment is the contraindication
    • Maintain hydration — the drug causes an osmotic diuresis
    • Foot care and daily foot checks: assess skin integrity, pulses and any new ulcer or infection
    • Assess for genital or urinary symptoms — itching, discharge, dysuria
    • Assess for perineal pain, swelling or redness with fever — Fournier gangrene is rare and rapidly progressive
    • Review diuretics and antihypertensives, which add to volume depletion
    2Vitals
    • Blood pressure, lying and standing — orthostatic drops are common
    • Heart rate
    • Weight and hydration status
    • Inspect the feet
    3Labs
    • Renal function before starting and during therapy
    • Ketones whenever DKA is suspected, regardless of the glucose
    • Glucose and HbA1c
    • Electrolytes, including potassium and magnesium
    • Note that urine glucose testing becomes meaningless on this drug
    4Education
    • Drink enough fluid
    • Report nausea, vomiting, stomach pain or breathlessness — even if your glucose readings look fine
    • Check your feet every day and report any sore, blister or colour change
    • Report genital itching or discharge, or burning on passing urine
    • Report pain, swelling or redness between the genitals and anus with fever — seek care immediately
    • Stand up slowly
    • Hold the drug and seek advice if you cannot eat or drink, or before major surgery
    Special populations
    • Severe renal impairment: contraindicated — it needs filtration to work.
    • Patients with peripheral vascular disease, neuropathy or prior ulceration: amputation signal — foot care is central.
    • Older adults and anyone on diuretics: volume depletion, orthostatic hypotension and falls.
    • Patients fasting, acutely ill or heading for surgery: euglycemic DKA risk — usually held.
    • Patients with recurrent genital or urinary infections: a predictable and often intolerable effect.
    • Type 1 diabetes: not indicated — DKA risk is unacceptable.
    Meglitinide
    no meal, no doserepaglinide
    Example drugsrepaglinide
    Mechanism of action
    • Stimulates rapid, short-lived insulin release from beta cells — the same channel as sulfonylureas but faster on and faster off
    • Designed to cover the meal and then stop
    • Works regardless of glucose, so it can cause hypoglycemia
    Therapeutic uses
    • Post-meal glucose control in type 2 diabetes
    • Useful where meal times are irregular, because doses track meals
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: hypoglycemia, weight gain, upper respiratory symptoms, headache
    • Serious: severe hypoglycemia, though usually shorter-lived than with a sulfonylurea; hepatic impairment increases exposure
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Dose with meals only — skip the meal, skip the dose. This is the defining rule of the drug
    • Give shortly before each meal, typically within 30 minutes
    • Assess for hypoglycemia, especially if a meal is delayed or small
    • Check hepatic function; impairment raises levels
    • Review interacting drugs — gemfibrozil is a notable one
    • Do not combine with a sulfonylurea; the mechanism is the same
    2Vitals
    • Capillary glucose, particularly after meals
    • Heart rate
    • Weight
    • Level of consciousness if a low is suspected
    3Labs
    • Glucose and HbA1c
    • Hepatic function
    • Renal function
    4Education
    • Take it just before you eat — and if you miss the meal, miss the dose
    • Never take it in advance of a meal that might not happen
    • Carry fast-acting glucose
    • Report repeated lows
    • If you add an extra meal, you may need an extra dose — ask how to adjust
    • Avoid alcohol
    Special populations
    • Patients with irregular meals or shift work: the group this drug suits, because dosing follows eating.
    • Hepatic impairment: levels rise; used cautiously.
    • Older adults: hypoglycemia risk, though usually shorter than with long-acting sulfonylureas.
    • Patients on gemfibrozil: markedly increased exposure — the combination is avoided.
    • Patients who fast for religious or medical reasons: doses are omitted with the meals.
    Glucose-elevating agent
    for the patient who cannot swallowglucagon
    Example drugsglucagon
    Mechanism of action
    • Breaks down stored hepatic glycogen to glucose and promotes gluconeogenesis
    • Raises blood glucose within about 10–15 minutes
    • Requires glycogen stores to work — so it is unreliable in starvation, alcoholic liver disease or prolonged hypoglycemia
    • Also relaxes smooth muscle, which gives it some non-diabetic uses
    Therapeutic uses
    • Severe hypoglycemia where the patient cannot safely swallow
    • Beta-blocker or calcium-channel-blocker overdose
    • To relax the GI tract for imaging
    Side & adverse effects
    • Common and expected: nausea and vomiting, headache, injection-site reaction
    • Serious: hypersensitivity; hypertensive crisis in pheochromocytoma; rebound hypoglycemia once glycogen is exhausted; hypokalemia
    Nursing considerations
    1Assessment
    • Turn the patient on their side — vomiting is common and an unconscious patient must be protected from aspiration
    • Give carbohydrate as soon as the patient can swallow safely — glucagon empties the glycogen store and the glucose will fall again without replacement
    • Teach caregivers and family to give it, since the patient will be unable to treat themselves
    • Pheochromocytoma is a contraindication
    • Recheck glucose after administration and keep rechecking
    • Expect it to work less well in malnourished patients or chronic alcohol use, where glycogen stores are depleted
    • Call for emergency help — glucagon does not replace that
    2Vitals
    • Level of consciousness — the response measure
    • Capillary glucose before and repeatedly after
    • Airway, breathing and position
    • Blood pressure and heart rate
    • Temperature if the cause is unclear
    3Labs
    • Glucose — repeatedly
    • Potassium, which can fall
    • Renal and hepatic function where the cause is being worked up
    • Consider alcohol and medication history
    4Education
    • For families: give it, place the person on their side, and call emergency services
    • Once they are awake and able to swallow, give food or a sugary drink — otherwise the glucose will drop again
    • Keep the kit where it can be found, and check the expiry date
    • Nausea and vomiting afterwards are expected
    • Every episode of severe hypoglycemia should be reported — the diabetes regimen may need changing
    • Practise the technique before it is needed
    Special populations
    • Patients with pheochromocytoma: contraindicated — can precipitate hypertensive crisis.
    • Malnourished patients, prolonged fasting, or chronic alcohol use: depleted glycogen means a poor or absent response — intravenous glucose is needed.
    • Patients on beta blockers: may have had blunted warning signs before collapsing.
    • Children: weight-based dosing; caregivers must be trained.
    • Patients with repeated severe episodes: the regimen itself needs review, not just rescue.
    Ch 01–06 · Slides 15–16, 24–25

    Self-test

    Both questions from the lecture, plus four drawn from the material above. Turn on quiz mode and answer before revealing.

    QuestionAnswer
    An IM injection is given to a 35-year-old male (165 lb) and an 18-year-old female (125 lb). Who absorbs the drug faster, and why?The male. He has more vascular muscle mass, and absorption from an IM site depends on blood flow to that muscle. The female has a higher body-fat percentage and less vascular muscle, so absorption is slower. (Lecture slides 15–16.)
    True or false: poisoning occurs when too much of a drug causes damage to multiple body systems.True. An overdose produces multi-system damage and requires urgent supportive care plus antidote therapy where one exists. (Lecture slides 24–25.)
    A patient with low serum albumin is given a normal dose of a highly protein-bound drug. What happens?More drug remains unbound (free) and pharmacologically active, so a normal dose can produce toxicity. Only free drug exerts an effect.
    Why can the oral dose of a drug be much larger than its IV dose?The first-pass effect. Orally absorbed drug passes through the liver via the portal vein and is partly metabolized before reaching systemic circulation. IV bypasses this entirely.
    A patient develops a rash on the first-ever dose of a drug. Is this most likely an allergy?Unlikely as a true allergy — hypersensitivity requires prior sensitizing exposure. Consider an idiosyncratic or secondary reaction. Still stop the drug, notify, and document.
    Which two organ systems, when diseased, most change how a drug behaves — and which ADME stage does each affect?Liver (metabolism) and kidneys (excretion). Impairment of either causes the drug to accumulate toward toxic levels at ordinary doses.
    Week 2 warm-up. Order: metoprolol 25 mg PO now. MAR: hold if systolic BP < 100. Current BP 88/54. Give it, hold and assess, or ask the patient?Hold and assess / clarify. The dose is correct, but a hold parameter is met. The “right dose” is not enough — assessment and clinical judgment come first. Asking the patient what they prefer does not resolve a safety parameter.
    Mini-case A. Patient says penicillin caused hives. New order: amoxicillin.Stop and clarify before giving. Hives is a true allergic reaction, and amoxicillin is a penicillin-class antibiotic — cross-reactivity is the concern. Verify the reaction, notify the prescriber.
    Mini-case B. Order: acetaminophen 650 mg. Available: 325 mg tablets.Proceed — this is a normal calculation. 650 ÷ 325 × 1 = 2 tablets. Two tablets is a reasonable answer for a dose twice the tablet strength.
    Mini-case C. Order to give now. Patient asks “what is this for?”Stop and teach before giving. Answer the question — name and purpose. An informed patient is the last safety check, and consent depends on it.
    Mini-case D. Order reads 0.5 mg. The MAR displays .5 mg.Clarify. A naked decimal is an ISMP error-prone designation — .5 mg can be read as 5 mg. Confirm the intended dose and report the display as a hazardous condition.
    Integrated case. Ms. Alvarez, 67, discharged yesterday, says she takes half of some pills when money is tight, uses an unlisted OTC sleep aid and herbal supplement, saw a post claiming supplements are safer than prescriptions, and asks what her new pain medicine is for. Order: acetaminophen 650 mg; available 325 mg tablets.Assess: full medication history including the unlisted OTC and herbal, last dose, allergies, pain, liver history (acetaminophen), and her understanding.
    Barriers: cost-driven dose-splitting, polypharmacy with undisclosed products, information quality from social media, a care transition, and a health-literacy gap.
    Teach: name and purpose, the acetaminophen ceiling and its presence in combination OTC products, why the supplement must be disclosed, and cost options — then teach-back.
    Math: 650 ÷ 325 × 1 = 2 tablets, if it is otherwise safe to give.
    Her four layers of a safe medication plan.1. Right patient and assessment — is this appropriate now? 2. Right medication plan — order, dose, route, timing, indication, monitoring. 3. Right calculation — units match, correct math, reasonable answer. 4. Right real-world plan — can the patient understand, obtain, and safely continue it?
    Medication safety = clinical judgment + calculation + communication + systems thinking.
